Remembering the pre-Google web, when search was an experiment

Ars Technica Long form August 07, 2026

“Most people have completely forgotten how chaotic it really was.”

In the mid-’90s, the web was exploding, but finding anything of actual value on it felt like an elaborate negotiation with whatever proto-search engine happened to be standing closest to the door. Unlike now, when Google is widely seen as both portal and gatekeeper, sites like AltaVista, Lycos, Excite, HotBot, and Ask Jeeves promised to tame the chaos, each with its own suite of quirks, charms, and flaws.

The real story of pre-Google search is not that early engines were inferior. It’s that they reflected a different Internet entirely, one where directories mattered, crawling was still an art, ranking was fragile, and the idea of “search” had not yet hardened into a single dominant interface.

The first thing to remember about the pre-Google Internet is that there was no built-in assumption that you could search for everything. Many users found pages through Yahoo-style directories, bookmarks, newsgroups, email signatures, and links from site to site because the web was still small enough that human organization could compete with machine indexing. It was an era of Wild West-style discoverability. Search engines existed, but they were only one part of a larger ecosystem that blended curation and accident.

Before those engines became the main public interface to the web, resources like Usenet were showing people how to organize and discover information online. Conceived in 1979, it gave users topic-based newsgroups and a culture of distributed discussion that made online information feel social and communal before the first major web engines arrived. Usenet helped establish the habit of navigating vast, messy digital spaces through categories and communities rather than a single search box.

Nicole M. Radziwill worked as a systems administrator, programmer, and project manager, among other things, in the ‘90s. She remembers Usenet as a portal to unearthing interesting content online. “It was the way to find out about websites that might interest you,” she said. “I got on Usenet in 1990 as a student in Durham, North Carolina… it was delightful, especially the alt.* and misc.* groups. People would put links in at the bottom of their posts, and awareness grew organically. And if you wanted safer or more reliable recommendations, you could limit yourself to moderated groups.”

It was an era when the term “discovery” carried actual weight, when you could authentically be one of the first people viewing a piece of content, regardless of its quality or how long it may have existed—an era of equal parts wonder and frustration.

“Then a couple of years later, webrings popped up,” Radziwill said. “You’d get a block of code and put it on the bottom of your site’s HTML page, and it would embed a link to the next website related to this one. Someone else would manage the list of what could come next, so it was a great way to increase your exposure. The people putting together the lists for the webrings were generally pretty upstanding, so we didn’t even think about sabotage.”

Webrings are another pre-Google artifact that recalls an era when microcommunities sprang up, not unlike those in the BBS era, from groups of people sharing niche interests, sometimes even local to one another in the real world. Before monolithic aggregators like Reddit, webrings were one of a handful of ways to find sites focused on the topics you were interested in.

That mattered because the web had not yet become a pure retrieval machine. It still had a culture of exploration, and many services were designed to help users browse topical categories rather than fire a query into a universal index. In that world, a webring or directory was not a compromise. It was often the main event.

Yahoo is the best-known example of this early logic. It began as a human-edited guide to the web, organized into nested subject categories and maintained by people rather than fully automated ranking systems. For a young web, that approach was surprisingly effective: Human editors could identify quality sites, filter obvious junk, and impose a sense of order on a medium that was still expanding rapidly.

“I was a sysadmin for an ‘ecommerce shop’ in 1995 and 1996,” Radziwill told me, “and when we would turn up websites for new clients, the highlight of our process was submitting the site to Yahoo. Yahoo was like the Yellow Pages, but only for websites. There was a form you would fill out, and you had to justify to the real people at Yahoo that this business you were submitting was legit and important enough to be in Yahoo’s main directory.”

That kind of human curation is almost unimaginable now.

“I remember one time submitting the website for a regional branch of the American Cancer Society and getting rejected because it ‘wasn’t significant enough,’” Radziwill said. “They recommended we contact the main ACS and have them link the site from their page… that they didn’t have yet.”

It was a time when getting accepted into a directory like Yahoo by their human moderators was a massive badge of honor. But the model had obvious limits. Human curation couldn’t scale forever, and it became more expensive and less timely as the web ballooned and content outpaced curation. The moment the number of pages outstripped the number of people who could reasonably classify them, the future belonged to crawlers and ranking systems.

Search engines of the era confronted the scale problem with software. Many of the first big commercial systems, like AltaVista, Lycos, Excite, and HotBot, used crawlers and indexes to automatically map a growing web rather than relying on editors to hand-classify every site. While these engines didn’t all work the same way, they shared a core ambition: to gather up as much of the web as possible and let the algorithm sort through the mess.

It may sound obvious now, but it was a leap at the time. AltaVista in particular represented a major step forward, combining a fast crawler with scalable indexing software, and was already handling millions of HTTP requests per day shortly after launch. It made search feel less like browsing a catalog and more like querying a giant machine.

AltaVista became one of the defining search engines of the 1990s because it was fast, broad, and unusually capable for the time. Later versions supported natural language-style searches and gave users the sense that the web could finally be approached as an indexable whole, even if the results were still rough around the edges. In a decade when many people were still learning what the web even was and grappling with its vastness, it felt close to miraculous. But it was still a very limited tool compared to the hyper-sophistication of an evolved engine like modern Google.

Mark Friend, director of the IT support firm Classroom365 Limited, worked as a systems operator in the late ‘90s. He remembers that in the pre-Google era, searching the web was both a technical skill and an art form.

“Most people have completely forgotten how chaotic it really was,” Friend said. “Back then, if you typed a question into AltaVista, the odds were stacked against you if you were looking for anything specific. You’d receive 40,000 results that would leave you just as confused as shouting into a crowded room.”

Compared with Google’s once-user-friendly UI and more relevant results, combing through an AltaVista results page required patience and genuine skill that was honed over time. But AltaVista did accomplish one important thing: It set the expectation that search should be immediate. That expectation proved decisive. Once users experienced a search engine that could quickly sweep a huge index, they stopped accepting sluggish, partial systems as sufficient. AltaVista didn’t win the search war, but it clarified the rules of engagement.

Lycos and Excite occupied an important middle ground. They were search brands, but they were also portals, meaning they strove to be destinations as much as tools. Search lived alongside breakouts for news, email, sports, weather, finance, and other content, all designed to keep users on the site rather than springing off to results pages.

These companies demonstrated how unsettled the category was. Some engines emphasized breadth, some emphasized speed, and some blended editorial channels with automated results in ways that feel alien today. The “search engine” label covered a wide range of products, from directory services and crawlers to portals with search bolted on as a tertiary feature.

HotBot earned a reputation as one of the more technically serious search engines of the era. It arrived during a period when users were beginning to notice that search quality depended on both the size of the index and the sophistication of the ranking system behind it—the scalable backend was provided by Inktomi. A fast crawl was not enough; people wanted results that were relevant, current, and not obviously gamed.

That tension exposed a weakness in the early generations of machine-based search. If a system leaned too heavily on on-page textual signals, people could just overstuff their content with word bloat to artificially boost ranking. If an engine relied mostly on easily manipulated on-page signals, marketing could overpower quality. The early web quickly became a laboratory for manipulation, even before anyone used the term “search engine optimization” (SEO) in the modern sense.

Ask Jeeves stood out because it tried to make search feel conversational, an idea that feels especially prescient in the age of the AI chatbot—though Ask Jeeves obviously did not offer anything close to the conversational interface based on today’s large language models. Mark Friend said Ask Jeeves felt genuinely futuristic because instead of asking users to think in keywords, it invited them to query in natural language, giving the impression of a web managed by a knowledgeable assistant.

The problem was that natural language is hard. Users didn’t always ask clean questions, and the underlying systems were not yet good enough to infer intent reliably at scale. Ask Jeeves was memorable because, without the underpinning of deep learning and LLMs, it purported to understand the user experience better than the technology of the time could support.

The pre-Google web was also a pre-industrial SEO environment. Site owners tried to improve visibility, but the modern system of search optimization had not yet become the massive, professionalized discipline it later became, with full departments of “experts” chasing ephemeral signaling from Google and attempting to predict its next mysterious pivot. Early engines were still relatively easy to influence with obvious signals like keyword repetition, metadata, and submission tactics.

“People didn’t talk about ranking back then,” Friend recalled. “They submitted their URL and waited patiently to see if it would show up in a search. Everyone took the Meta keyword tag seriously and the practice of utilizing ‘white text on a white background’ to hide hidden keywords was a legitimate tactic that webmasters would use to include keywords in their website for search engine crawlers. There was no fear of penalties, and you built a website, crossed your fingers, and hoped for the best.”

By the late ’90s, engines were identifying the white-on-white approach as spamdexing and taking action. In any case, that meant ranking was both simpler and more fragile than it is today. The early search web was an experimental stage where the rules had not hardened, and the feedback loop between publishers and engines was still manageable and easier to test and interpret. Once search became the main gateway to the web, that open-ended environment collapsed into a more adversarial one.

“The hard truth that most people do not want to face is that scraping and ranking turned the Internet into a manufacturing facility of content,” Friend said. “Websites went from being written for people to being written primarily for search engine crawlers.”

Google’s crucial contribution was not that it discovered search; it was that it changed the logic of ranking. Among other things, PageRank treated links as signals of authority, which made relevance partly a question of how the web itself pointed to a page. It marked a major shift because it made results seem more trustworthy and made simple manipulation harder, though obviously not impossible.

Just as importantly, Google paired that ranking approach with a stripped-down interface and a results page that got out of the way. The clean design mattered because it reinforced the sense that search should be a utility, not a portal amusement park. In practice, Google made the search box feel like the front door to the whole web, with the same intrinsic, vital importance that a front door serves in a home.

In retrospect, the pre-Google era was slower, messier, and in many ways less efficient. But it also had more competing ideas about how information should be found, categorized, and judged, alongside a lawless atmosphere that suggested unlimited potential. Some systems trusted people. Some trusted crawlers. Some trusted directories, and some trusted questions phrased in plain English.

“The Internet contained an inherent level of clutter and chaos,” Friend remembered. “But at the same time, it was a much more humanized place before. It’s why many of us feel nostalgic for that time. The Internet had an artisanal feel to it. It was made by real people using text editors such as Notepad and Dreamweaver. You might start at one destination and find yourself at a fan site of an obscure band, and then end up at a forum discussing vintage synthesizers, and ultimately end up on a NASA page.”

That diversity is worth remembering because it shows that search was never necessarily destined to look the way it does now. The pre-Google engines weren’t just failed precursors. They were serious attempts to address a problem that the web had made urgent but not yet solvable in one obvious way. Google won by combining technical rank, usability, and scale at exactly the moment the rest of the Internet was ready to abandon the old order.

'Cowboy builders' targeted in new government clampdown

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:44:02 GMT

People carrying out home renovations will gain greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards, the government has said.

Traders signing up to the scheme launching next month will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

The National Federation of Builders said the changes would not stop rogue operators while the Tories suggested there would be added paperwork for firms already operating legitimately.

Citizens Advice has said home renovations are one of its biggest sources of consumer complaints.

The government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months have experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority suggesting customers lost more £10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

BBC News has previously reported on "bait-and-switch" locksmith scams, where customers were given an initial cheap quote before hidden charges and unnecessary work were added.

Under the new traders' scheme, customers' money will be held in an account and released in parts after certain milestones in projects are completed.

The National Federation of Builders (NFB) told BBC Breakfast there are already schemes in place to find trustworthy builders.

Adas Rico Wojtulewicz-Richmond, the NFB's director of policy, said: "Is this scheme going to stop bad actors operating and ripping people off? I don't think it will."

He said a better approach would be for every project to have a "passport" which records all the work done.

"It protects consumers because you can find out which companies are doing a poor job, and it brings up the industry standards," he said.

The prime minister said rogue tradespeople gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and would be "putting the cowboys out of business".

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said that, while home improvements can be stressful, "we're taking action to protect consumers, support reputable traders and make sure people can spend their money with greater confidence and security".

Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith said the announcement looks like "the sort of government initiative that risks the unintended consequence of piling more paperwork onto the majority of businesses who already do the right thing".

He said: "The government would do far better to beef up law enforcement and have tougher sentences for the minority who fraudulently rip off customers. Those who break the rules will keep breaking them regardless of whether there is an app in the way."

Liberal Democrat business spokesperson Sarah Olney said: "Rogue builders cause real harm and ruin real lives every year. The current system is simply not fit for purpose and this half-baked announcement falls frustratingly short from fixing it.

"A voluntary code for tradespeople completely misses the mark. Rogue operators won't voluntarily sign up - they will simply keep exploiting families in the shadows."

Alongside action on rogue tradespeople, the government has announced plans to regulate private bailiffs in England and Wales, to protect people in debt from "intimidating behaviour, unfair treatment or being pushed into excessive repayment arrangements".

Under the changes, people facing enforcement action will have access to an independent complaints process, and private bailiffs will be held to professional standards.

Sarah Sackman, minister for courts and legal services, said bailiffs did an important job, but "with that responsibility must come high standards".

As part of the changes, the government will look at how organisations such as Trading Standards work with regulators and enforcement bodies "so consumers are not passed from pillar to post".

Last year, a Freedom of Information request by Which? revealed that understaffing in trading standards teams was leading to more scams and dangerous products being sold.

Rape and sex offence specialists on all police forces by 2027, PM says

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:30:39 GMT

Investigators specialising in rape and sex offences will be introduced to every police force in England and Wales by the end of 2027, the government has said.

Ministers are speeding up the rollout of the scheme, previously announced by Sir Keir Starmer's government, by 18 months as part of efforts to tackle violence against women and girls (VAWG).

They are also offering more money for some forces to boost protection orders.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the previous plans were "too slow" and ministers should be "laser focused" on tackling such crimes.

One charity has welcomed the measures, but says they represent "only a small portion of what is needed" for victims.

The Home Office initially announced the plans last year and was due to have teams in place by summer 2029.

Burnham said: "The scale of violence and abuse suffered by women and girls in this country is unacceptable.

"We're taking action to accelerate the roll out of specialist rape and sexual offence teams, who will go after perpetrators, enforce strict new protection orders to protect survivors, and invest in programmes to intensively manage offenders to break the cycle of abuse."

Up to 10 police forces across England and Wales will also get a share of a £13.3m pot to boost the teams managing protection orders, where offenders are subject to electronic monitoring, exclusion zones and other measures, the Home Office has said.

Minister for Safeguarding Satvir Kaur said violence against women and girls was one of the "most critical challenges of our time" and the government was strengthening its response by "relentlessly pursuing perpetrators and helping victims live their life without fear".

The charity Refuge welcomed the changes, but suggested the government should go further.

Its head of policy and public affairs Ellie Butt said the measures "represent only a small portion of what is needed to ensure all survivors can access timely and effective support".

She said the charity hoped the announcement would be the "first step of many" in Burnham's plans to tackle VAWG, adding that protection orders were "highly underutilised" and "enforcement is often inadequate".

"Survivors often avoid reporting the abuse they've experienced to the police for fear of being disbelieved or undermined, so for protection order teams to increase uptake of these tools, genuine efforts are needed to build women's and girls' confidence in policing and ensure abuse does not go unreported," she added.

In December, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood described violence against women and girls as a "national emergency" as she announced plans for the specialist investigation teams.

She told the BBC at the time that the way police forces investigate cases was "too much of a postcode lottery".

The accelerated rollout comes as the prime minister has been facing pressure over the early release scheme, designed to avert overcrowding in the country's prisons.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected to reveal the findings of a review of the scheme next week when MPs return to Parliament from their summer recess.

The plans were paused earlier in the summer, and the eligibility for the scheme was also changed, removing the right of those convicted of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming to have their sentences cut.

However, domestic abuse commissioner Nicole Jacobs said not excluding domestic abusers was "wrong and puts victims lives at risk".

She said earlier this month: "It is critical that no abuser is released in October unless I am confident that victims' safety is not being compromised."

Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:07:05 GMT

US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.

Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.

He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.

In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.

There is no universally recognized international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.

Trump's latest order directs the US Department of the Interior to update the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US - to reflect the name change, the president said.

Canada, however, does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials have dismissed the idea.

Premier of Nova Scotia Tim Houston said on Thursday, "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.

As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".

Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".

"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.

"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.

There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.

Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".

"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".

Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.

Clean-up of illegal waste supersite costs taxpayers £6m

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:00:48 GMT

The clear-up of one of England's largest illegal waste tips has been completed - landing taxpayers with a £6m bill.

The government has vowed to recoup the clearance costs for the Kidlington dump in Oxfordshire - and seven other sites - from the criminals responsible.

In 2025, around 22,000 tonnes of domestic and commercial rubbish was dumped at the spot, between the River Cherwell and the A34. It is one of nearly 30 so-called "supersites" first uncovered by a BBC investigation.

The government, which launched a crackdown on waste crime last week, said it would do more to force criminals to pay for clean-up operations by confiscating their money and assets.

But figures obtained by the BBC show that, in the past five years, the Environment Agency has so far managed to claw back just over £7m from waste criminals using Proceeds of Crime Act (Poca) confiscation orders.

At the same time, the agency says waste crime costs the economy £1bn a year.

Campaigners have labelled the amount taken from convicted criminals as "derisory" while the Country Land and Business Association (CLA), which represents rural landowners, asked: "Where is the deterrent?"

The amount paid by criminals so far was revealed by an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) request to the Environment Agency by the BBC.

It shows there have been 66 confiscation orders between January 2021 and March 2026, totalling £7.3m.

Fourteen orders have yet to be fully paid, leaving around £1.4m still to be recovered.

The figures cover those larger illegal sites for which the Environment Agency is responsible, and do not include confiscation orders for smaller fly-tipping offences, which fall under the remit of local authorities.

Baroness Sheehan, who chairs the House of Lords environment and climate change committee, said the figures obtained by the BBC showed "consistent, decisive enforcement" was lacking.

"With clean-up costs at sites such as Kidlington far exceeding these sums, and enforcement still lagging, the taxpayer continues to foot the bill," the Liberal Dem peer said.

"The Environment Agency must do more to secure and enforce confiscation orders against those responsible, so criminals pay - not communities."

As well as the work at the Kidlington site, the Environment Agency has also stepped in to clear a supersite at Hoads Wood, near Ashford in Kent.

The cost of these two clearances alone has been budgeted at £20m by the Environment Agency - although the Kidlington project has come in under the original £7.3m contract.

The government estimates that 20% of waste in England is illegally managed.

In the Waste Crime Action Plan, launched under Keir Starmer's administration, the government said the Environment Agency would step in "on an exceptional basis to clear sites where that waste presents an untenable risk to the public and the environment".

Private landowners whose land is used for illegal waste dumping are normally expected to pay for the clear-up.

Last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a nationwide crackdown on waste crime and plans to clean up three more of the largest illegal tips in England.

In total, six supersites have been earmarked to be cleared using public money, but they will be assessed first. They are:

Environment secretary Dame Angela Eagle said: "After years of waste crime being allowed to fester, we are taking decisive action.

"By putting more officers on the frontline and using drones to catch offenders in the act, we're putting the criminal gangs on notice that there is nowhere left to hide."

But many more illegal supersites remain - and it is not known if or when they will be cleared up, and who will be made to pay.

This includes one supersite in the countryside of Over, Gloucestershire, which Charlie Coats, chairman of Highnam Parish Council, is calling for the Environment Agency to also deal with.

He told the BBC that the amount of money taken from waste criminals was "derisory" and added: "It acts as absolutely no deterrent whatsoever because the income that they can derive from this dwarfs anything by way of any fine."

The Environment Agency told the BBC that some of the unpaid confiscation orders were outstanding "because they are still within the six-month payment period allowed for settlement" and the failure to pay was a matter for the courts.

It added that more money could still be seized if further information is uncovered about the offenders' assets.

Four men have so far been arrested in connection with the illegal waste tip at Kidlington. All have since been released while the investigation continues.

Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 20:39:16 GMT

Contains some upsetting scenes.

Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.

The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.

The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.

The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.

In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.

If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.

Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's lawyer, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopaedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.

Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www. befrienders. org.

In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc. co. uk/actionline.

What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 20:38:48 GMT

Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.

Search and rescue operations are continuing after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss".

There are risks of more floods: a lake of rising water has formed at a site along the China-Nepal border - prompting fears it could burst its banks.

Here is what we know so far.

Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood.

However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.

The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.

Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said.

Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.

Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".

Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.

He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.

He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet.

He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."

One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.

Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.

A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu.

Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.

In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.

Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.

In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.

Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.

The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear.

Nepali police say at least 389 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East.

In its latest update on Thursday evening, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing. This included 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepal Army and 28 Nepal police officers.

Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.

Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.

The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.

It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.

The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response.

China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.

In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance".

UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.

The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.

Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including:

Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

Manager Derek McInnes says he takes "full responsibility" for Rangers' "embarrassing" Conference League exit at the hands of Jablonec.

Rangers, who held a 1-0 lead going into the second leg of the play-off in Czech Republic, lost 4-3 on penalties on Thursday to crash out of Europe completely.

Derek McInnes' side actually led early in the shootout, only for Findlay Curtis and James Penrice to miss their final two penalties.

It leaves them without European football beyond August for the first time since the 2-1 aggregate defeat by Luxembourg's Progres Niederkorn in the Europa League first qualifying round in 2017.

Rangers out of Europe after wretched penalty defeat in Jablonec

Get Rangers news notifications in the BBC Sport app

And it ratchets up the pressure on McInnes after a hapless start to his reign at Ibrox, which included a Europa League exit against Jagiellonia Bialystok and a draw and defeat in their opening two Premiership games.

"I'm embarrassed with the performance," the Rangers manager said.

"The only people who represented the club well tonight were my staff and the supporters who were outstanding, getting behind the team despite watching what we all watched.

"I'm not going to make any excuses. Yes there's been a big turnover of players, yes we looked inexperienced at times but the responsibility is mine to make sure we're better than what we served up tonight.

"We're elite in everything we do in terms of preparation and the performance lacked in everything."

This video can not be played

McInnes 'mortified' at Rangers' European exit

The stats back up McInnes' anger. Rangers had just over 46% possession during the 120 minutes in the Czech Republic, and just one shot on target.

They won fewer than 70% of their 16 tackles and committed 17 fouls.

"I can't accept, and we shouldn't accept, losing individual battles, duels, second balls, not winning enough tackles and just getting the momentum of the game going our way," the former Hearts manager added.

"I thought we looked young, inexperienced at times. We're trying to make some signings to help with that side of it but we need to do so much more as a team.

"We got what we deserved. If we'd won on penalties we would have taken it, of course, but it would only have covered over the cracks.

"I'm mortified with the performance. I know you can lose games of football but we should have enough in the building to take care of that tonight."

Rangers had won their two previous games - a 5-1 win over St Mirren in the League Cup and the 1-0 victory against Jablonec at Ibrox - after drawing at Dundee United and losing at home to Hibernian in their opening two Premiership matches.

But McInnes - who confirmed that no bid has yet been received for the absent Nico Raskin - feels this latest result may set them back.

"We went into this game scrambling for some sort of confidence, some positivity," he said. "But I just thought the team that deserved to go through went through tonight and that's hard for me to take."

An extra 200 police officers are being sent to support an investigation into a car crash and a house fire which left nine people dead, a council leader has said.

Seven people, including two police officers, died in the crash at South Bank near Middlesbrough on Saturday, followed by a house fire in Grangetown on Wednesday that claimed the lives of a woman aged 34 and a seven-year-old girl.

Alec Brown, leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, said armed officers, dog units and "community bobbies" were among the additional personnel supporting local detectives.

Cleveland Police said it was receiving support from neighbouring forces, but exact numbers were "changing all the time".

It confirmed staff from the National Crime Agency, and the Northumbria, Durham, Humberside and North, South and West Yorkshire forces were supporting local officers.

Earlier Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "all of the support will be provided to get to the heart of what has happened" over the past days.

In an update on social media, Brown said: "Over 200 extra police officers from forces around the country are here and are on route, from detectives to armed response.

"If it is any reassurance at all, jobs called in to the police are actually down this week, however the seriousness of the ones that have been called in need serious and swift action."

Speaking to the BBC, the Labour councillor said: "Let's not forget two police officers lost their lives in the line of duty, so of course colleagues from around the country are going to want to come and support Cleveland Police.

"Yesterday we had a horrific house fire in Grangetown... and within hours there were two arrests being made.

"Police that were mourning the loss of their colleagues only three days beforehand were on site having to deal with some horrific sights of a lady and a poor little girl losing their lives."

Earlier Brown told Radio 4's Today programme that residents deserved to "feel safe in their own homes" and he understood people from the area might feel "left behind".

"I'm from an estate, from the same ilk," he said.

"You live around people that may be suffering poverty or other social issues, it can be that uniform sort of consciousness that 'we're left behind'.

"But I can assure the people of Grangetown and South Bank they're as important to me as people from any other estate in the borough."

Local Labour MPs Anna Turley, Luke Myer, Andy McDonald, Jonathan Brash and Chris McDonald issued a joint statement in which they welcomed the help of other police forces during the past week, but called for more long-term support to protect residents who had expressed "safety concerns" for "far too long".

Myer said current national funding formulas for the police and fire service did not take into account the "seriousness" of the crime people in Teesside faced.

"We essentially have a metropolitan style of crime and also risk of fire but with a sort of rural-style funding," he said.

"This is why we need to see a real overhaul of the funding formula."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told the Press Association the events in and around Middlesbrough over the last week were "deeply worrying".

On Saturday, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died when a Volkswagen Passat, which was going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank, hit their vehicle.

The five young men in the Volkswagen also died and inquests into all seven deaths opened on Thursday.

Police said 17 people, aged between 18 and 61, had been arrested across Teesside as part of an investigation into the lead-up to the crash.

They have been held on a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

Cleveland Police are also investigating another crash in which a vehicle hit the wall of a house in South Bank in the early hours of Thursday morning.

The property had been empty at the time and the force said it had "not yet been confirmed whether this incident is linked to wider organised crime".

On Wednesday, Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece Valentina Foster in the fire in Grangetown.

Natalie's mother, Lisa Kirton, described her as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Valentina, who was known as Tina, was staying at the house for the summer holidays and had been "dancing around the living room" only the previous night.

Lisa said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape after the friend "kicked out a window" upstairs.

Natalie's brother, Josh Kirton, said she had not been involved with "anything to do with gangs" or the crash on the A66.

"That's what makes this so senseless," he said.

"There's some terrible people in the world and now my sister and Valentina have gone."

The fire also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital, while another three people suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, were arrested on suspicion of murder and remained in custody.

Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind" about the fire and said it could not "rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

Mike Ashley attacks Burnham plans as 'populist'

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 20:03:34 GMT

Billionaire Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised recent cost of living and retail policies from Andy Burnham as "populist reactions".

In a letter to the prime minister, the entrepreneur accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons", while "disastrous" business rates policies and increases to the cost of employing workers were causing businesses to struggle.

He also described a previous proposal of increasing business rates on large warehouses to help reduce them for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life - like energy, water and housing - are affordable again."

Promises including cutting VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms is "just the start", they added.

Earlier this month, Burnham promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" high streets by helping councils block new vaping and betting shops.

He also brought forward a plan to end subscription traps and ban shops using misleading recommended retail prices, which can make it seem like discounts are larger than they really are.

In Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times, he hit out at announcements made since Burnham succeeded Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

The businessman called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 27 October, to lower costs for employers and change the government's position on business rates.

Pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April, while a review has been launched into how the tax, which high street firms have long called for reform to, is calculated.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer," Ashley said in the letter.

Ashley has repeatedly called for a fundamental overhaul of the tax, including levelling the playing field between High Street retailers and online rivals.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," he wrote.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty high street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media, with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business, still owned by Ashley but run by his son-in-law Michael Murray, this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

Ashley also used his letter to ask Burnham how the prime minister intends to revive Harvey Nichols, which has faced financial challenges in recent years.

Referencing comments by Tory peer and former Marks & Spencer boss Lord Rose, who called the announcements "hot air", Ashley said "I agree with him".

"It is the disastrous business rates position (which I have raised many times over the years) and the dramatically increasing cost of employing people that are really causing business to struggle," Ashley said.

"You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he added.

Ashley said the High Street will be "further devastated" without major reforms, and warned Burnham's suggestion he will consider further business rates changes in the coming Budget are "too little, too late".

He also used the letter to attack Burnham's plans to clamp down on the use of recommended retail prices, saying instead the real issue is "price fixing in sporting goods and other markets" - where he cited the rising cost of official football merchandise.

Werro's push for the world record stretched out the field in Zurich

European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark of one minute 53.28 seconds, set 43 years ago.

Roared on by a 25,000-strong capacity crowd at the Zurich Diamond League, the Swiss hit the final 100m almost in stride with the infield pacing lights which had been set for a world record.

However Werro, straining hard against the clock, could not quite find the finishing pace she needed, clocking 1:53.70.

Still, the third-fastest time in history shaves another tenth of a second off the 22-year-old's personal best and only increases the sense that she will break the record sooner rather than later.

"As far as the world record is concerned, I saw the light, but there was a lot of movement during the race and it was not calm," said Werro, who caused second-placed Femke Broeders-Bol to check as she overtook the Dutchwoman at the start of her kick for home on the back straight.

"I still had enough energy at the end of the race to accelerate and to stay in the lead. Yes, it was tight for the world record, it was not meant for today.

"I am so proud to be able to run those sub-1:54 times, which shows that I can run consistently and fast now and this is good for the future."

Werro has improved every year of her top-level career and now, having finished her studies and concentrating on the track, has shown ruthless consistency. She has four of the top-10 all-time 800m times, all clocked this summer.

For Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, who withdrew from the meeting after her exertions in taking continental silver behind Werro in Birmingham, it only emphasised the challenge she faces in the event.

Not only does she have to contend with Werro's burgeoning form, but Broeders-Bol, the world 400m hurdles champion who has switched up to two laps this season, gave another impressive showing in her debut campaign over 800m.

The Dutchwoman, who took out the pace initially, clocked a new national record of 1:54.71, beating Hodgkinson's training partner and Commonwealth 800m champion Georgia Hunter-Bell, who finished in 1:55.03, into third.

Broeders-Bol's long, languid stride and sprint speed have already made an impression in the event and she is gaining tactical knowhow fast as she acclimatises to the bump and hustle of middle distance.

"I was hoping to be in these sort of fights, but to be honest, I didn't expect it at all in the first season," she said afterwards.

"I thought I needed at least one or two seasons to get into the 1:54s, but here I am."

When Athing Mu-Nikolayev, Hodgkinson's American nemesis who beat her to gold at the Tokyo Olympics and Eugene 2022, slipped off the scene, the Briton had hoped to dominate the 800m.

With less than two years until she defends her Olympic crown in Los Angeles however, new rivals are looking ever more threatening.

Hodgkinson, like Werro and Broeders-Bol, has qualified for the Diamond League final in Brussels on 4-5 September. It could be an intriguing benchmark for the season's end.

While Werro fell short in her world record attempt, two new marks were set in an astonishng night of action.

This video can not be played

Dos Santos breaks 400m hurdles world record in Zurich

First, Brazil's Alison dos Santos defied expectations to smash the 400m hurdles world record.

The 26-year-old has been in excellent form this season, undefeated in the event, but there was little to suggest that Karsten Warholm's 2021 mark of 45.94 seconds was in danger.

But, with Warholm a distant second, Tokyo 2025 silver medallist Dos Santos cantered off the final hurdle and pushed through to clock 45.80 seconds.

His previous personal best stood at 46.29 and was set four years ago.

Just 75 minutes later, another world record fell in front of the 25,000-strong capacity crowd

Masai Russell, the Olympic champion, capturing the 100m hurdles mark was less surprising, considering the American has finished within a tenth of a second of Tobi Amusan's 12.12-second landmark five times in the past two seasons.

The 26-year-old celebrated her 12.09 clocking with a finger to her lips as the crowd erupted. Just like Warholm, Amusan had a prime view of her record being broken, finishing second.

Amy Hunt, winner of four golds at the European Championships earlier this month, found things tougher against some of the world's finest 100m runners.

Left in the blocks, the Briton had to watch on as Olympic champion Julien Alfred inflicted Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's first defeat over the distance in two years, edging out the American in a 10.70-second photo finish.

David Rudisha's 800m world record of one minute 40.91 seconds, set en route to gold at London 2012, survived unscathed as his Kenyan compatriot Emmanuel Wanyonyi came home in one minute 41.76 seconds.

France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:29:38 GMT

France has temporarily relaxed rules for making some of its best-known cheeses after the summer drought drastically reduced the amount of grass available to feed milk herds.

Government decrees to grant dispensations to manufacturers of Abondance, Beaufort and Comté cheeses - which come from mountains in eastern France - appeared on Wednesday.

Several other cheeses are expected to receive similar waivers, allowing farmers to feed livestock with grass and hay brought in from outside their strict geographical zone.

These include Cantal, Bleu d'Auvergne, Fourme d'Ambert, Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, Reblochon and the goats cheese Rocamadour.

The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for other protected produce because of the effects of the summer heat.

Products that will benefit include some types of Calvados and cider from Normandy, Crémant d'Alsace fizzy wine, lamb from Poitou-Charentes, and Reine-Claude plums.

Certificates of origin allow farmers to sell at a premium, but they come with strict regulations governing the location and method of production.

The aim is to preserve the unique identity of cheeses, wines and other foodstuffs, supposedly linked to their particular terroir - a French concept that links locality and tradition.

Because of a 2026 drought - which the INAO now describes as "historic" - farmers are being allowed to bend the rules for a short period.

Makers of Abondance cheese in the Alps, for example, will be authorised to reduce the amount of pastured grass in their animals' diet from 50% to 15%. They will be entitled to import forage from outside their zone, and use some supplements.

Makers of Comté cheese in the Jura mountains will be able to replace the local green maize they usually give to their cattle with maize from elsewhere.

The derogations are allowed in French and European law for periods of exceptional weather. Similar measures came in after the dry summer of 2022.

It will be interesting to see if the changes lead to any detectable change in the taste or quality of the cheeses - or to the quantity produced and how it is priced.

Longer term, the measures raise questions over the viability of the existing labels of origin in France and elsewhere.

If changing climate means that certain foodstuffs can no longer be produced in their traditional localities, then the idea of terroir will be stretched to its limits.

Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:12:01 GMT

Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.

BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.

At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.

You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.

One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.

Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.

Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.

The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.

I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"

The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years.

"I am," he said, "a musician".

Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.

I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries.

You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.

I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.

He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.

In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically pure Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.

Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way.

My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb.

We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.

General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

Norwegians have laid flowers in front of the palace in Oslo after the royal household said King Harald V's condition in hospital had become "extremely serious".

His wife, Queen Sonja, and his son, Crown Prince Haakon, cancelled royal engagements to be at his bedside at Oslo University Hospital with other members of the family.

They all stayed for several hours, and then during the evening Haakon was seen returning with Crown Princess Mette-Marit.

The 89-year-old has been in hospital for 10 days receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. Late on Thursday afternoon the palace issued an update to say his condition was unchanged.

Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state.

Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story.

Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king.

Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape.

King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus.

Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday.

"The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement.

The king has had multiple health problems in recent years which have forced him to scale back his royal duties.

He was fitted with a pacemaker in 2024 after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia.

The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026.

Crown Princess Mette-Marit received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018.

The transplant came two days after Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and is to appeal the sentence.

Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure.

Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:02:33 GMT

President Donald Trump said John Ratcliffe's trip to Russia was a "semi-routine" visit but there is nothing routine about the CIA chief making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow.

Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials on Tuesday - notably his opposite number in Russia's overseas spy agency, Sergei Naryshkin - after arriving unannounced on a US military plane, the Kremlin confirmed.

It's been nearly five years since his predecessor William Burns made this trip and that was at a similarly tense time, just as Russia was drawing up plans to invade Ukraine. So, this is probably serious.

In the absence of any official US comment on the reason for the mission, it is being widely reported Ratcliffe's trip was to warn Moscow not to escalate in relation to the stalemate in Ukraine - possibly by taking action against Nato members.

One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".

The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.

And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.

News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.

But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.

Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.

So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.

These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.

It could entail expanding the undeclared "hybrid war" that Russia is already suspected of waging against Nato countries, using sophisticated cyber-attacks, drone incursions and using not-so-sophisticated criminals to carry out arson attacks on munitions factories.

But at the even more alarming end of the scale there are other potential scenarios which the Kremlin may be considering, urged on by hardliners.

One is to distract attention from its obvious failure to win the war in Ukraine by testing Nato's resolve through a limited attack on a Baltic state. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were all once part of the Soviet Union, effectively ruled from Moscow until 1991.

Today they are all members of Nato, while still being home to substantial Russian-speaking communities.

Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.

In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.

Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.

If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.

Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.

Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.

Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.

Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.

That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.

But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 16:00:12 GMT

Actor Peter Cullen, who voiced popular characters including Optimus Prime in Transformers and Eeyore in Disney's Winnie the Pooh franchise, has died at the age of 85.

The Canadian actor began his most famous role - as the heroic deep-voiced Optimus Prime - for the Transformers TV series in 1984, then returned for seven Hollywood films from 2007 to 2023 and other spin-offs.

He voiced depressive donkey Eeyore in TV animation The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games.

His other memorable voice parts included KARR, the evil counterpart to KITT in TV show Knight Rider; the clicking vocalisations of The Predator in Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1987 film; and the roars of King Kong in 1976.

He died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, a statement said.

"Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family - and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide.

"His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember 'be strong enough to be gentle'."

Cullen started his career on Canadian TV and radio and was then a regular on programmes like The Sonny & Cher Show before deciding to concentrate on voice acting.

His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero".

"He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.'

"And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime."

Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death.

The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

BBC News Thu, 27 Aug 2026 15:14:26 GMT

A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.

Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ's College in Finchley, north London, assaulted the boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.

On Thursday, a jury at Harrow Crown Court found the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after deliberating for six hours and 29 minutes.

One complainant told the court he had sex with the teacher "about 20 or 30 times" over several months. He said he visited her at home, considered her his girlfriend and had fallen in love with her.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court she had "drummed it" into him that he must not tell anyone about them and to keep it a secret.

A second complainant told jurors he had kissed Bowen in a café after being "goaded" into it by other boys.

A former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that she acted like she was in "a Sabrina Carpenter video" while in the classroom and "dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers".

"The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual," said Oliver, who did not know the complainants.

He recalled incidents where Bowen flashed her underwear to a class while sitting on a table and went through and discussed a "sex manual" a student had brought in, which Oliver believed to be the Kama Sutra, with the class.

Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered receiving a complaint from the first alleged victim's mother after she was worried that her son was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.

During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were a "total fabrication" and that she had a medical condition which had not been diagnosed in the late 1980s and made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was granted bail.

She will be sentenced on 20 November.
