Glaciers in the Alps are on track for record-breaking ice loss

New Scientist August 27, 2026

I am climbing Switzerland’s Rhône glacier when I feel a thump deep under my feet, then another. The glacier is shifting and cracking as it slides down the mountain, opening new crevasses within. Dazzling blue melt streams grow and multiply across the sooty ice. Every few minutes, melting glacial remnants on the valley wall unleash rocks that crash down with the rumble of cannon fire, raising clouds of dust. Suddenly, the 20 metres of ice under my crampons doesn’t feel very solid.

A 4-metre aluminium tube has emerged so far from the ice that it has nearly tipped over. Andreas Bauder at ETH Zurich in Switzerland pulls it out. For two decades, he has been drilling stakes into glaciers to measure how much of the surface melts away during the warm months. But this year caught him off guard.

“I make sure that they’re drilled sufficiently that they survive. Except when we have some special conditions like this summer,” he says. “There was too much melt.”

Advertisement

A series of heatwaves have hit Europe this season, including the continent’s worst-ever heatwave in June. As a result, more than 9 metres of ice have melted off the surface of the Rhône glacier. While the stifling weather finally broke in mid-August, forecasters warn temperatures could remain above average through autumn, and another heatwave is possible.

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

If that happens, glaciers in the Alps will probably experience record ice loss this year, says Bauder, beating even 2022, when dark Saharan dust blown across the Mediterranean sped up the melt. This would mean another 6 per cent of all glacier ice in the Alps would disappear.

“No final answer, but we are definitely on the way to break the record, or at least come close to [it],” says Rainer Prinz at the University of Innsbruck, who has been monitoring glaciers in Austria.

Bauder and his colleagues were taking measurements on the Rhône glacier as part of ETH Zurich’s long-term monitoring of more than 100 glaciers. Extreme melt years are occurring more frequently in the Alps, unleashing devastating avalanches of ice and rock and threatening to shrink major rivers. More than 1000 Swiss glaciers – 40 per cent of the total – have vanished in the past 50 years. Another 30 glaciers could join them this summer, in what the Swiss media has dubbed a “massacre”.

The bright face of the mountains is dimming. The world’s last year-round ski area has temporarily closed due to unsafe conditions on the glacier under the Matterhorn’s distinctive rock fang, and a famous ice tunnel passing through a glacier in Chamonix has had to be closed.

The Rhône glacier has lost 30 million tonnes of ice this year, enough melt to fill 12,000 Olympic swimming pools. A hole dozens of metres across has torn open the glacier’s lower flank. At its bottom is a river of silty, grey water dotted with boulders and chunks of ice. As we climb the glacier, we have to circumvent the hole, hopping across a spiderweb of crevasses. Members of the team start setting up a ground-penetrating radar to detect water flows at the bed. Meltwater trickling down through vertical shafts has formed a subglacial river that collapsed the ice here, says Ilaria Santin at ETH Zurich.

Free newsletter

“More ice is melting quickly because more water is flowing down there,” she says. “More holes will open on that side of the glacier.”

The Rhône glacier features in the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger as a steep cascade of gnarled white ice next to the Belvédère Hotel. Today, it has retreated almost 2 kilometres back into the valley and the hotel has been abandoned.

A glacier’s lifeblood is snowfall. In summer, the snow starts melting at lower elevations, exposing the ice underneath to warm air and sunlight. If the melt has only reached midway up the glacier by the next winter, new ice can form above it when fresh snowfall compacts the older snow. The flow of new ice from the top compensates for ice melt below.

But snowfall was scarce in the Alps this winter, and the melt began early due to an unusual May heatwave. Glacier loss day, the point when summer melt in the Swiss Alps exceeds winter snowfall, came on 2 July. “It should be in late September,” says Prinz.

We climb a steep icefall to almost 2600 metres, where we find another melt stake falling over. Bauder pulls it out and drills in a new one. In previous decades, the summer melt rarely reached this point. This year, it has crept above 3100 metres and counting.

While the melt line may not reach the top of the Rhône glacier, at 3600 metres, it already has for many lower glaciers. In that case, “it’s just a matter of time,” says Mauro Werder at ETH Zurich. “They will disappear.”

Under current climate policies, more than 97 per cent of glaciers in the Alps will be gone by 2100, along with most of those in Scandinavia, Russia, the tropical Andes and western Canada and the US. Only 5 per cent of Rhône glacier will be left.

That would deplete many critical water sources. Rhône glacier, for instance, is the source of the Rhône river. This great waterway flows through Lake Geneva and into France, where 19 major hydroelectric power plants line its course. Its waters cool the reactors at four nuclear plants and carry up to 5 million tonnes of goods on barges each year.

The Rhône also irrigates the Grenache, Viognier and Syrah grapes of famous French wine-making regions like the Côtes du Rhône, as well as much of the country’s fruit production.

5 graphs that show how heatwaves are getting more dangerous

Glacier-fed rivers like the Rhône, Po, Rhine and Danube have shrunk to record lows this summer, revealing woolly mammoth remains and forcing power plants to shut down. That was mostly due to drought and meagre snow melt. But glaciers in the Alps have already passed “peak water”, meaning the melt they contribute to rivers in summer is gradually drying up. Europe will have to consider adaptations like building new reservoirs.

“The situation is really treacherous because, with every day of the heatwave, we’re using up the reserves of ice, the stocks that have been built up many decades or centuries ago,” says Matthias Huss at ETH Zurich. “Ten or 20 years from now… drought will be even more problematic.”

Permafrost, the icy glue that holds the mountains together, is thawing along with the glaciers. This is what increased rockfalls onto the Birch glacier near the Swiss village of Blatten. In May 2025, the glacier fractured, burying the village under 20 million tonnes of rock and ice, and killing a shepherd. Experts monitoring the glacier evacuated 300 inhabitants nine days before the collapse.

Last month, researchers showed that laying a fibre-optic cable across a glacier can detect crevasses hidden 25 metres down, a far cheaper way to monitor fracturing than seismometers. They were surprised to discover that 8 per cent of the volume of a glacier in Valais was empty crevasses. Scientists may be underestimating the damage to glaciers’ stability, says Thomas Hudson at ETH Zurich, one of the study’s authors.

In the past, monitoring was really all about protecting the glaciers, he says. “We now need to put more of our focus on monitoring for prevention of disasters.”

As we take a breather on the glacier, I ask Werder if attempts to preserve glaciers with geotextiles or reflective clay granules could work. He says the outcomes of these geoengineering approaches are highly uncertain.

While ski resorts have covered parts of eight other glaciers with geotextiles, spreading them across Switzerland’s large glaciers would cost £1.3 billion a year and only slow ice loss, not stop it. But if humanity could limit global warming to 2°C, the number of glaciers surviving to 2100 would almost double, including 269 in the Alps.

“All other solutions are pretty desperate,” says Werder. “We really should just reduce CO2 fast.”

The Crown Range Rd is also closed this morning between Eastburn Rd and Cardrona, due to “adverse weather conditions”, NZTA said.

Area warnings are in place for SH6 from Haast to Hokitika on the West Coast, State Highway 8A from Tarras to Luggate in Otago, and State Highway 8 from Omarama to Clearburn in Canterbury, because of surface flooding.

Snowfall yesterday has also resulted in area warnings for State Highway 73 from Springfield to Otira.

Flooding and rockfalls have affected a swathe of Queenstown and surrounding areas overnight as a late-night deluge hit the town amid a significant winter storm across the South Island.

Snow, heavy rain and slips are causing hazardous travel conditions, while some residents were evacuated from their homes amid concerns about land stability.

Firefighters attended 16 flooding-related jobs during the night, mostly related to water entering homes, Fire and Emergency southern shift manager Lyn Crossan said.

Numerous other calls had also come in regarding flooding on properties and roads. Most jobs were in Queenstown, Frankton, Arrowtown, Lake Hawea and Wānaka, with more expected this morning.

Some Queenstown residents had been evacuated due to concerns about the stability of the ground around Fern Hill and Bowen St, including at a campground, Crossan said.

However, evacuees on the Fernhill side could not get into Queenstown as flooding and debris had completely cut off the Fernhill roundabout. Two fire trucks were also unable to get through for several hours.

The roundabout, at the intersection of Fernhill Rd and Lake Esplanade, was closed from 10.30pm to 2.30am. Evacuees were sent to the Heritage Hotel, while those on the Queenstown side were sent to the Civil Defence’s welfare centre at the Memorial Centre.

The rain had eased around 1am.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

Crossan said one car had become stuck in the water at the roundabout, although nobody was trapped.

“Sometimes in inclement weather people continue to go out and drive around. It just puts everybody more at risk, including our firefighters.”

A van is stuck in debris from a slip in Wānaka, around the 9km mark on Mt Aspiring Rd, according to a social media post from the council just before 7am. Other vehicles can still get around the slip.

The council urged people to avoid non-essential travel, warning there were multiple other slips, washouts, rockfalls and surface flooding, including on Haast Pass Rd, Luggate Hill, Tarras Rd, and Kingston Rd.

“Expect delays, traffic management, and ongoing disruptions throughout the day,” the council said.

The Crown Range Road – which was closed earlier due to rockfall – had reopened thanks to “an outstanding effort from our wonderful crews” early this morning, the council said.

“There’s still a few minor slips which have been clearly marked, so you can safely travel the route.”

Surface flooding was also affecting several roads and the Fernhill/One Mile roundabout, while Queenstown Hill was unaffected. Gorge Rd remains closed near Bowen St.

Along the Glenorchy-Queenstown Rd, flooding and slip issues were affecting the One Mile pumping station and roundabout, with only minor surface flooding and isolated rockfall beyond Sunshine Bay.

Around 2.30am, the council said that while the rain was beginning to ease, people should avoid unnecessary travel and take care on the roads, especially at night as surface flooding, debris and other hazards could be present.

People in Fernhill, Sunshine Bay, Queenstown CBD and Frankton Rd were being told to conserve water.

Northland volunteering: Cost-of-living pressures make recruitment difficult

New Zealand Herald August 27, 2026

Volunteering Northland community connections co-ordinator Verena Pschorn and manager Bev Giles. Photo / Brodie Stone

Rising living costs are making it harder for some Northland organisations to recruit and retain volunteers, community groups say.

Non-profit Volunteering Northland says finding volunteers has become an obstacle in recent years.

“People get into that headspace where they can’t even think about doing something to help someone else because they’re in that survival mode,” manager Bev Giles said.

The organisation connects groups with volunteers and provides networking opportunities, support and professional development.

Giles predicted a “crisis” if volunteers could no longer contribute.

“I think a lot of people wouldn’t imagine that someone that just saved their life was a volunteer as well.”

Community connections co-ordinator Verena Pschorn said volunteering had become “more of a luxury” and people were questioning whether they could help at all.

“It just takes that joy and that community spirit totally out because you have to consider surviving.”

The national volunteer and foster manager for the SPCA, Viv Moore, said living costs meant people had to “carefully consider” their finances.

“We have heard from many volunteers across the country that the ongoing cost-of-living pressures are having a significant impact on their ability to volunteer.”

Some had reduced volunteer hours or taken paid work to make ends meet, she said.

The challenge came amid increased demand for animal de-sexing and rehoming, and with kitten season looming, the SPCA needed extra hands.

North Haven Hospice chief executive Helen Blaxland also cited volunteer recruitment as a “significant challenge” in the past three years.

Volunteers were generally retired and in their early 70s, but others included beneficiaries unable to find paid employment.

Volunteering was a “catch-22” for those who lacked disposable income, she said.

Some stopped volunteering when fuel prices spiked in March, and others could help only once a week despite wanting to commit more.

Some parents’ capacity to volunteer had been reduced because they were taking a more active role in childcare as working parents tried to save costs.

More nurses and healthcare assistants had been called into the inpatient unit to fill gaps, reducing income, Blaxland explained.

“Our expenses are going up as a result.”

Patient support had taken a hit too, with twice-weekly biography services now occurring once a month.

Good Bitches Baking Whangārei chapter lead Kristin Rewha-Langdon said it was becoming difficult to fill the baking roster as volunteer numbers dipped.

The charity provided baked goods for people in need across the region.

Though living costs were tight, Rewha-Langdon also pointed to winter illness, holidays and funerals as reasons for lower volunteer numbers.

“I think for me, like some of it is life, it doesn’t get in the way, but life happens to us volunteers as well, and then that impacts on those that we are wanting to serve.”

In the past 12 months, the chapter delivered 995 boxes.

“People are just so grateful, and I suppose when you think about it, if your ordinary diet’s simple, to have a box of homemade baking is just a treasure,” Rewha-Langdon said.

Some volunteers were baking more often to help fill gaps.

The Hato Hone St John district operations manager for Te Tai Tokerau, Ben Lockie, said recruiting and retaining ambulance volunteers had become “increasingly challenging” in recent years for a range of reasons.

The pressure was greatest in rural and remote communities, where people commonly volunteered for more than one organisation.

Lockie said economic and demographic changes were also factors.

“Many people are working longer hours or remaining in employment later in life, while younger people often move away for work or study.”

Increasing levels of violence and aggression made attracting and retaining volunteers difficult, he said.

Coastguard said finding volunteers depended on the size of the town they were drawing from and whether people were already volunteers.

The cost of living had not been cited as a trigger for a change in numbers, a spokesperson said.

“Where volunteers do leave a unit, time constraints tend to be the main reason we hear.”

Units including Houhora, Whangaruru and Whangaroa were seeking volunteers.

Others, like the new Mangawhai unit, had a strong membership.

Brodie Stone covers crime and emergency for the Northern Advocate. She has spent most of her life in Whangārei and is passionate about delving into issues that matter to Northlanders and beyond.

One dead, critical police probe underway after head-on crash on Alfriston Rd, Manurewa

New Zealand Herald August 27, 2026

A car and ute have been involved in a serious crash on Alfriston Rd, Manurewa overnight.

One person is dead and a critical investigation is underway after a stolen vehicle fleeing police collided head-on with a ute in a serious crash in a Manurewa street overnight.

The crash happened on Alfriston Rd, near the Fleming St intersection, just east of Gallaher Park.

Police confirmed this morning that a person died at the scene and a second person was taken to hospital with moderate injuries.

Counties Manukau District Commander Superintendent Shanan Gray said that around 9.36pm police were called to an address on Greenmeadows Ave following a report of an aggravated robbery.

“An alleged offender was believed to have stolen a vehicle from the property, after presenting a crowbar at the occupant.

“As police units approached the area, they observed a vehicle being driven in the middle of the road, without headlights.”

Gray said it was later confirmed the vehicle was the one stolen from Greenmeadows Ave.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

They signalled for the vehicle to stop but it raced off.

“Around 9.42pm the vehicle has travelled onto Alfriston Rd, where it has collided head-on with a vehicle coming in the opposite direction.

“Officers immediately rendered first aid; however, the driver and sole occupant of the stolen vehicle was pronounced deceased at the scene.”

Gray said the occupant of the second vehicle was taken to hospital with moderate injuries.

The Serious Crash Unit had completed its examination of the scene and the road had since reopened.

Several investigations were now underway to work to establish all the facts surrounding the incident.

This included notifying the Independent Police Conduct Authority.

“We are also working to support those affected and their families, as well as our staff who were involved.

”All those involved in the initial report of aggravated robbery are believed to be known to each other, and there is no ongoing risk to the public."

Gray said that as part of the investigation, police were seeking information from witnesses who might have been in the area at the time, or before the fatal crash.

Photos from the scene show a small silver hatchback and a red ute both facing in the same direction, with debris strewn across the road.

Police tape is strung across Alfriston Rd, while a white sheet covers what is believed to be a body on the road.

Sirens and the Police Eagle helicopter could be heard in the area around the time of the crash.

Security footage of the incident posted to a social media page showed a car travelling at high speed on Alfriston Rd before colliding with the ute.

A large number of police were already in Manurewa following the killing of two people in Wattle Downs on Thursday afternoon.

Hato Hone St John was called at 9.45pm and sent a rapid response unit, an ambulance and an operations manager, while Fire and Emergency sent two fire engines after being called at 9.49pm.

Both agencies referred further queries to police.

The Herald has requested comment from police.

Rotorua man says spinal surgery in Turkey gave him his life back after 25 years of pain

New Zealand Herald August 27, 2026

Rachael and Adrian Crothers have recently returned from Turkey where Adrian had life-changing spinal surgery. Photo / Kelly Makiha

Turkey’s medical tourism scene is famed for hair transplants, dental work and cosmetic surgery. But Rotorua’s Rachael Crothers says it’s not just a place to “get skinny and pretty”. It’s where her husband, Adrian, had long-awaited back surgery and got his life back. They speak to senior journalist Kelly Makiha.

“Good as” was Adrian Crothers’ standard answer if anyone asked if he was okay.

But he wasn’t.

He was battling intense back pain from a 25-year-old rugby injury. He was bent over, felt “crippled”, had lost his quality of life and was hitting the painkillers and relief remedies hard.

He spent about three years going through the various stages of the health system, including battling ACC to pay for his surgery.

His personal health insurance wouldn’t cover a pre-existing condition. Without ACC, he was faced with a long wait in the public system or paying an estimated $175,000 to have surgery in a private hospital.

That was until his wife, Rachael, “did some googling”.

“He was in so much pain that day and was groaning at the end of the couch,” Rachael said.

“So I Googled, ‘Can you have orthopaedic surgery overseas?’”

One of the first options that came up was in Turkey.

“So I Googled ‘How much is a disc replacement and disc fusion in Turkey?’ and it said 40 grand.”

Rachael blurted this out to Adrian and said, “We can do that”.

The pair had been saving for a new ute for Adrian - his one with the “dumped-on 20-inch mags” made for a bumpy and impossible ride with his back injury.

As Adrian put it: “It’s uncomfortable as hell but s*** it looks cool.”

Rachael said if the back issues were resolved, they would not need a new ute.

That was the moment that changed Adrian’s life.

Fifty days later, he was on a plane to Turkey.

Adrian said he was playing rugby in Manawatū in 2001 when he formed a scrum and heard a “pop”.

“Typical bloody male, I thought I’d stretch it out. I went in for another scrum, because they reset it, and then I realised ‘Nah, I’m out.’”

By the time he got to Whanganui Hospital after an hour-and-a-half team bus ride, Adrian was locked in a 90-degree position.

Diagnosed with a spinal sprain, it was thought he would come right in a few weeks.

But he said the back issues never went away. The couple moved to Rotorua in 2003 and, not long after, Adrian experienced pain again.

“I didn’t realise the original [ACC] claim was still open, so I made another claim.”

About two to three years ago, the flare-ups started to happen more consistently, so he went to his doctor. But they couldn’t find his original claim for the rugby injury.

A Rotorua specialist referred him to an Auckland specialist. He learned he needed a combined disc fusion and disc replacement.

Adrian said that, in the meantime, ACC found the original rugby injury claim, but wanted the original X-ray report, doctors’ notes and physio notes.

“My doctor had retired, the physio didn’t keep records past 10 years and we found the physical X-ray but not the X-ray report.”

The X-ray was so outdated that supposedly no one was able to read it to write a report, Adrian said.

ACC told him it was “unable to determine” his accident caused his condition, and declined his request for surgery cover.

The Crothers used an ACC advocate to challenge the decision, without success.

Adrian said he went back to his GP a year ago to get on the public surgery waiting list.

He was told he needed a specialist appointment, which would take 16 to 22 weeks. They expected a letter by January.

Ironically, it did not arrive until May 5 - the date Adrian had surgery in Turkey.

They laugh about it now, but the letter referred them to the same specialist at Rotorua Hospital they saw three years earlier, and who had referred Adrian to Auckland.

“It was an absolute stuff-around,” Rachael said.

Rachael said her investigations online suggested Adrian’s surgery could have cost an estimated $175,000 at a New Zealand private hospital.

She said Adrian’s pain had become so bad, they felt stuck.

He was “crippled” and using fentanyl slow-release patches

”If he kept busy he was all right, but once he stopped, he seized up and was broken.”

They bought a new bed, changed mattresses and bought expensive mattress toppers. But Adrian’s tossing and turning usually sent one of them into the spare room.

They tried reiki, healing massages and mirimiri. He lived in their spa pool and used Deep Heat daily.

“Sprays, lotions, potions, oil, balm, codeine: I was taking eight ibuprofen a day to get through.”

They gave up favourite pastimes including seeing live music and fishing trips with the boys.

Rachael said on one occasion Adrian’s response to her asking if he was okay wasn’t his usual “good as”.

”He said, ‘If I give in to the fact that I am crippled, I will break down mentally.’”

Moana McRae, originally from Rotorua, runs medical trip business Oceanscape Group in Turkey, and helped the couple plan Adrian’s mission.

The surgery cost less than expected, $21,000, so they added a holiday, including experiencing Anzac Day in Gallipoli.

“We thrashed what was left of Adrian’s back,” Rachael said.

The couple said McRae was with them throughout the process and at Anadolu Medical Centre there was a translator available at every step.

Adrian said he could not believe the efficiency in Turkey. Waits between doctors, specialists and MRIs were minutes, not the months he had faced at home.

Rachael said some people “pooh-poohed” their plans.

“They thought he’d end up in a bathtub full of ice with no kidneys.”

Rachael said they had faith in McRae, despite her never having organised a spinal surgery trip.

“She hand-picked the surgeons because we have heard there are some backyard butchers overseas.”

They said the surgery he had was less invasive than that recommended in New Zealand.

Adrian said he knew his back was healed the next day, even through the pain from surgery.

“I sent a Snap out saying, ‘Don’t want to brag but … Today I put on my own socks and shoes!!!”

Rachael said she couldn’t believe her eyes when Adrian got off the hospital bed the next day and stood up straight, as opposed to peeling himself off and slowly moving.

“It’s been a long 25 years since Adrian was broken … but we got an amazing holiday and a hubbo with a refurbed back.”

Adrian said the process included two years’ insurance cover to return to Turkey if there were any complications.

McRae said being able to support the couple through their life-changing trip was “incredibly special”.

She said travelling overseas for surgery was a huge leap of faith, particularly after years of pain and uncertainty.

“Watching Adrian and Rachael take that leap together was incredibly moving, and continuing to follow Adrian’s progress from here in Turkey, seeing him regain his mobility and get his life back, has been so rewarding.”

While Adrian said he was “stoked” to have his life back, he was still sad New Zealand could not give him the care he needed.

The couple, who own Rotorua-based business Electrical Solutionz BOP, said they had paid taxes and ACC levies all their working lives, and felt let down.

ACC head of service operations Phil Riley said it received the request from Adrian’s surgeon in February last year.

“ACC can only contribute to treatment costs when there is a link to a covered injury. The medical information available didn’t support this link and the request was declined.”

Riley confirmed this was reviewed at Adrian’s request, but no further supporting clinical information was found. Adrian withdrew the review after his overseas surgery.

ACC Minister Scott Simpson and Health Minister Simeon Brown declined to comment on Adrian’s case, saying it was a matter for ACC.

Neither responded to a general request for comment about the health system and Kiwis seeking urgent surgery overseas.

Adrian said after hitting “brick wall after brick wall” with the New Zealand health system, he couldn’t recommend Turkey enough.

Rachael said it was great to have her husband back.

“It’s not just somewhere you can go to get skinny and pretty, they will also fix you,” Rachael said.

More than four months on from surgery, Adrian said he was better than “good as” - he was “mint”.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Waikato film industry grows beyond Hobbiton as region attracts major productions

New Zealand Herald August 27, 2026

Waikato is trying to turn The Lord of the Rings movie magic into something bigger. Pictured is Matt Hicks, a director and producer from Cambridge.

Twenty-five years ago, a little-known farm outside Matamata became Middle-earth.

Now Waikato is trying to turn that movie magic into something bigger.

Hobbiton remains the region’s most famous connection to Hollywood, but beyond the green hills and round doors, a different screen industry has been quietly taking shape.

Film-makers are making films, festivals are showcasing them, cinemas are putting local work in front of audiences and an increasingly sophisticated network is helping major productions set up shop.

Cambridge director and producer Matt Hicks has seen that change first-hand.

A decade ago, Hicks was making his first film while moving dog kennels and figuring filmmaking out as he went.

Now he has produced the Waikato-shot feature Home Kills, which premiered at the New Zealand International Film Festival, and made his feature, The Tavern.

He never went to film school.

“I think sometimes naivety is a superpower,” Hicks said.

“If I had fully understood how hard it is, maybe I wouldn’t have done it.”

That willingness to have a go is something Hicks said ran through Waikato’s screen community.

“The most beautiful thing about it is everybody’s operating from almost like a pure sense [of filmmaking],” he said.

“There’s not too many politics. There’s not too much ego. Everybody’s just turning up for the love of the game.”

In Waikato, a film crew still attracts attention, he said.

It is still a novelty, and Hicks reckons that can be an advantage.

For The Tavern, the team approached Cambridge Raceway hoping to film one horse-racing scene. Instead, they were welcomed in entirely.

Farmers opened their properties, locals became extras, and businesses got involved.

Some were paid little more than a box of Waikato Draught and a bottle of spirits.

But they wanted to see their town on screen.

“That’s the coolest thing about the Cambridge community,” Hicks said.

“I feel any success that The Tavern has had, they’ve had as well.”

When the film toured New Zealand, people who had once drunk at the real Cambridge tavern that inspired it came out to screenings.

One man told Hicks he had been the bouncer there in 1972.

“It was so cool to show our town all around the nation,” he said.

That grassroots enthusiasm is now alongside something considerably more professional.

Waikato Screen, the region’s film office, has grown over the past three years and now supports seven of the Waikato region’s nine councils.

Attraction and facilitation manager Erin Griffiths said the scale of change was significant.

“In the past four years, we’ve had more productions filming in the Waikato than we had in the previous 20 years combined,” she said.

Waikato Screen’s role includes helping productions find locations, crew, businesses and services, while navigating the practicalities of filming across the region.

Location manager Peta Sinclair, who recently worked on the international production Minecraft, said having an established film office had made a significant difference.

A production needs more than a beautiful landscape: accommodation, service providers, a unit base and infrastructure capable of supporting large casts and crews, Sinclair said.

Waikato Screen could provide location leads, make introductions and help productions navigate council permissions, logistics and filming requirements, Sinclair said.

Waikato is also becoming an attractive alternative to Auckland, particularly for large international productions that might struggle to operate at scale in the big smoke.

“Waikato Screen has become a major player within the filming process for both international and the local domestic market,” Sinclair said.

“The future is looking extremely bright for the land of Mooloo.”

Hicks puts it more colourfully.

“We’re not the poor cousin of Auckland,” he said.

“I reckon we’re like the hot, rich sister.”

The recent list of productions using the Waikato is hard to ignore.

A Minecraft Movie and its sequel used Huntly, including the town’s streets and power station, while Netflix’s Beyond Goodbye filmed in Raglan.

The region also hosted productions including Chief of War, The Gone, Sweet Tooth, and Don’t Make Me Go.

Earlier productions filmed in Waikato include The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian and Pete’s Dragon.

Recent productions such as Minecraft have given locals a glimpse of what featuring in a movie could mean.

Hicks remembers sitting beside two Huntly councillors at an Auckland preview as Huntly Power Station appeared on screen.

“It’s a real buzz,” he said.

But bringing productions into the region is only half the battle.

The other question is who will make them.

Misty Flicks film festival director Paige Larianova has spent a decade watching Waikato’s filmmaking community develop.

The festival began as a two-hour short-film showcase and has grown into a three-day event featuring workshops, pitching sessions and training programmes.

Larianova said many Waikato-made films found success overseas.

“There are heaps of short films on the festival circuit around the world being made here, and no one even knows about them [locally],” she said.

“Wouldn’t it be cool if people could actually see what local filmmakers are creating?”

Another challenge, she said, was developing the people behind the camera.

“Everyone is trying to be a director, but we need more producers and people who understand the different roles on a film set if we’re going to make bigger productions more often.”

That is also the thinking behind the new Waikato Screen Charitable Trust.

The separate organisation will focus on education, training, mentoring, scholarships, upskilling, cultural storytelling and pathways into film, television and the creative industries, while Waikato Screen concentrates on attracting and facilitating productions.

At Hamilton’s Lido Cinema, manager Nigel Corboy sees the film community developing from another vantage point.

The independent cinema hosts local premieres, Q&As and screenings for Waikato productions.

“You see a lot of the same people working together, which is great,” he said.

“It’s a small scene, but it’s vibrant.”

Corboy said audiences were also increasingly backing New Zealand-made films.

“It makes me proud to see Kiwis flock to Kiwi films,” he said.

“We really do turn out for these films.”

Meanwhile, for Hicks, Waikato’s film future lies in keeping that community spirit while giving people more opportunities to make ambitious work.

When he decided to make The Tavern, he went to Whangamatā, locked himself in a room for a week and wrote.

No internet. No distractions.

He produced about 200 pages of what he called “absolute garbage”, cut it to 130 pages and eventually took another 40 minutes out during the edit.

The finished film was the realisation of a life dream.

“It was my life dream to make a feature film, and I’d done it,” Hicks said.

“If I died tomorrow, it was great to know that I’d achieved something of significance.”

He is already working on his next film.

His advice to anyone considering entering the industry:

“Just do it.”

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before joining the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Coroner finds speedwing pilot misjudged final manoeuvre in fatal crash at Avalanche Peak

New Zealand Herald August 27, 2026

A day flying in the mountains ended tragically for Connor Knox in February 2025. The speedwing pilot, who loved the outdoors, was killed while executing a final manoeuvre too close to the ground. Photo / 123rf

A thrill-seeker’s fatal leap from a mountain peak was filmed by a nearby tramper who watched his final manoeuvre before he collided with the ground.

Connor Knox had launched himself off Avalanche Peak in Arthur’s Pass National Park after two failed attempts with his speedwing when wind conditions weren’t right.

A speedwing is similar to a paraglider, but smaller and designed for fast, steep, dynamic descents close to the ground.

The “bold and brave” 25-year-old loved to try new things, but was a risk-taker, leaving little margin for error, a coroner found.

Knox’s death from head injuries underscored the importance of pilot compliance with aviation regulations, appropriate training and the use of equipment that was fit for purpose and matched the pilot’s flying skills, Coroner Amelia Steel said in findings this year.

The case featured in the Chief Coroner’s latest Recommendations Recap, published last week. The recap contained summaries of coronial recommendations and comments made between January 1 and March 31, 2026.

Knox, who worked as an industrial abseiler at high levels using specialised ropes, died near Avalanche Peak on February 2 last year.

The “happy and adventurous individual” enjoyed the outdoors, was widely travelled and pursued rock climbing, biking and paragliding.

His parents, Mark and Lisza Knox, told NZME their son was a private person and they preferred to say little out of respect for the likelihood it’s what he would have wanted.

“We are grateful to have had him as a son.”

Tributes posted online in the wake of Knox’s death revealed a young man who lived life to the fullest.

One tribute said he loved fully and with abandon.

“He loved the thrill of adventure, he loved climbing, and the mountains and sharing them with people.

“He loved pasta, his family, gingernut cookies, and any kind of strange concoction with enough carbs and calories.”

He also loved having a yarn, playing rumi, chess and riding bikes.

On that summer’s morning he travelled from his home in Christchurch with other paragliders and speedwing pilots, planning to launch from an approved site at Avalanche Peak.

Access to the area is described by the Department of Conservation as an 1100m vertical climb from Arthur’s Pass Village.

The friend Knox was with described him as a beginner or intermediate flyer.

He said Knox was “very comfortable” using a larger speedwing he had completed hundreds of flights with.

The friend had seen Knox complete low-altitude and low-energy manoeuvres which left little margin for error, and was aware others had spoken to Knox about taking risks with his flying.

Cloudy conditions upon their arrival at the site delayed launch by a couple of hours.

Knox launched first after two aborted attempts because of insufficient wind.

On one attempt, he snagged a line on an obstacle and had to complete a makeshift repair on a trim tab at the rear of the wing, Coroner Steel said.

The Civil Aviation Authority said in a report to the coroner the glider was airworthy to fly with the repair in place, and it would have had minimal effect on Knox’s final flight.

He gained plenty of height after successfully launching, completed a “super nice” spiral to get closer to the ground with the wing his friend said was performing well.

Knox then went out of his friend’s sight, but was seen by trampers crashing heavily into the ground.

The coroner said medical assistance was given but he quickly died from his injuries.

Contact the Open Justice team

Among the online tributes was one who said he and a friend had reached Knox minutes later, and wanted his parents to know he was not alone in that moment.

“I am so deeply sorry we could not save him,” the person wrote.

A nearby tramper recorded the crash on his cell phone. Knox’s friend told police, who sought his opinion on the footage, that it appeared Knox had attempted a manoeuvre without sufficient height to complete it safely.

The witness video showed Knox’s ground speed was slow before he entered the turn, resulting in the glider “diving” more.

Knox was wearing a lightweight climbing helmet. The clip broke on impact and the helmet came off, leaving minimal damage to the helmet, Coroner Steel said.

“Tragically on February 2, 2025, Mr Knox misjudged the amount of height and speed he required to successfully complete what was his final manoeuvre and crashed into the ground,” she said.

“I find that due to the severity of his injuries, he died rapidly after this impact.”

The New Zealand Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association (NZHGPA), which provided technical assistance to the CAA in its report to the coroner, said Knox did not hold the required association membership nor an appropriate pilot certification.

The CAA noted Knox’s association membership had expired three months earlier.

Training records showed he achieved a beginner paragliding rating in November 2023 and a novice rating a little over a year later, followed by speedwing training in April 2024 but did not hold a rating in the use of the canopy type.

The CAA said the crash was the result of an error of judgment combined with Knox’s “high-risk appetite and limited experience”.

The NZHGPA reiterated the importance and benefits of membership which not only ensured compliance with CAA regulations but also connected pilots to a national safety culture, structured training pathways, equipment checks, and public liability insurance coverage.

Coroner Steel said after Knox’s death, the association accelerated its safety education campaign “Fly Like a Bird, Think Like a Pilot”.

“I emphasise the critical importance of NZHGPA’s safety messaging designed to keep individuals safe and manage risk in what is inherently a high-risk adventure sport,” Coroner Steel said.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

After grieving the loss of a bandmate, a Beastie Boy makes his solo return

Sydney Morning Herald August 28, 2026

Mike D says his sons, and the influence of the late Adam Yauch, helped him realise it was time to make music again.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

From the age of 16 to 46, New York City-born rapper, musician and producer Michael Diamond, aka Mike D, spent most of his time in a band with his two closest friends, Adam “Ad-Rock” Horovitz and Adam “MCA” Yauch.

As Beastie Boys, the trio forged a successful career that included their 1986 debut Licensed to Ill (the first rap LP to top the Billboard 200 album chart, it has shipped more than 10 million units in the US alone), 1989’s sampledelic masterpiece Paul’s Boutique, and 1994’s Ill Communication, a cutting-edge blend of hip-hop, punk and funk that cemented their place as unassailable signifiers of cool.

Then, on May 4, 2012 – a year and a day from the release of Beastie Boys’ eighth and final album, Hot Sauce Committee Part Two – Yauch succumbed to cancer at the age of 47. For Horovitz and Diamond, who is now 60, the freewheeling party came to a crashing end, and Beastie Boys’ time was up.

“Yauch’s passing was a shocking death because he was so tragically young,” says Diamond, post-band rehearsal in Los Angeles. “To have this figure who’s so close to you in life die, and then go through the grieving of that.

“My entire adult life until that point we were very fortunate as a band because, even if we would sometimes take long periods of time between projects, we would always have that to go back to. So it was certainly a very different thing to have this quiet time [afterwards] and there was a lot for me to unpack, obviously.”

With the preciousness of time starkly underlined, Diamond redirected his full-time focus to being a dad to sons Skyler and Davis (now 22 and 23, respectively; their mother is filmmaker Tamra Davis). Any attempts at making new music during that period were aborted due to the grief it would trigger.

Things started to shift, says Diamond, during the pandemic. His sons, who make music as the indie-pop/electronic duo Very Nice Person, began pulling out Diamond’s vintage equipment and messing around with it in the backyard pool house, causing the stay-at-home dad to rethink his retirement.

“The COVID times were very instrumental to me making my record,” he says. “My kids took over all the gear from my studio and they set up our home studio properly. That became our sanctuary and the place where we had the luxury of time to just get creative.

“That was what inspired me. It just lit this thing inside me of ‘I’m ready now to return to this happy place of making music on my own schedule’. It took a while to eventually get there but that [period] definitely was critical.”

Knowing that it was the right time to focus on music again (one of the new tracks is even titled It’s Time), Diamond hunkered down with his band 5D (Skyler, Davis, Will Graefe and brothers Eddie and Milo Ruscha) to finish his lively and experimental debut solo album, Thank You. The LP takes the Beasties’ familiar penchant for genre-blurring into the 21st century while still managing to throw in a few surprises (see: the drum’n’bass-influenced Switch Up and the tender, guitar-led title track).

Despite it being a neat reminder of exactly why the Beastie Boys were seen as coolness personified, it still leaves Diamond confronted with a hard truth that all parents must face. “Making music with my sons is nice because there’s this built-in honesty where they’re gonna call me out on stuff because I’m never gonna be cool in their eyes, right?” he says.

“Occasionally they’ll see something [Beastie Boys did] and be like, ‘that was pretty cool’, but never to the point where they actually would think that I am cool.”

I ask Diamond if anything from his friendship and long working relationship with Yauch played a part in influencing the new album. “Yauch always inspired us to think that however inconceivable or far out there an idea seemed, that was never a reason not to do it. So that was something that was very present for me when I was making this record,” he says.

“Also, whenever any of us were doing something enriching on our own outside of the band, Yauch was always, very clearly, ‘that’s great, you should definitely do that’. I felt almost like this nudge from Yauch – like, ‘just do it; block out all the noise, you should be doing this’.”

Diamond also felt compelled to tell his other former bandmate Horovitz that new music was percolating. “I actually felt really happy that I was able to call up this old friend of mine and say, ‘hey, I just need to let you know I’m making this record, and the boys have been helping me so much on it, and we used your old SP-1200 sampler on something’,” says Diamond.

“It was just cool to be able to let him know and have him be just cool and supportive about the whole situation.”

Diamond says the gratitude that’s expressed on Thank You is for his past as much as for his present. “I’m thankful for all of it – for having grown up in New York City when I did,” he says. “It was when it was the only place in the world where you had all this music absolutely popping off at the same time.

“Then you had the birth of hip-hop happening, and that started to permeate the clubs. Within blocks of each other you’d have all this incredible music and be exposed to it. We were a band but it was really just us as friends being teenagers and being able to run wild amongst all of this incredible music.”

And what advice would he give that wild, music-loving teen, with the benefit of hindsight? “Try to be kind. I’d also say don’t waste so much time – but you kind of have to waste time when you’re a kid,” he says. “Because how else are you gonna figure out the value of it?”

Thank You by Mike D is out now.

Wigan rise to occasion against Hull KR as town unites to remember Sir Billy Boston

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:40:24 GMT

Super League: Wigan Warriors 46-0 Hull KR

Liam Marshall bags hat-trick of tries in rout

On the night when Wigan Warriors celebrated one of their greatest entertainers, perhaps it was fitting that Matt Peet’s class of 2026 produced a performance Sir Billy Boston would have been proud of on their charge, potentially, towards another Super League title.

There are some nights where the result is dwarfed by the occasion. Where sport, in truth, comes second. This was undoubtedly one of those, as what felt like the entirety of this town where rugby league is more akin to a religion than it is a pastime came together in grief to remember the life and career of their most cherished adopted son.

In the week Boston passed away at the age of 92, Wigan’s players were challenged by Peet to deliver a performance rugby league’s first knight would have adored. At times, it was a game that was played in conditions Boston himself would have been familiar with during the sport’s winter seasons; biblical rain and utterly horrendous conditions.

But Wigan, just like Boston did in his own career, made light of those difficulties to register a 13th consecutive Super League victory, extending their own modern era record and returning to the top of the table. Leeds Rhinos will get the chance to return serve on Friday when they face St Helens, but it is obvious it will take some team to stop Wigan this year.

It would be remiss not to mention the immense help the Warriors were handed here by Hull KR opting to effectively surrender this game before a ball had been kicked. The defending champions have been dragged into a battle just to make the play-offs with three rounds remaining, and should the Saints beat Leeds on Friday, they will be level in sixth and seventh.

But at the end of a run of four games in 14 days, Willie Peters took many of his key men out of the line of fire, throw in a number of youngsters and hand out a plethora of debuts. The end result was what many feared: a heavy loss for the Robins. This night alone does not prove they are big outsiders to retain the title, but this is their third consecutive defeat.

However, the best teams offer little sympathy to such situations. Wigan also had the added motivation of following on from a wonderful tribute for Boston pre-match, when there was barely a dry eye in the house. It was difficult not to be moved by the Warriors’ many tributes, including leaving the usual seats of Boston and his late wife, Lady Joan, empty.

Few clubs do nights like these like Wigan. And they made good on the promise to honour Boston on the field, leading 28-0 by half-time as they picked Hull KR’s fringe team apart. Fittingly, four of the five tries in that first half went to wingers, with Liam Marshall and Zach Eckersley both scoring a brace, along with a well-taken finish from Jai Field.

That Wigan were still able to score points as the torrential rain began towards half-time is a very good sign for the play-offs, when conditions typically deteriorate. They did not relent after the break either, with Adam Keighran finishing a wonderful team move, Marshall completing his hat-trick and Jake Wardle ensuring all of Wigan’s three-quarter line scored.

As for Hull KR, this was the first time they have failed to score under Peters. He has won every trophy on offer with the Robins but his time in charge looks likely to end with a whimper.

These two sides have contested the last two Grand Finals with one win apiece. The odds on a third are lengthening by the week with only one looking like they will be at Old Trafford. If Wigan needed any more motivation, they have likely now found at it the end of a tragic week: honouring their greatest player with another league title.

Fightland review – 50 Cent’s farcical boxing show is featherweight at best

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:05:38 GMT

This boxing drama wants its sex, drugs, bling and violence – but isn’t willing or naughty enough to truly go for it. Instead, it ends up as just a long, bruising slog

Fightland is what you might, for a joke, have called a drama that’s like MobLand but with boxing. That they have gone with that as the title of the new show from G-Unit Film & Television, the production company founded by the rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson, is an immediate warning that this is not a series that bursts with originality, passion or technical finesse. At best, Fightland asks whether what it’s got will just about do, and hopes you’ll distractedly say yes.

Howard Charles is Maduka “Duke” Kilroy, a British boxer who, when we first meet him, is in Las Vegas, winning the world heavyweight championship. Everything’s going for him: he’s the champ and Joy (Deborah Ayorinde), the woman he enjoys a post-bout warmdown with on the silk sheets of a penthouse suite, seems receptive to his plan to take their relationship further. It’s a risky goal given that Joy’s husband is Kingsley Marshall (Nicholas Pinnock), Duke’s manager, who is also London’s top drug dealer; we’ve seen him brutally break the leg of a journalist who asks him about the secret drug-based wing of his empire.

Sure enough, later that evening Duke is set on by goons, presumably hired by Kingsley after discovering that his golden boy has double-crossed him. The resulting fracas leaves Duke bereaved and, after he fights back a little too much, in prison. On his release six years later, he returns to London, bent on revenge. His plan is to pose as a penitent lost son, rejoin the Marshall crime/boxing family and bring it down from the inside. But Kingsley has gone awol, so instead Duke is up against the big man’s two heirs, who are a two-for-one cliche of a gangster patriarch’s pampered adult children: Zeek (Charles Babalola) is weak, vain and impetuous, while Cece (Anita-Joy Uwajeh) is smart, ruthless and overlooked.

The setup sounds simple enough, but Fightland fumbles it on account of its fundamental flaw, which is that nobody’s motivation for anything is ever clear. Perhaps because it’s banking a big twist for the back half of the season, the show is coy to the point of outright confusion on who knows what about the affair and the attack on Duke, what the repercussions of his imprisonment were, and where Kingsley might be. In scenes in which characters ought to discuss these things, they awkwardly don’t, although if there’s a plot point the show wants to remind us of, oh boy does it crowbar that into the dialogue. You are evidently meant to let it wash over you; viewers who have a tendency to say, “Wait, why did they do that?” or “Hang on, that isn’t going to work because …” are in for a long, bruising slog.

Fightland wants its violence, sex, bling, betrayals and bricks of illegal powder, and isn’t too fussed how it gets there. Except, it’s not interested enough in any of those things. If we’re going to do a sex-and-violence crime caper, let’s get properly naughty with it. But Fightland has almost no bedroom mojo and the fight scenes are perfunctory and weirdly short. They often offer tantalising premises – a duel to the death with a coked-up, machete-wielding strip club owner, for example, whose blade keeps clanging against the stage’s chrome pole – before petering out. If you can’t be excellent, at least be excessive; Fightland constantly holds back. Even boxing, which offers all kinds of ready-made metaphors for the power games played by businesspeople and criminal kingpins, is relegated to the background. The scenes in boxing gyms could be taking place anywhere.

Charles is a formidable presence but he’s far too good for this material, as is Pinnock, which makes the decision to quickly remove the latter from the action even more bewildering. They are both more than capable of fronting a rich, layered character drama, which Fightland doesn’t attempt, or a knowingly camp romp, which it can’t muster the energy for either. The script is deliberately funny on occasion, but so rarely that you almost question whether it is deliberate; it’s not as unintentionally funny as you’d hope, either, although Duke’s homemade photoboard of the Marshalls and their acolytes, featuring the scrawled caption “DRUG CONNECT??”, is one highlight.

Fightland moves quickly and smoothly enough that all this may not matter too much. Maybe Cece’s nonsensical plan to make millions by introducing casino sportsbooks to the UK, a country that already has an established betting shop/online bookmaker industry, will somehow work. Maybe the South American cartel Duke is in league with will conquer London, despite their British operation apparently consisting entirely of Duke and one guy they have sent over. Maybe Fightland will survive and be allowed to rumble on for three or four seasons. But it’s a featherweight contender.

Fightland aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now

USA’s Russell and Brazil’s Dos Santos smash world records on ‘crazy’ night in Zurich

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 21:05:05 GMT

Dos Santos and Russell smash hurdles world records

Werro comes within 0.42sec of 800m world record

Bednarek and Wanyonyi clock world-leading times

Masai Russell and Alison Dos Santos each set a world record while Mondo Duplantis won a historic pole vault on a frenetic Thursday night in Zurich.

The Letzigrund Stadium had a raucous sell-out 25,000 crowd and the still, balmy weather conditions helped the athletes no end.

Brazil’s Dos Santos was the first to make a mark, clocking a sensational 45.80 seconds in the 400m hurdles to beat the previous mark of 45.94sec set by Norway’s Karsten Warholm in the final of the Tokyo Olympics.

“I have been showing great form throughout the season – that I am fast, I am strong,” said Dos Santos, with Warholm finishing second and dubbing their discipline a “crazy event”.

“As soon as I knew I was coming here, I was excited. The weather’s good, the track’s amazing,” the Brazilian added.

Then came US star Russell, the Olympic champion, timing 12.09sec in the 100m hurdles to beat the previous best of 12.12sec set by Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan at the Eugene world championships in 2022.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Dos Santos and Russell will leave Zurich with a cheque each for $80,000 for having broken their respective records.

The world records were punctuated by a scintillating competition in the pole vault, eventually won by double Olympic and triple world champion Duplantis. The US-born Swede came under real pressure from Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis, who vaulted a personal best of 6.20m. Duplantis cleared 6.25m for victory, while both vaulters tried a possible world record 6.32m, in a truly thrilling showdown that gripped the stadium’s attention.

It was the first time in vaulting history that two athletes had gone beyond the 6.20m mark.

“It’s not every day two people go for the world record, so that was nuts,” said Karalis.

The icing on the cake came in the women’s 800m, with the star attraction Switzerland’s own Audrey Werro. Werro also did not disappoint, registering the third fastest time ever in the two-lap race, 1:53.70, as she edged ever closer to Jarmila Kratochvilova’s Cold War world record of 1:53.28 set in Munich in 1983.

“It was crazy, I am very proud. Thank you everybody!” the 22-year-old said.

Femke Broeders-Bol finished second as she continues to improve in her transition from the 400m hurdles in which she was twice a world champion.

“Being in a great event with a great time – amazing,” the Dutch athlete said.

Kenya’s world and Olympic champion Emmanuel Wanyonyi held off Algeria’s Djamel Sedjati for a nail-biting victory in the men’s 800m.

Wanyonyi has said that going for David Rudisha’s world record of 1:40.91 is like running a marathon under two hours, and the mark once again proved elusive as he timed a world lead of 1:41.76 for the win. Sedjati was just 0.07sec adrift.

“When I see the world records being broken, I know my time will come. There is time for everything,” said Wanyonyi.

Danny Welbeck leads Chelsea past Luton as Fernández misses Carabao Cup tie

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 20:40:13 GMT

Emiliano Martínez is on his way but another high-profile Argentinian is likely to be wearing a different shade of blue soon. Chelsea have dealt with their biggest weakness, satisfying Xabi Alonso’s wish for a new goalkeeper by agreeing a £7.5m deal to sign Martínez from Aston Villa, and it will surely not be long before they have put an end to the Enzo Fernández saga.

Fernández was the most notable absentee as Chelsea eased into the third round of the Carabao Cup with a 2-0 win over Luton. There is a desire to move on from the circus. Manchester City are poised to bid for Fernández and, with the noise around the midfielder becoming a distraction, Alonso and the club decided to leave Chelsea’s supposed vice-captain out.

Alonso explained that he had to think about the team. Chelsea’s manager was diplomatic. Alonso said that Fernández has been training well. He offered political answers but did not douse the sense that Fernández has played his last game for Chelsea, who host Leeds in the next round.

It is for the best. Fernández has been looking for a way out since March and Chelsea need committed players.

Alonso wants to improve the squad’s culture and the attitude against Luton was good. Danny Welbeck, still going strong at 35, can be a standard bearer after joining from Brighton. The striker is not here to make up the numbers and played a key role in this win, grabbing his first goal since joining when he open the scoring early in the second half.

“Danny was the patient player,” Alonso said of Welbeck breaking Luton’s resistance by leaping to head home a fine cross from Malo Gusto. “He did what he does best: score and to be in the right place.”

Welbeck will provide competition for João Pedro in attack this season. He also adds a vital dash of experience to a young squad. Chelsea can cope without Fernández, even though they will need to replace him if he goes to City.

The early vibes under Alonso are encouraging. He has been decisive with the goalkeeping position, as exemplified by his ruthless response to Robert Sánchez’s skittish display against Fulham. There is nothing left to see with Sanchez. He is not good enough and Chelsea had to be opportunistic when offered the chance to sign Martínez. Mike Penders made his debut in goal here. The 21-year-old Belgian is highly rated but will be behind Martínez in the pecking order.

Alonso is trying to win now. Although Chelsea have no Europe this season it was surprising that they named such a strong side three days after their helter-skelter win over Fulham in the Premier League. Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer were part of an exciting attack and were supported by a thrilling display from Estêvão Willian on the right.

Third in League One, Luton battled to stay in contention during a first half in which the shot count was 17-3 in Chelsea’s favour. Rogers crashed an effort against the bar and Jack Wilshere’s side were defiant in defence. Josh Keeley made excellent saves from Palmer and Reece James, starting in midfield for the second time in three days despite his injury problems.

Russia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack Nato

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 19:26:01 GMT

Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles

Russia has said it could retaliate against the UK for its support of Kyiv by striking military targets inside and outside Ukraine, amid reports that the director of the CIA warned the Kremlin against attacking Nato during a secretive visit this week.

Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, said on Monday the UK would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start ⁠its own production of Storm Shadow ​long-range ​cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology. Maria ⁠Zakharova, Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Thursday Britain and France were “playing ⁠with ​fire”.

Responding to the latest Russian threats, a Ministry of Defence official reiterated UK support for Ukraine. “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies,” they said.

The Wall Street Journal reported that a visit by John Ratcliffe, the CIA chief, to Moscow on Tuesday had followed a US intelligence assessment that Russia could be planning to test Nato with a limited assault on an allied country. This could range from a cyber-attack to a small-scale incursion, probably in a Baltic nation.

Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies during the war, including thinly veiled nuclear threats and others apparently aimed at diplomatic missions in Kyiv.

Asked ‌to comment ‌on the reports of Ratcliffe’s visit – and despite Thursday morning’s threat against UK targets – Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has ‌nothing to do with reality and nothing to do ​with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”

The intense scrutiny around the Ratcliffe trip and Russia’s intentions comes amid a new report over shortfalls of missile interceptors available in Europe.

A report by the Associated Press says the US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, according to a US defence official in Europe and a Nato official, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack.

The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involved Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.

Russia is believed to be contemplating a further escalation of its war with Ukraine after months of escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s oil refining infrastructure and other sites, which are imposing an increasing economic toll.

The Kremlin has adopted ever more bellicose rhetoric, much of it aimed at a domestic audience, as the war in Ukraine has been brought to its doorstep.

In the space of a few days Russia has invoked the threat of its nuclear arsenal against Japan over its territorial claim to the disputed Kuril Islands. It has described relations with the US as a “crisis” and at a historic low point.

Ratcliffe’s reported warning mirrored one made by his predecessor, William Burns, in 2021 before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – which Moscow also denied it was contemplating.

Concerns over Moscow’s intentions have been increasing amid a rise in incidents of Russian hybrid warfare attributed to Moscow across Europe, from cyber-attacks and drones to arson, at facilities associated with supporting Ukraine’s war efforts.

Russia and the US have tried to play down Ratcliffe’s meeting with his Russian counterparts: Trump on Wednesday described the visit as “semi routine”. However, the unusual nature of the encounter has caused intense speculation in the west and Russia.

The US president continued to play down the encounter on Thursday, telling Axios that Ratcliffe had arrived in Moscow with “no message” and claiming there was “nothing unusual” about the meeting.

Asked later by reporters about reports about the CIA director Ratcliffe had delivered a warning to Russia, Trump replied: “I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack.”

Nato countries neighbouring Russia have moved quickly to increase their military readiness. Poland this week announced it had taken delivery of its first shipment of South Korean Black Panther main battle tanks, which will be deployed near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region.

Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s deputy defence minister, said this month Warsaw was preparing for the possibility of a full-scale conflict.

Tomczyk told Super Express media: “We are preparing for war, hoping it never happens.”

Uefa raises stakes with criminal complaint in battle to unseat Infantino

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 19:00:36 GMT

Uefa has begun a legal process against the embattled Fifa president but it will still be an uphill struggle to remove him

Anyone who interpreted Uefa’s decision to withdraw a proposed boycott of Fifa competitions, revealed by the Guardian on Wednesday, as a backward step in the attempt to remove Gianni Infantino as Fifa’s president has been quickly disabused of that notion.

In a stunning development that overshadowed one of the biggest days in the European football calendar as national football federation and club executives gathered for the Champions League draw in Monte Carlo, Uefa announced it was preparing to make a legal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland alleging “criminal mismanagement” for his role in the failed World Cup sell-off plan.

Uefa, having removed the immediate pressure on Fifa on one front by permitting European teams to play in next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup and October’s senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers, has dramatically increased the stakes on another.

The first step in that legal process is seeking disclosure in the United States of documents relating to the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, which Uefa described in a 56-page document sent to three US courts as having an “absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn” (£14.7bn).

From the moment it became clear Infantino would not resign after withdrawing the FFE plan four days after it became public, Uefa has been pursuing the valuation issue, which if the sale had progressed would have enabled Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital to buy 21% of future Fifa revenues in perpetuity for $4.2bn.

The Guardian revealed on 6 August that Uefa was commissioning an independent valuation of FFE amid concerns Infantino was planning to sell off football’s crown jewel on the cheap, a feeling exacerbated by the fact Fifa’s sales deck did not contain any information on the valuation process or evidence of a competitive tender.

As one source who questioned Fifa’s valuation said this month: “We need to find out if they were selling the World Cup at a knockdown price.” The intention to bring a criminal complaint is the logical extension of this process.

Even the most cursory of inquiries over the past few weeks vindicated Uefa’s concerns. Fifa’s revenue for the four-year cycle that culminated in this summer’s World Cup was $15bn, leading market analysts to suggest that $20bn was a low valuation, particularly as the proposal did not appear to include provisions to prevent expansion and the creation of new tournaments.

Kushner’s subsequent purchase of the LA Lakers with the former Disney chief Bob Iger for $12.5bn further convinced Uefa that Thrive Capital had been given a sweetheart deal by Infantino, a conviction underlined by its suspicion that Infantino was lining up a lucrative role worth tens of millions of pounds a year as FFE’s chair after standing down as Fifa’s president, which he plans to do in 2031 if he wins a further, final term.

Infantino’s determination to cling to office – demonstrated by his decision to enter campaign mode by attending a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union last weekend in the Dominican Republic where, as the Guardian revealed, he suddenly approved several funding projects – emboldened Uefa further.

Uefa has taken the legal route after being thwarted in numerous requests to Fifa to disclose documents. It has made court filings in New York, Florida and Colorado to obtain papers it may submit to Swiss courts seeking criminal charges.

Just as significant as the attempt to take Infantino to court in his adopted country is Uefa’s attempt to rally Fifa members behind it in its attempt to unseat him via March’s presidential election.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

For all Uefa’s public bullishness that Infantino’s race is run, several senior figures there and among its allies at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – have admitted concerns to the Guardian that they are struggling to get many member associations outside Europe to turn against him.

Over the past few weeks several FAs have privately indicated it may take evidence of criminal activity, or at least proof that Infantino would have been personally enriched by the FFE venture, for them to abandon him.

Even those with a brief knowledge of Fifa’s history would agree that the rebels concerned about momentum to unseat Infantino stalling have a point. Although he loves to paint the world governing body as the ultimate democracy underpinned by a one-member, one-vote system, the reality is anything but. Although elections are held every four years there have been only three permanent presidents in the past 52 years, and the last to leave office after a vote was England’s Sir Stanley Rous in 1974.

Rous’s conqueror, the Brazilian João Havelange, resigned after 24 years and was later found to have accepted bribes related to the sale of media rights by a Fifa ethics committee. His successor, Sepp Blatter, stood down after winning five elections in the midst of an FBI investigation in 2015, which has resulted in more than 20 criminal convictions in the US and could lead to more.

Any hope among the rebels that the Swiss authorities will come to their aid and bring Infantino to court should be tempered by those authorities’ long history of turning a blind eye to Fifa corruption, which meant intervention from the FBI was required to expose and punish it.

Actor Peter Cullen, voice of Optimus Prime and Eeyore, dies aged 85

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:56:50 GMT

Montreal-born actor also voiced KARR in Knight Rider and the monster in Predator, having started his career on Canadian TV and radio

Peter Cullen, the actor behind the voice of characters including Eeyore in Disney’s Winnie the Pooh franchise and Optimus Prime in Transformers, has died aged 85.

He died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, a statement said.

The Canadian actor began his biggest role – as Optimus Prime, the honourable leader of the Autobots – for the Transformers TV series in 1984. He returned for seven Hollywood Transformers films from 2007 to 2023 and other spinoffs.

Cullen voiced the melancholic donkey Eeyore in The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh TV series from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games.

His other notable roles included the roars of King Kong for the 1976 remake, and KARR – Knight Automated Roving Robot, the evil counterpart to KITT – in the Knight Rider series in 1982 and 2009.

The actor is also credited with coming up with the eerie clicking sounds that emerged from the mouth of the monster in the Arnold Schwarzenegger film Predator in 1987.

His family said: “Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family – and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide.

“His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember, ‘be strong enough to be gentle’.”

The Montreal-born actor began his career on Canadian TV and radio and was then a regular on programmes including The Sonny & Cher Show and The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour before deciding to concentrate on voice acting.

Cullen said Optimus Prime’s resonant and authoritative voice was inspired by his older brother Larry, a retired captain in the US Marine Corps who had served in the Vietnam war, who suggested he should play the character as “a real hero, don’t be a Hollywood hero”.

“He said, ‘Don’t go yelling and screaming. He’s strong enough to be gentle’,” Cullen recalled. “And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime.”

Cullen gave Larry a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his brother’s death in 2011.

In a 2014 NPR interview, Cullen acknowledged that he initially approached playing Optimus Prime with puzzlement. “I auditioned like everybody else,” he said. “I was told it was a hero, and I was told it was a truck.”

The actor’s performance earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

When the director Michael Bay resurrected the Transformers franchise for a film in 2007 starring Shia LaBeouf, Cullen told IGN: “I describe it as kind of slipping into an old pair of very comfortable shoes that you haven’t worn for a while. I just slipped right into them, and they felt as good as the last time I put them on.”
