Burnham accused of U-turn after initially backing political donations cap to fall below £500k

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:51:40 GMT

Exclusive: Campaigner says PM wrote in email he believed £500k cap should be reduced over time to guard against undue influences

Andy Burnham recently supported an even lower donations cap than previously reported, according to correspondence seen by the Guardian, as the row over next week’s elections bill escalates.

The prime minister wrote to a campaigner in May outlining his support for a £500,000 individual donations cap, which he said would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.

In a follow-up email seen by the Guardian, Burnham went on to say he believed the cap should gradually be reduced – a proposal now being put forward by the Labour MP Stella Creasy.

Campaigners are accusing Burnham of a U-turn after the Guardian reported the prime minister had decided not to back the attempts by Creasy and others to introduce a donations cap in next week’s elections bill.

In his first message to Shaun Bowler, who runs the website wakeupgb. co. uk, Burnham wrote: “I do think there should be a cap on political donations. This would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.

“As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”

In a second message, the then would-be MP for Makerfield said: “[I] would definitely want to see that reduced over time. I am in complete agreement that there needs to be wholesale culture change in Westminster.”

Bowler has now written to the prime minister accusing him of abandoning his previous commitments. He wrote: “It appears you are going to break your promise to me – and the nation …. Weeks after being elected, you have made your first major U-turn.”

He added: “This is your chance to actually deliver the start of that cleanup. Show us that politics can be clean and trustworthy. Don’t surrender to the mess.”

Other campaigners, including the broadcaster Carol Vorderman, are also urging the prime minister not to back down in the face of opposition from trade unions, who have warned that a donations cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.

Senior figures at groups including Transparency International, Spotlight on Corruption and Greenpeace have also written to Burnham. In an open letter, they call for a “low and hard cap on all political donations”, adding: “We know you agree that politics should not be for sale. Please take action now to ensure it will not be under your leadership.”

The issue will come to a head next week when MPs debate the next stage of the elections bill. The bill will lower the voting age to 16 and cap donations by Britons based abroad, but not on domestic donations.

Creasy had put forward an amendment to cap domestic donations at £100,000, while her colleague put forward an amendment to cap them at £1m.

Creasy has now changed her amendment to set the cap at £500,000, reducing in the second year to £100,000 unless ministers intervene to set it at a different level. The proposal, which has cross-party backing, mirrors what Burnham told Bowler he would support in May.

The prime minister’s aides say that while he is not backing a donations cap next week, he is not ruling one out in the future. A Labour source said: “This bill was designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and to strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising. But we’re not ruling out taking further steps to protect our democracy in the future.”

Officials also said the government would not support an attempt by the Labour MP Anneliese Dodds to reduce the amount political parties can spend during an election campaign after the limit was raised by the previous Conservative government.

Alcaraz, the defending champion in New York, has not competed in singles since sustaining a right wrist injury at the Barcelona Open in April, with the Spaniard missing the French Open, where he was also the defending champion, and Wimbledon. He was understandably rusty and tentative with his first serve when making his first competitive appearance since the injury alongside Serena Williams in the mixed doubles event on Tuesday, with the pair losing in the quarter-finals and the 44-year-old Williams even outperforming him during large parts of their time on court. His opening match against the world No 98 Safiullin, who has risen more than 100 places in the world rankings this year after returning from injury and defeated Alcaraz indoors at the Paris Masters in 2023, will be a significant first challenge.

Between the uncertainty surrounding Alcaraz due to his lack of match play and the absence of the world No 1, Jannik Sinner, who was forced to withdraw due to a knee injury, the men’s Flushing Meadows draw is as open as it has been in years. As the second seed, Alcaraz’s section includes both the eighth seed, Ben Shelton, and the 10th seed, Arthur Fils, the winners of the Canadian Open and Cincinnati Open respectively, the two ATP Masters 1000 events leading up to the US Open. Fils will face a high-profile first-round opponent in the former world No 3, Stefanos Tsitsipas.

The four-time champion Novak Djokovic will begin his latest attempt to become the oldest singles grand slam champion in the open era as the fourth seed in Alcaraz’s half of the draw. He faces Mariano Navone in the first round with the out-of-form seventh seed Daniil Medvedev the highest-ranked seed in the Serb’s quarter. Alexander Zverev, the French Open champion, is the top seed at a grand slam tournament for the first time and faces the Italian Lorenzo Sonego in his opener.

While a large group of players have an opportunity to make a career-defining breakthrough in the men’s draw, it will be difficult for the rank-and-file competitors to stop the strong group of elite players at the top of the women’s draw despite their differing form. Aryna Sabalenka, the defending champion, will begin against Camila Osorio as she tries to hold on to her No 1 ranking after a difficult few months.

The highest ranked players in Sabalenka’s half are the in-form third seed, Jessica Pegula, a potential semi-final opponent, the Wimbledon champion and sixth seed, Linda Noskova, and the seventh seed, Karolina Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon. However, considering Sabalenka’s recent results, even a potential third-round match with the two-time grand slam champion and 27th seed, Barbora Krejcikova, cannot be taken for granted.

The strong bottom half of the draw, meanwhile, is overflowing with title contenders.. Elena Rybakina, the second seed, seemed to be in an ideal position to usurp Sabalenka at the top of the rankings but her form is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati last week due to a leg injury.

Mohammad Abbas pegs back England as improved Pakistan make their mark at Lord’s

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:20:18 GMT

Second Test, day one: England 248-9 v Pakistan

Jordan Cox and Jamie Smith hit back with half-centuries

Footage of Brydon Carse kept flashing up on the big screens at Lord’s on Thursday. Not that footage, of course, but rather the headline-grabbing fast bowler enjoying a refreshing can of the fizzy apple juice that is English cricket’s “official drinks break partner”. In fairness, both clips make a decent advert for sticking to the softies.

In Carse’s absence – not that he was likely to play in the second Test – the metaphorical clouds hanging over this England team made way for the real thing. After being stuck in on a nibbling slow surface, a Swiss clock-precise seamer like Pakistan’s Mohammad Abbas was only ever going to be a handful.

Abbas duly stamped his mark by nipping out four wickets that, with three from the more expressive Mohammad Ali, lifted Pakistan’s mood significantly at 1-0 down. But for Jordan Cox’s 55 and 61 from Jamie Smith, England’s eventual 248 for nine from the 56 overs that were possible would have been considerably worse.

In a new-look England top seven still to fully congeal, these were also important knocks for the pair. Both have reputations as dashers but, with the ball in the ascendancy – unless it was dropping short of the slips – they played the percentage cricket that Joe Root is desperate to instil in his second spell as Test captain.

Cox in particular held the innings together, with 217 minutes of watchfulness – interspersed by punishment of the bad ball – continuing the good impression he has made at No 3. It took a jaw-dropping catch from a substitute fielder to remove him, with Salman Ali Agha – captain last week, dropped the next – as wide-eyed as anyone after the ball stuck in his diving right paw at third slip.

This brought an end to a precious 67-run sixth-wicket stand with Smith and while the wicketkeeper kicked on for a spell, he eventually became one of three men clean bowled before the gloom became too great. Given how one-sided events were at Headingley, the honours felt even in one respect but Pakistan’s in another.

Either way, the series badly needed this kind of contest after the grim affair in the first Test. It remains to be seen if Marylebone Cricket Club can breathe a little easier about the pitch, however, because the nine wickets to fall could easily have swelled further had Ollie Robinson not been denied a late burst.

So far the surface is not quite the minefield witnessed during that rapid-fire Test against New Zealand in June, primarily because the bounce, while low, appears more consistent. Although after rain forced an 80-minute delay to the start of play, it still looked like one that Abbas in particular would enjoy.

It took a little while for Pakistan to find their radar as 20 runs flowed from the first 19 deliveries. But once Abbas had Emilio Gay strangled down leg – not the first time the left-hander has fallen this way in his nascent Test career – he then wiped out Root and Ben Duckett in more familiar fashion.

Trapped lbw for 17 on review, Duckett was Abbas’s 900th wicket in first-class cricket. That only 123 of these had come in the whites of Pakistan is a head-scratcher. Indeed, the 36-year-old has played just 25 Tests out of 59 since starring in their last win at Lord’s eight years ago, despite averaging 22.5. Go figure.

Root, meanwhile, had spent far too much time in the buildup to this Test dealing with the Carse situation, bandwidth he would have preferred to put towards his own game. Not even a life gifted on one helped as, with Mohammad Rizwan up to the stumps, Abbas caught him on the crease for his eighth lbw in 11 innings.

after newsletter promotion

At the other end Ali was struggling with the front line and already combustible due to the earlier catch going down off Root. Things improved for Ali on the stroke of the 2pm lunch, at least, when he bowled Harry Brook for 15 – a ball that deviated lavishly off the seam and whistled past an ambitious straight drive.

England reaching 80 for four at lunch made it Pakistan’s session, clearly, only for Cox and Smith to flip this before tea. One wicket fell for exactly 100 runs in the second session and it was self-inflicted too, Dan Lawrence run out looking to pinch a non-existent single off the spin of Ali Usman and trudging off in disgust.

Lawrence did not look entirely at ease for his 17, it must be said, not least compared with Cox at the other end. His penchant for the leg-side risks made him easy to tie down. Had Shan Masood not dropped a simple chance at mid-wicket to deny Khurram Shahzad, Lawrence would have fallen for 10.

Indeed, for all that Pakistan upped their game from last week, their fielding – Agha’s wonder-catch off Cox aside – continues to hold them back. The most damaging missed opportunity came when Smith was dropped on 15 by Rizwan. It was a low chance, granted, but bad positioning given what little carry was on offer.

Ali was the bowler to miss out, his exasperation one of the enduring images of the day. He eventually took his colleagues out of the equation, cleaning up Smith and Robinson with balls that nipped in. Abbas repeated the dose for Jofra Archer late on to leave this second Test looking more intriguing than the last one.

Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 18:03:09 GMT

Flash floods have killed at least 389 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 389 people and left more than 1,300 missing.

Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Videos from Wednesday’s disaster showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.

Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.

Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.

Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.

Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.

“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”

Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”

Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”

Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. He said: “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”

People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.

Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.

The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”

More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.

Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.

Police in Nepal said 389 ⁠bodies had been recovered by Thursday afternoon local time, while Chinese state media reported three dead on the Tibet side of the border.

Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.

Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.

Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.

“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”

Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.

Scant information has emerged from the Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.

Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups & experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”

She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.

The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: prepare for more climate-linked disasters

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:40:35 GMT

Medicine, food and other supplies are the urgent priority. But the rising risks from shrinking glaciers must be faced too

Thousands of people in Nepal and Tibet are in desperate need of emergency assistance following Wednesday’s disaster. With 360 people confirmed dead, more than 1,300 others are still missing as search and rescue operations continue. The precise sequence of events linking glacier collapse to flash floods is yet to be confirmed. But there is no doubting the enormous destructive power of the brown torrent that can be seen on video clips surging down the steeply sided Himalayan valleys, sweeping away everyone and everything in its path.

Testimony from survivors about terrifying near-escapes and losses is reminiscent of previous disasters, including the 2004 tsunami. With some of the worst-affected areas still cut off and accessible only by helicopter, there is a high level of uncertainty about the total number of people who have died or homes that have been destroyed. Existing medical, food, shelter and sanitation supplies will need to be replenished. Pledges of help for locally led relief efforts from foreign governments and agencies, following reports that hundreds of those missing were tourists or pilgrims, must lead to swift action. People need basics including electricity and clean water before they can start to rebuild and recover.

Satellite images of the glacier and affected rivers are among crucial pieces of evidence used by scientists to piece together an account of what happened. Initial reports of an earthquake were later discounted, with seismic activity instead attributed to the impact of the glacier collapse and ice-rock avalanche. Nepalese authorities have issued warnings about the high risk of further floods. Women and children who have been displaced are particularly vulnerable to further harm, including disease and trafficking.

As with other disasters that are widely recognised to be climate-related, it is unwise to jump too swiftly to conclusions. Tectonic movement, which leads glaciers to change their shape over time, is a natural process. But already, multiple glaciologists and other earth scientists have pointed to global heating as a crucial destabilising factor. Higher temperatures are well established to be altering mountain environments worldwide, with the Himalayas warming twice as fast as the global average. As the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has pointed out, this puts the region and its people at heightened risk not only from avalanches, landslides and floods, but also from freshwater shortages caused by retreating glaciers.

The implications of this may seem overwhelming. While millions – and perhaps billions – of people around the world accept that greenhouse gas emissions have altered the Earth’s atmosphere, the impact of human activity on the geology of mountains is a less familiar idea. Once the immediate humanitarian crisis in Nepal has eased, and survivors have been helped to safety, this is the reality that must be addressed.

Mitigation of the climate threat through the transition away from fossil fuels remains essential. But resilience and adaptation measures also offer vital protection, particular to communities in exposed locations. As mountains become more dangerous, early-warning systems must be strengthened. Disaster preparedness should be prioritised at a national level and in aid budgets so that agencies are better equipped to react. Governments must rally round the people of Nepal and Tibet, and prepare to support similarly afflicted parts of the world in future.

The Guardian view on energy costs: vulnerable households need help with their bills

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:39:46 GMT

Soaring prices are plunging struggling families into debt. The government must support them in the short term as it invests in a clean energy future

Fuelled by the consequences of Donald Trump’s disastrous war on Iran, household energy debt in Britain is continuing to soar, rising to a record £6bn by the end of June. That figure is set to hit £7bn by the end of the year, as the government’s cap on gas and electricity prices goes up to a three-year high in October. The human cost among the less well off will be more people regularly choosing whether to skip meals, ignore other bills or stay cold this winter.

Such is life at the sharp end of the cost of living crisis, which Andy Burnham has made it his priority to address since arriving in Downing Street. The day after he became prime minister, Mr Burnham announced that VAT would be removed from electricity bills from the beginning of October. But the Middle East-related rise in the price cap, announced on Wednesday, more than wipes out the effect of his cut. In an era of geopolitical volatility, high energy costs have become the new normal.

The government is right to stress, as the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, did again this week, that completing the transition away from fossil fuels holds the key to bringing future costs down. As well as being the right thing to do, clean renewable energy will eventually deliver cheaper bills and end Britain’s exposure to fluctuations on international gas markets. But as families’ finances are tipped over the edge by fuel prices they simply cannot afford, short-term solutions are needed if Mr Burnham is to deliver on his pledge to give them “breathing space”.

The warm-homes discount for vulnerable households was set at £140 in 2011; it has gone up by a miserly £10 since then. A new social discount scheme is desperately required, which can properly insulate the less well off from financial pressures that neither they nor the government can control. Emergency crisis and resilience funds run by local councils need to be boosted.

Gordon Brown has suggested that the latter could be done through the introduction of a new betting and gaming tax. The Trades Union Congress has lobbied for the financing of a new social tariff through a windfall tax on banks. Flexibility, as Mr Brown has also observed, can be sought within the fiscal rules Mr Burnham has inherited. With the requisite political will, the money can be found.

At the same time, the government needs to drive the necessary investment in the green transition and find a way to shift more of its financing on to the broadest shoulders. In part, that should mean switching more environmental costs away from household bills and into general taxation. Research indicates that some low-income households spend three times more of their net income on levies than wealthier ones. Britain’s climate goals make moral and economic sense, and are supported by the public. But an overly bill-focused approach to green investment helps those seeking to present net zero as the problem rather than the solution.

Following Ofgem’s announcement of the price cap rise, Mr Burnham acknowledged the impact it would have. A further, bigger spike in January is predicted if market volatility continues. The prime minister’s VAT cut on electricity bills was welcome. But as the Conservatives and Reform UK exploit high energy costs to create dividing lines over the green transition, the government’s approach needs to become bigger and bolder.

A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.

Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London, assaulted the teenage boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not appear to show any emotion as a jury at Harrow crown court returned majority verdicts finding the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after six hours and 29 minutes of deliberations.

One complainant told jurors he had sex with the teacher “about 20 or 30 times” over several months. He would visit Bowen’s home, considered her to be his girlfriend and had fallen in love, the court heard.

In his evidence, the man – who cannot be named for legal reasons – said he kept their relationship secret because he felt compelled to protect the teacher, who he said had drummed it into him that he was not allowed to tell anyone.

“I never, ever spoke to anyone about it,” he said. “I was always really aware, she drummed it into me.” He added: “Years she got to teach because I remained silent.”

He said in a police interview that the experience had been “the destruction of my education”.

Madeleine Wolfe, prosecuting, told jurors in her closing speech that the man’s evidence had “a real visceral quality to it”. She said: “There can be no doubt that there was a lasting impact on him. It’s not a schoolboy fantasy, is it? He’s started this account in 2014 – this has real-life implications for him, remained with him for decades.”

It was not until he became a parent himself that the man began to realise what had happened to him, Wolfe said.

The second complainant said he and Bowen kissed once in a cafe when he was goaded into it by other boys.

Another former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that Bowen acted as if she was in “a Sabrina Carpenter video” while in the classroom, and “dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers”.

Oliver, who did not know the two victims, told jurors: “The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual.”

Bowen had no boundaries and “felt more like trying to be one of us, like our friend, than a teacher,” he said. Bowen was “very flirtatious” in class and told them how she enjoyed giving oral sex to her boyfriend, he said.

He recalled an occasion when a boy in Bowen’s class was reading a “sex manual”, which he believed to be the Kama Sutra. He said Bowen went through the book and discussed “the merits of different sexual positions” with the students.

Oliver also described how on another occasion Bowen sat on a desk and caught the attention of the class before slowly opening her legs, revealing her underwear.

Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered a complaint from the first victim’s mother that she was concerned the boy was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.

During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were “total fabrication”. She said she had had a medical condition that in the late 1980s had not been diagnosed and had made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Her partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, giving evidence, said Bowen had not been aware of her condition when they met in 1990, and sex had been “clearly not enjoyable for her” as a result.

Asked under cross-examination how she had dressed in the classroom, Bowen replied that she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher” in her mid-20s. She told the court she did not flirt with students and was “just friendly”.

She denied having a relationship with the first complainant. “Absolutely not, no relationship whatsoever. Student-teacher,” she said.

She denied knowing the second complainant, saying she did not remember him even after seeing him give evidence in court.

Allegations against Bowen featured in the Tortoise Investigates podcast Lucky Boy last year.

Bowen was granted bail until her sentence hearing on 20 November.

The former Barclays boss Jes Staley has denied having sex with a woman dressed as Snow White, after being questioned about an infamous email exchange about Disney princesses with Jeffrey Epstein.

The comments were detailed in newly released transcripts from a closed-door interview last month with US lawmakers as part of their investigation into Epstein, who died in prison in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

In the email exchange on 9 and 10 July 2010 Staley and Epstein referred to Disney princesses. In those messages, the details of which have been circulating in the media since 2021, Staley tells Epstein: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.”

Epstein then asks: “What character would you like next?” to which Staley replied: “Beauty and the Beast.” Epstein responded: “Well one side is availble [sic].”

During his congressional testimony, Staley, who spent more than three decades at JPMorgan Chase before joining Barclays in 2015, was asked: “Did you ever have sex with a young woman in a Snow White costume?

“No, I did not,” Staley said.

Lawmakers then questioned Staley about another email, sent to Epstein by an unnamed individual on 10 July 2010 and which said: “the snow white was f.. ed twice as soon as she put her costume))”. Epstein appears to have asked an unnamed individual to buy a Snow White costume weeks before those exchanges, on 20 June 2010.

“Why would this young woman have sent this email to Mr. Epstein if the two of you had not had sex while she was wearing a Snow White costume and if Mr. Epstein had not instructed her to do so?” a congressional representative, whose name has been redacted from the transcript, asked.

“I have no idea who else she was with. I – it has nothing to do with me, though,” Staley said. When pressed further, he said: “I may have seen her in apartment [sic] and prompted that email. But I was not with a person dressed as Snow White outside of potentially crossing at his apartment.”

The representative asked: “So you may have seen her in his apartment, later emailed Mr. Epstein and said, ‘That was fun,’ but it was not because you had sex with her?”

“That’s correct,” Staley said.

In the transcript, Staley is then asked: “Would you agree that’s a pretty incredible coincidence, that you email him on July 9th, saying, ‘That was fun, say hi to Snow White,’ and then [the unnamed individual] emails him the next day, reporting back on something that just didn’t have anything to do with you?”

“Sure. Why not?” Staley said.

“That’s pretty hard to believe,” the representative said.

The former banker was also asked whether he and Epstein used “Disney princesses as code names for selecting women for sexual encounters”, to which Staley replied, “No.”

Staley’s reputation has been tarnished as a result of his well-documented friendship with the child sex offender.

Staley originally met Epstein in 2000 after he became head of JP Morgan’s private bank, where Epstein was a client. Staley later took over as chief executive of Barclays, one of the UK’s largest banks, in 2015 but was forced to step down in 2021 after City regulators opened an investigation into his relationship with Epstein.

Staley was eventually banned from taking any job in the UK’s financial sector for playing down those ties. He tried and failed to overturn that banking ban last year in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship.

Trump’s war on Iran is rapidly draining US navy budget, documents and interviews reveal

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:00:34 GMT

Exclusive: Experts and former officials say accounts are running dry, and funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge

Donald Trump’s war on Iran has driven the US military into a severe financial crisis, with the US navy forced to transfer money from its payroll and other sources to cover the costs of combat, according to documents obtained by the Guardian, and interviews with navy officials, contractors and defense analysts.

The US-Israeli operation, which has depleted US munitions stockpiles and prompted retaliatory Iranian strikes that have wrecked strategic bases across the Middle East, is piling pressure on budgets across the military.

One Pentagon memo about navy funding seen by the Guardian warns that there are “shortfalls in payroll” accounts due to the department “raiding” them to fund combat operations.

Experts and former officials say the accounts are running dry. “The piggy bank is broken,” said Harlan Ullman, a retired naval officer. Ullman is a member of the National Commission for the Future of the Navy but he said he is not speaking on the commission’s behalf.

One official and one navy contractor said non-emergency maintenance on shore-based facilities has been deferred because of the cash crunch.

When Trump started the war on 28 February, it quickly strained the military’s existing budgets – particularly that of the navy, which not only helped launch the initial wave of attacks but was later responsible for an extensive naval blockade. The White House eventually asked Congress for emergency funding to pay for the war efforts, but prospects that the request will be approved are dim amid the unpopularity of the war.

A navy official who was briefed on how the service is planning to address the shortfalls said money is shifted around in imaginative ways. “The money for payroll,” he said, “was robbed to pay for overseas contingencies and is being backfilled by money that hasn’t been spent. They are backfilling payroll so we get enough money in our paycheck.”

The navy’s budget for 2026, almost $300bn, has different batches of money allocated by Congress for various requirements: personnel, shipbuilding, procuring specific weapons systems and “operations and maintenance”, the day-to-day running of the fleet and its bases. The law limits how money can be rejiggered throughout all those batches of money.

The issue has occasionally surfaced in some hearings on Capitol Hill. Susan Collins, in a 21 July hearing of the Senate appropriations committee, said: “I’m told some military services face near-term solvency challenges.” A staffer said the navy was one of the services Collins was referring to.

In a statement, a navy spokesperson said maintenance and operations funds have not been depleted. “The Department of the Navy,” the statement said, “is actively managing its resources to meet current pay obligations on time. We continue to work closely with Congress to address ongoing operational demands and sustain our personnel and readiness throughout the fiscal year.”

Inside the service, the cash shortage is no secret. “They’re just not speaking publicly about it,” said Todd Harrison, a defense analyst at the conservative American Enterprise Institute. “And I suspect that is a deliberate decision of the civilian leaders in the Pentagon, starting at secretary, that this is for political reasons, that they don’t want to look like they’re damaging future military readiness over a war that is becoming increasingly a political liability.”

The military knew the crisis was coming. In mid-May, Adm Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, cautioned Congress that the crunch would hit in July. “The FY ’26 budget didn’t bake in Epic Fury,” he said. “I do fear that I’ll have to start making decisions in the July timeframe on how I do force generation. That could make differences between how I do exercises, how I do routine operations in order to make sure that I … have the funds necessary to continue the war effort for Epic Fury.”

Pete Hegseth has pushed Congress for emergency funding, without which, he said in July, “we face critical shortfalls”. The defense secretary testified that the Iran war cost $35.7bn, but it’s unclear if that is a full accounting of the war’s costs.

When the Trump administration asked Congress for $67bn in emergency funds for the defense department, it didn’t break down how much would be for the navy. The House passed a $1.15tn defense bill in July and a separate budget authorization that would provide $73bn for the war in Iran, but it’s unlikely either will become law.

Ullman noted that during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, funding was more forthcoming from Congress because those conflicts were authorized by a resolution. “There is no authorization to use force in this case. Is Congress obliged to pay for a conflict it did not authorize?” he said.

The fact that the navy is broke – or at least out of money for now – may be something of a slap in the face for Trump.

The president has often evoked what he sees as his affinity with Theodore Roosevelt, who was president from 1901 to 1909 and presided over the expansion of the US navy, deploying the so-called “Great White Fleet” that steamed around the world. Instead of a Great White Fleet, Trump’s administration has embraced the term “Golden Fleet”. Among his naval ambitions: plans for mammoth “Trump class” ships – the largest battleships in US history.

Trump’s micromanagement has included directing the navy to redesign an aircraft carrier so it launches jets with a steam and hydraulic catapult system rather than by an electromagnetic system. As the Guardian reported, every year since 2017 he has opined about his preferences in carrier launch catapults.

At this point, however, funding a war with no clear endgame is the main challenge. A former military officer now working for a navy contracting company, who has been briefed on the shortfalls, said: “They’re fucked. They shot all their weapons; they trashed all their ships; they ran out of their money.”

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:00:33 GMT

Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form

Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Dolly Parton may have had a record 25 US country No 1 singles, released 66 studio albums and earned six Golden Globe nominations, among many other achievements, but the Tennessee-born star also had an incredible number of fashion moments. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”, she famously quipped when asked about her style. As we bid her farewell, six Guardian writers reflect on their favourite Dolly looks.

‘About as far from the Glastonbury aesthetic as it is possible to get’

Head-to-toe white rhinestones, long red fingernails strumming a matching white bejewelled guitar. Teased platinum wig, blue eyeshadow. About as far from the Glastonbury aesthetic as it is possible to get, but on that Sunday afternoon in 2014, a 180,000 strong crowd fell in love with Dolly. Her charm, her wit, her voice, and just the pure ballsy goodness of her. In her own words: “Don’t judge me by the cover, ’cause I’m a real good book.” Amen. Jess Cartner-Morley, associate editor (fashion)

‘She proved the best way to live is in a look you love’

While Parton wore a plethora of looks, sometimes up to 10 a day, you always knew what you were going to get. For over 60 years she held firm to her signature style – a silhouette that emphasised her tiny waist, along with high heels, higher hair and a heavy sprinkling of sparkle. In today’s world of image architects and constant reinvention, her continuity felt even more refreshing.

Speaking to Vogue in 2023, Steve Summers, Parton’s longtime stylist and creative director said: “Designing for Dolly is great, because there are so many [Dollys].” “I’ve got the philanthropist, the singer, the actress, the theme-park owner. The canvas is always very broad.” Here we have godmother Dolly, at the age of 76, performing with her goddaughter Miley Cyrus in 2022. And her look perfectly captures her attitude to style, as well as her outlook on life. Belting out I love Rock ‘n’ Roll, Parton didn’t have time to entertain any boring discourse about age-appropriate style. She was too busy living. And as Parton proved, the best way to live is in a look you love. Chloe Mac Donnell, deputy fashion and lifestyle editor

‘It’s almost meta’

Among Dolly Parton’s greatest quotes, the most iconic must surely be “I’m not offended by dumb-blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb … and I also know I’m not blonde.” So much has been said about Parton as an artist who took her craft seriously but not herself, and this rhinestone-embellished, yellow “dumb blonde” top is emblematic of that. It’s almost meta. Every bit of her aesthetic, modelled after a bold, flamboyant and glamorous woman in her local Tennessee who was derided as the “town tramp”, was intentional. Art not artifice. A paean to women who wouldn’t make themselves smaller, who would not only wear society’s prejudices but throw them back with a lip-glossed kiss. Jason Okundaye, assistant opinion editor

‘Formed the blueprint for everything I thought was glamorous’

I first watched Steel Magnolias aged 7 and Dolly’s glamorous style was instantly seared into my brain. Not to miss the point about Dolly – it was all about the rhinestones, the teetering heels and the long red fingernails. In a world of algorithmic, Pinterest-board taste, where it can be hard to tell whether your style is even your own, there’s something almost medicinal in that. Ellie Violet Bramley

Tim Curry obituary

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 17:00:25 GMT

Actor and singer best known for his roles in The Rocky Horror Show and the 1990 Stephen King TV miniseries It

In June 1973, I went to the Royal Court to see one of Edward Bond’s best plays, The Sea. On my way out, I met a colleague who said he had a spare ticket for something called The Rocky Horror Show in the Court’s studio space, the Theatre Upstairs, starting at around 10.30pm.

We had no idea what this was going to be about. There was a gantry rigged above us and, astonishingly, suddenly, crawling along it was a frizzy haired chap in fishnet stockings, suspender belt and lurid makeup. This was Tim Curry, as the deranged scientist and debauched sex magnet Dr Frank-N-Furter, introducing himself in song as “just a sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania”.

Thus was launched Richard O’Brien’s hilarious, addictive glam rock musical that went on to become a cult classic, after moving, with Curry, along the King’s Road to a former cinema, then crossing to Broadway in 1975, and later being performed in productions all around the world.

It was adapted for the screen in 1975 as The Rocky Horror Picture Show, directed by Jim Sharman, with Curry reprising his role, and O’Brien appearing as Riff Raff, the scientist’s butler, along with Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick as the young couple who seek shelter in Dr Frank-N-Furter’s castle after their car breaks down.

The film arguably lacked the stage show’s element of subversive innovation and unbridled glee, but it became a huge cult hit with audiences, with both movie and theatre-goers dressing up in glam costumes, and joining in with the dance moves of Time Warp, the show-stopping song led by O’Brien.

Curry, who has died aged 80, became a big star on both sides of the Atlantic in film and on stage. He went on to prove himself a class act in stylish comedy and hit musicals, including a rocked-up version of The Pirates of Penzance in 1982 at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, and Stephen Fry’s smart version of Me and My Girl, doing the Lambeth Walk as Bill Snibson on a 1987 US national tour, and as King Arthur in Monty Python’s Spamalot (2005-07), directed by Mike Nichols on Broadway and in London.

His celebrity was certainly matched by his talent, and his innate charm was equally matched by his louche lifestyle which, for a period, involved party-going with David Bowie – a huge fan of his – and cocaine-fuelled benders with Truman Capote.

Cruelly, he was struck down by a severe stroke in 2012 and was a wheelchair-user for the rest of his life. He summarised that life in a beautifully written and generously expressed, almost self-deprecating, memoir, Vagabond, in 2025.

Curry was born in Grappenhall, on the outskirts of Warrington, the second child of Jim Curry, a Methodist chaplain who had served in the Royal Navy, and his wife, Maura (nee Langmead), a school secretary. He was educated as a boarder at Kingswood school in Bath – after the family had relocated to Plymouth – and took a degree in English and drama at Birmingham University.

His first professional engagement was in the tribal rock musical Hair at the Shaftesbury theatre in 1968 – where he first met O’Brien. That cast included Elaine Page, Paul Nicholas and Marsha Hunt. Between Hair and Rocky Horror, he appeared in David Mercer’s After Haggerty (1969) with the Royal Shakespeare Company at the Aldwych, and as Puck in A Midsummer Night’s Dream in Regent’s Park in 1972.

After the Rocky Horror film took off, he spent three years in New York recording and touring as a rock singer. This culminated in his Broadway role, from late 1980, as Mozart in Peter Shaffer’s Amadeus, losing out on the Tony best actor nomination to Ian McKellen as Salieri. His theatrical appetite re-boosted, he returned to London.

Back in the capital he brought vim and vigour to his notable stage role as the Pirate King in the production by Michael White – the commercial producer behind the Rocky Horror Show – of Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Pirates of Penzance. He was nominated for an Olivier award for his performance.

In 1983, Curry appeared at the National Theatre as Bob Acres in Peter Wood’s sumptuous, elegant production of Sheridan’s The Rivals, which placed the Royal Crescent of Bath on the Olivier stage and co-starred Michael Hordern as Sir Anthony and Geraldine McEwan as Mrs Malaprop (“All men are Bavarians” – instead of barbarians). This show also marked the professional debut of Fiona Shaw. Less successful was the NT’s revival of Brecht/Weill’s The Threepenny Opera in 1986, in which he played Mack the Knife.

Other films included Annie (1982), in which he played the con-artist Rooster, Richard Eyre’s The Ploughman’s Lunch (1983), written by Ian McEwan, the black comedy mystery Clue (1985), and The Three Musketeers (1993), in the role of Cardinal Richelieu.

He was the clown Pennywise in the 1990 TV mini-series adaptation of Stephen King’s novel It, and also appeared in the films Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992) and Muppet Treasure Island (1996), as Long John Silver. He was a lifelong friend of the art critic Richard Cork with whom he had been to school.

His sister, Judy, predeceased him.

Timothy James Curry, actor and singer, born 19 April 1946; died 25 August 2026

Five MPs on Teesside have called on the government to provide more help to local police and fire services after a week in which nine people have died in two incidents.

The MPs said the communities they represented should get the “strongest possible backing from the government”.

Police have said two fatal incidents may be linked to organised crime. On Saturday, seven people including two police officers were killed in a head-on crash on the A66. On Wednesday, a 34-year-old woman and her seven-year-old niece were killed in a house fire that police believe was started deliberately. The house in Grangetown is less than a mile from the scene of the A66 crash.

Andy McDonald, the Labour MP for Middlesbrough and Thornaby East, said gangs and the drugs trade were “clearly featuring” in a series of incidents in the area. He said Cleveland police had been underfunded for many years.

He told BBC Radio 4: “We do suffer those metropolitan levels of crime, and yet comparatively our funding looks much more like a rural area, and it simply cannot continue like that. We’ve got to put resources where the demand is most high, and that is Cleveland, and that’s the message to ministers.”

On Thursday evening Alec Brown, the Labour leader of Redcar and Cleveland council, said more than 200 extra police officers had been, or would be, deployed from around the country to support Cleveland police.

Earlier he said people deserved to “feel safe in their own homes”.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the government would offer “all of the support that the authorities need” after the incidents. On a visit to south Wales, he told reporters it was “too early to jump to conclusions” about whether the Grangetown fire and the A66 crash were connected.

“The important thing [is] it’s a terribly tragic event that’s happened, with the loss of a young woman and her seven-year-old niece,” he said. “Utterly devastating. I’m sure there’s a whole community that is grieving.”

Inquests were formally opened into the deaths of the seven people in the A66 crash. The two police officers who died were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.

The Teesside area coroner, Paul Appleton, said that in the early hours of 22 August there was a collision on the A66 at South Bank between a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat. He told the hearing: “All occupants of both vehicles were sadly pronounced dead at the scene.”

Appleton said: “At this stage it is understood there had been a police pursuit of the Volkswagen Passat. It [the Passat] entered the A66 carriageway against the flow of traffic, at which stage the pursuit was aborted. A short time after … the Volkswagen Passat collided with a police vehicle which had not been directly involved in the prior pursuit.”

He said the provisional cause of death for Blades was head and neck injuries and for Clough was neck injuries.

Later, inquests were opened and adjourned into the deaths of the Passat occupants, named as Cole Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak.

The victims of the house fire have been named as Natalie McDonald and her niece Valentina Foster.

Local residents insisted their deaths had nothing to do with the A66 crash. McDonald’s brother Josh Kirton told reporters: “My sister was not involved with anything to do with gangs or the [crash on the] A66. That’s what makes this so senseless. There’s some terrible people in the world and now my sister and Valentina have gone.”

Cleveland police have arrested two men aged 23 and 31 on suspicion of murder in connection with the blaze. They remain in police custody.

Police also released details about two other crimes in the area but did not say if they could be linked. One was a report of a vehicle crashing into a wall at an empty property in South Bank in the early hours of Thursday. The other was an assault with a bladed weapon in Eston at midday on Thursday.

The five Labour Teesside MPs – Andy McDonald, Chris McDonald (Stockton North), Luke Myer (Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland), Jonathan Brash (Hartlepool) and Anna Turley (Redcar) – said they had met the policing and crime minister, Sarah Jones, to discuss the pressures being felt locally.

“These pressures did not emerge overnight,” they said. “They have built up over many years and were made significantly worse by the savage cuts during the austerity period.”

Students are being set up to fail by compulsory GCSE resits

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 16:38:05 GMT

Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article calling for mandatory exam resits to be scrapped in a first step towards education reform

I was delighted to read Polly Toynbee’s demolition of compulsory GCSE resits (How can we stop destroying the prospects of a generation? Scrapping compulsory GCSE resits will be a start, 24 August). Of course, level 2 qualifications in maths and English should be accessible to all school leavers who need them. However, the depressing treadmill of resitting resits is thin educational gruel and Michael Gove should be ashamed for espousing such a killjoy policy.

As a governor at a large further education college in Bedford, I find it depressing to receive data at every single board meeting focusing on GCSE resit results for thousands of students who “failed” maths and English just a few months previously. Speaking to students and staff, it is apparent that resitting exams is counterproductive. Compulsory GCSE resits are a negative learning experience, offering no reflection on how to improve. In most cases students merely fail again.

It does not have to be this way. The potential stepping-stone qualifications are a positive idea and lessons from the past need to be considered. I began my career teaching mature students (aged 17 to 70) GCSE English at evening classes in the 1980s. We did not force them to do the same course over and over. Rather, we offered “mature” syllabuses, avoiding the repetition of school failure and using more creative approaches to learning and assessment. It is no surprise that the number of those not in education, employment or training has risen in an age of compulsory resits. John ButcherEmeritus professor of inclusive teaching in higher education, The Open University

Polly Toynbee’s excellent article describes just how damaging our exam system has become. Failing the 11-plus in 1960, when only one boy from my large working-class West Yorkshire primary school class passed, negatively affected the rest of my life. I eventually got to university, but was unable to do a BA, which I wanted to do, because of a lack of an O-level foreign language – it was not taught at my school. I struggled through a BSc.

I subsequently had a career as a secondary school teacher and have been appalled by how Tory governments negatively affected the educational experience of students from the late 1980s, starting with the absurd “quart in a pint pot” Kenneth Baker national curriculum and marketisation of schooling. More recently, the manic Michael Gove “reforms” have destroyed local education authority control and accountability, wasted colossal amounts of money on “free schools” and academy chain bureaucracies, imposed a punitive inspection system, narrowed the 14-16 curriculum and turbocharged norm-referenced overassessment. All these changes have been driven by a nostalgia for a selective and academic elitist education that is unsuited to modern times.

The third of students unable to pass maths and English GCSE and condemned to the resit treadmill are victims of Tory arrogance and folly, and will feel this “failure” just as I did with the “stupid” (invoking Govian terminology) 11-plus for the rest of their lives. Philip WoodKidlington, Oxfordshire

Polly Toynbee’s article should be read alongside Pete Crockett’s letter on the same date (Let’s focus on what people with special needs can do, rather than what they can’t, 24 August). Grades 1 to 3 are not “fails” for many students with additional needs – they are successes, built on the hard work of students, teachers and teaching assistants, often against the odds. Ruth EversleyPaulton, Somerset

We need new reservoirs – and it’s a job for the state, not private companies

Pete Ford (Letters, 20 August) rightly reminds us that “The Victorians … built reservoirs, aqueducts and local water-storage infrastructure.” But who were these “Victorians”? Generally speaking, they were local councillors and their professional engineers.

Taking my own town as an example, within 40 years of its incorporation as a borough in 1868 it had built five new reservoirs, as well as taking over others previously provided by ad hoc groups of commissioners, with water delivered through 240 miles of mains. By 1897 it was one of 610 urban councils with their own water undertakings.

As recently as 1971, Queen Elizabeth opened Scammonden dam (a joint project of Huddersfield Corporation Waterworks and the Ministry of Transport, which also carries the trans-Pennine M62 motorway). With new reservoirs now urgently needed, perhaps the Burnham government will see this once again as an appropriate role for mayors and combined authorities, rather than failing private companies. David GriffithsHuddersfield, West Yorkshire

I so agree with Sheila Carey-Thomas’s suggestion that communal underground water storage could be incorporated into new housing estates to take advantage of our wet springs (Letters, 20 August).

Similarly, heat-exchange shafts could be sunk and shared to tap heat from underground. Surely, too, by locating any planned datacentres near new housing estates, the cooling water could be piped to centrally heat the houses, rather than wasted. All of the above could be incorporated into estates during the construction phase without adding hugely to the cost of each individual house. Kevin WhatelyAspley Heath, Bedfordshire

Government must prioritise heat pump installation to tackle climate chaos

It is hardly surprising that many who were optimistic and supportive of Andy Burnham becoming prime minister, but who also prioritised tackling climate chaos, are becoming increasingly unsure about him, given his tardiness in emphasising this threat as an overriding policy objective (Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved, 19 August).

One of the problems he faces is that the political debate around energy is obsessed with relatively short-term fossil fuel supplies. Instead, the focus should be on drastically and rapidly cutting fossil fuel use in a way that reduces bills and generates secure jobs through a devolved energy programme for every postcode.

Key to this must be a public commitment to rapidly “get off gas”. This must prioritise a rapid nationwide programme of increasing the installation of heat and cooling pumps in all properties and making buildings more energy-efficient.

An immediate source of labour could come from giving work to existing workers made redundant by Keir Starmer’s ill-thought-out policy to cut energy bills by dropping investment in energy saving. Nothing concrete was put in its place and Andrew Warren, chair of the British Energy Efficiency Federation, has pointed out that a staggering 12,100 skilled professionals have already been made redundant, with a further 80,000 estimated to be made redundant in the next 12 months.

A final social advantage to this approach would be that the future labour force could come from apprenticeships that create the skilled workers required and would help tackle today’s youth unemployment problem. Colin HinesConvener, Green New Deal Group

Surprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematicians

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 16:37:42 GMT

Whether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI depends on what it is that society values in the human intellect, writes Dr Henry Bradford

I share Kasra Rafi and Bruce Schneier’s impression that recent mathematical breakthroughs by AI consist in clever recombination of existing ideas, not development of truly novel theory (No, AI doesn’t mean the end of mathematics – at least not yet, 25 August). The question is: what happens to mathematics if this changes?

Like many mathematicians, I have done much soul-searching in recent weeks, especially since a key problem in my own field of group theory (the existence of non-sofic groups) was solved this month by OpenAI’s Astra model. Astra’s proof consists largely in a slight twist on theorems by my colleagues Gabor Kun and Andreas Thom. That said, even a few months ago I would have found the idea that AI was capable of such a breakthrough incredible, so it seems foolhardy now to bet against AIs achieving superhuman capabilities in all areas of mathematical thought in the coming years.

This forces the question: what is the purpose of mathematical research? Is it simply to prove new theorems (at which task future AIs may be far better than humans)? The great American mathematician Bill Thurston thought not: in his 1994 essay On Proof and Progress in Mathematics, he wrote that mathematicians “discover ... that what they really want is usually not some collection of ‘answers’ – what they want is understanding”. In other words, mathematics consists in the ideas living in human brains, with new theorems serving as markers for our progress in understanding and sharing these ideas.

This matters, because the development of AI will stimulate debate about the value of mathematics as practised by human beings. If AI can churn out research papers faster and cheaper than humans, then administrators within cash-strapped universities will surely be tempted to regard their mathematical researchers as superfluous. On Thurston’s view, this would be a mistake, because the value of those researchers’ work consists less in the papers they write than in their contributions to the preservation and furtherance of mathematical knowledge among people.

Whether mathematics thrives or perishes in the age of AI is not merely a technical question about the capabilities of future machine intelligences. It is a collective decision that society makes about what it is in the human intellect that we choose to value. Dr Henry BradfordFellow of mathematics, Christ’s College, University of Cambridge

Britain’s Josh Tarling pulls out of event mid-stage

Tadej Pogacar outsprinted Enric Mas to claim victory in stage six of the Vuelta a España on Thursday, his third stage win of the race.

The Slovenian and Mas outshone their rivals on the gravel in the stage’s final climb, and Pogacar held off the Spaniard when arriving in Castellón de la Plana to extend his general classification lead. The five-time Tour de France winner Pogacar, the overwhelming favourite for the Vuelta, is aiming to complete a Grand Tour grand slam.

Ramses Debruyne grabbed the third spot on the podium, finishing in a group including Primoz Roglic, Richard Carapaz and Felix Gall, 46 seconds behind the leaders. UAE Team Emirates’ Pogacar, who had a brief scare as he came off the road on the final descent, now leads Movistar’s Mas by 3min 34sec and his compatriot Roglic by 4min 21sec overall.

There was a big battle to get into the break but it took a long time for an escape to form. Finally 15 riders moved clear and established a two-and-a-half minute gap on the peloton with 40km remaining. The final climb of Puerto El Bartolo split up the break and then peeled on to a gravel road, where Pogacar attacked and picked off the riders ahead of him. Mas was hot on his tail and the Spaniard dug deep to charge past Pogacar and come over the top of the climb ahead. Pogacar came off the road and into a grassy section after misjudging a corner, but he swiftly recovered to get back on Mas’s trail. The four-time Vuelta winner Roglic, Gall and Debruyne were chasing the front two, but Pogacar and Mas worked well together to keep their advantage. Pogacar led out towards the finish line and Mas could not catch him.

It was a bad day for Oscar Onley, who lost more than a minute and a half on his general classification rivals.

Earlier in the day, the Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling abandoned the race with around 120km of the stage left, with his team not giving a reason. The Briton’s brother Finlay Tarling died in the Tour of Portugal after a crash with a vehicle, but Josh decided to race in Spain in honour of his sibling. “Josh Tarling’s brave La Vuelta has come to an end and he’s decided to stop. We couldn’t be prouder,” said Netcompany Ineos on social media.

Tarling produced a strong display in the first stage individual time trial, coming third behind Pogacar and Ethan Hayter.

Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 16:12:15 GMT

Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide

From the archive:

Fourteen years a fugitive: the hunt for the Butcher of Bosnia

Ratko Mladić will die in jail. But go to Bosnia: you’ll see that he won

Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague.

Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.

Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.

A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day.

“Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.

Described by the former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction, Mladić was one of the most notorious figures of the war that killed more than 100,000 people and left more than 1 million homeless.

He commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of Bosnian Muslim people and had boasted of being a “Serbian god”.

The news of Mladić’s death was first broken on Serbian state television after his son, Darko, had spoken earlier about his father’s declining health.

Mladić was sentenced by a UN tribunal to life imprisonment in 2017 over genocide and war crimes committed during Bosnia’s 1990s war. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run.

The slaughter in Srebrenica was the culmination of a brutal war that had lasted more than three ⁠years, during which Mladić oversaw the siege of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, which was pounded daily by artillery, tank and sniper fire, killing 10,000 people.

The goal of the Serbian leadership, which Mladić was tasked with implementing – as determined ⁠by the UN’s international criminal tribunal for ⁠the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) – was the forcible expulsion of ​Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian land for the creation of a greater Serbia.

The tribunal found that Mladić, together with the late Serbian president Slobodan Milošević and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadžić, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

“I do not recognise this court,” Mladić said at an ⁠ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced, he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”

The Serbian campaign culminated in the horror of Srebrenica when, after the withdrawal of Dutch UN peacekeeping forces, thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves.

Mladić had the siege filmed to show him praising his “lads” and haranguing the UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands.

“We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who had once held the area as part ‌of the Ottoman empire.

The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for slaughter.

after newsletter promotion

When Nato tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.

The son of a second world war partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was, according to his family, born in March 1943 in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, putting his age at death at 83 (though official documents recorded his date of birth a year earlier, in 1942).

Mladić was an officer in the communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991.

When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was chosen to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down, as 22,000 troops with the UN Protection Force stood by, more or less helplessly, under orders not to take sides.

A combination of western pressure, Nato strikes and covert US arms and training for Croats and ⁠Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladić’s army. After the war, Mladić went into hiding, with the reformists ruling post-conflict Serbia not daring ​to move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

Mladić continued to insist he was “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. He had a heart ​attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.

This month, a UN doctor said Mladić’s death “may occur at any time”, possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected.

Munira Subašić, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. “Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans,” Subašić said. But while 31 years later mothers of victims were “still carrying the pain in our souls … we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladić was a hero for the Serbs”.

Elizabeth Evenson, the international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander found guilty of genocide, including the massacre of up to 8,000 Bosnian men and boys after the fall of Srebrenica, Bosnia, in July 1995, is a reminder of the ongoing need for justice, truth, and reparations in the western Balkans.

“Full accountability for such terrible crimes, in Bosnia and elsewhere, demands commitment by governments to justice, even decades after the events themselves.”

The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.

The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.

The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.

The navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. In a statement to MS Now about the decision to pursue a non-judicial punishment for the sailor, a navy official said that “the Navy is fully committed to the health and wellbeing of every Sailor”.

“We strive to foster environments that support mental health by removing barriers to seeking help, increasing awareness of resources, and taking appropriate action when someone is in need,” they added. “Mental health resources are available to our Sailors 24/7, and asking for help is a sign of strength.”

The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.

Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.
