Food allergies when flying are no joke. That’s why nuts should be banned on planes

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 15:00:32 GMT

People with allergies must be able to travel without fear, and a compassionate society should respect that

What are you most scared of? Perhaps snakes send a chill down your spine. Or heights leave your knees weak. Peanuts may sound like an odd source of phobia, but they have taken on an absurd bogeyman quality for me since my daughter was taken to hospital by ambulance after eating peanut butter when she was six months old. Just the sight of a bowl on a pub bar, or their shells discarded on the pavement, can raise my heart rate – even when I’m not with her.

Nowhere is the sight of peanuts more confronting than at 30,000ft, especially now when millions are jetting back from their holidays. Travelling with a severely allergic child can be a nightmare for all sorts of reasons, but the idea you could be sat next to a passenger consuming the very thing that has hospitalised them is its own kind of hell.

Most airlines will make an announcement asking passengers to avoid consuming nuts if you let them know that somebody in your party has a severe nut allergy. But I brace for impact when these announcements are piped out. On almost every flight there is at least one passenger who sighs or makes some inane comment, loud enough for everyone to hear, about how annoying it is.

Oh, I’m sorry – is not being able to eat nuts for a few hours inconveniencing you? Does one passenger’s desire to consume peanut M&M’s trump someone else’s right to stay alive? I didn’t realise the right to eat nuts was a civil liberties issue. How utterly absurd.

And yet, people get disproportionately upset about being told not to eat things. Chloë Dickson, who runs the Instagram account peanutfreezone, recently posted a horrifying video of her experience flying with a severe peanut allergy and a man behind her responding, “Really?” to an announcement asking passengers not to eat nuts. He “then proceeded to make comments throughout the entire journey about eating peanuts around me, along with two other people nearby,” the caption reads.

I am mystified by this mean-spiritedness. Allergies are not a lifestyle choice but a medical condition. And yet, they seem to inspire a lack of empathy in the public consciousness. Perhaps it’s due to a misunderstanding of what allergy actually is. For people such as Chloe and my daughter, we’re not talking about skin irritation or a dodgy stomach, however unpleasant that might be. Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can affect multiple body systems and commonly impacts breathing or consciousness. The primary treatment is adrenaline via an EpiPen and it requires immediate medical attention.

But I suspect many people do know what severe allergy can look like, they just think this level of caution is overblown and are frustrated by having to make accommodations. Take a look at some of the comments under Chloë’s post and you’ll see what I mean. They are staggering in their stupidity. “Fly private or DON’T FLY AT ALL. Don’t make other people’s lives miserable just to please yours!” one reads. “I travel with a bag of peanuts for these moments,” says another. There really are people who seem to believe that those with allergies should just not travel at all. Or not go out to eat. Or not be able to participate fully in life outside their own homes. I wonder if they would feel that way if it was their children who were diagnosed.

Allergic people can’t be wrapped in cotton wool. Some of the best advice I got when my daughter was small, from an angelic NHS allergy nurse, was that you do your very best to keep her safe and then you carry EpiPens as your insurance policy. That’s given me lots of comfort over the years when gauging risk. But when you’re trapped in a metal tube in the sky with no possibility of medical attention, the stakes feel much higher.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

What scares allergic people most is not necessarily the risk of an airborne reaction, which is vanishingly rare, it’s the possibility of cross-contamination. That peanut dust on someone’s fingers could then spread to the tray table, the seat, perhaps the toilet door. That a rogue peanut from a previous flight has fallen between the seats or touched the seatbelt. On quick turnaround budget airlines with minimal cleaning, the risk you may come into contact with the allergen starts to feel frighteningly high. And even tiny amounts of nut protein can trigger a life-threatening reaction for some people.

Banning nuts on planes seems like a no-brainer. And I say nuts because of all the common allergens, they are the least likely to be outgrown in childhood and have a higher rate of causing severe reactions. That means telling passengers not to bring nut products on board. But even just stopping the practice of serving them on flights would drastically reduce the risk of cross-contamination when travelling. And it would take the pressure off anxious, allergic passengers to advocate for their safety. Of course, no ban could be watertight, which is why airlines should make a blanket rule that anyone with severe allergy should be offered priority boarding to clean their own seats before takeoff as a precaution.

Allergic people shouldn’t have to justify their medical needs to people who don’t understand them. Banning nuts on planes could send an important message to the broader public. That people with allergies should be able to travel without fear. That compassionate societies make accommodations.

Lucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editor

What caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet – and how does a glacier collapse?

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 14:53:58 GMT

A glacial collapse registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border on Wednesday morning

Hundreds of people have died in catastrophic flash floods in Nepal. Here’s what we know so far about what caused the disaster.

On Wednesday morning local time, a landslide of ice and rock resulted in a torrent of mud, water and debris bursting the banks of the Trishuli River, also known as the Bhotekoshi, which runs between China and Nepal. Homes, roads, bridges and power plants were swept away.

Experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said water levels on the Trishuli River rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Trishuli, was most affected, they said.

Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, told the country’s parliament on Wednesday that initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the ⁠area that triggered a landslide.

However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) subsequently said that a glacial collapse was responsible for the seismic event and for the flooding itself.

The USGS noted that the glacial collapse had registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, occurring near the border between Nepal and China at 8.37am local time on Wednesday.

According to Daniel Shugar, a geomorphologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary in Canada, initial satellite analysis showed a 0.2 sq km chunk of ice had “collapsed about 1.2km vertically”.

“What I can see in … satellite imagery from Planet Labs, the lower part of a glacier broke off at about 5,200 metres and crashed on to the valley floor about 1,200 metres below,” he ​said.

The imagery seemed to show that a large ‌amount of snow had melted in the 24 hours prior to the disaster, he said. “Some of the glaciers in the valley were covered in snow yesterday and today they are mostly bare ice. So in other words (and I haven’t seen any weather station data yet), it was probably warm.”

Shugar said construction could also be a factor.

Prof Andrew Mackintosh, a glaciologist at Monash University in Melbourne, said it was unclear whether the collapse was isolated to the glacier, or was the “whole mountainside collapsing that included part of the glacier”.

“When a glacier of that scale collapses, it generates a lot of water, and then there’s a cascading sequence of events … where the water and the sediment combine and bulks up and creates the flood.”

“These sorts of large glacier collapses are really shocking,” Mackintosh said. “It’s hard as a glaciologist not be alarmed by these events that seem different to what we’ve observed previously.”

However, he said there had been “so few of these documented that we’re not really able to make very clear statements about the specific relationship between glacier collapse and climate change yet”. Scientists do, however, “have very high confidence in the relationship between glacier retreat and climate change”.

“We also know that mountain permafrost is degrading under a warming climate,” Mackintosh added. He described permafrost, ground that is frozen year round, as being akin to a “glue that holds the rock and sometimes adjacent glaciers … together on very steep slopes”.

The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods.

The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating. An assessment published that year found that the Hindu Kush Himalayan glaciers had disappeared 65% faster between 2011 and 2020 than in the previous decade.

In 2021, a Himalayan glacier broke off and caused flash flooding in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, leaving 200 people dead or missing. Subsequent research suggested that a 27m-cubic-metre avalanche of rock and glacier ice had transformed into “an extraordinarily large and mobile debris flow”.

Though not thought to be a cause of the August 2026 event, mountain areas are also at risk of “glacial lake outburst floods”.

Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached.

Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist, polar engineer and associate professor at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia, said: “With a warming climate, glaciers recede, ice becomes water, that water gets trapped.”

More than 12,000 deaths have already been attributed to such floods globally. According to the UN, Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, of which 21 are considered potentially dangerous.

With Reuters and Associated Press

Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 14:47:20 GMT

Burnham has nothing to hide as he prepares to meet president he once called poisonous. It may actually win him more respect

It makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago, Keir Starmer was falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him.

Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war.

No such misgivings for Andy Burnham. This week, the prime minister was reminded that when he had been mayor of Greater Manchester, he had said The Donald wouldn’t be welcome in his city and that he could take his poisonous politics elsewhere. Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist.

Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word.

This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had been mayor of “some town”. To be fair to Agent Orange, it’s quite likely he had never heard of Manchester before. Neither geography nor an interest in other people have ever been his strongest suits. All he had known about Andy was that he was “extremely liberal”. Which in Maga language is the same as saying he’s a “Commy bastard”.

So here was Burnham’s deal. He wasn’t planning to go out of his way to insult the US president, but neither would he be offering unexpurgated sycophancy. Instead, we would be getting a very British type of pragmatism. He would do what was necessary in the UK’s interest but not much more. They would be polite and try not to accentuate their differences, but there would be no pretence of any lasting friendship. Just stick to the matters in hand and get the hell out. After New York, Andy wouldn’t be sending weekly WhatsApps. Out of sight, out of mind.

Weirdly, this performative show of an ersatz friendship – the US and UK are meant to be more or less on the same side, after all – is likely to be far more effective than Keir’s more needy approach. Because this is the type of language The Donald understands. Although he craves the fawning, he has no respect for those who offer it. He takes it as a sign of weakness. Equally, no amount of flattery is ever enough. There is a hole in Trump’s psyche that can never be filled.

With Burnham, there is going to be more a meeting of equals. Two world leaders who are doing what it takes to get along with each other. It’s as close to respect as a sociopath like Trump can get. Andy hasn’t taken a backward step, or attempted to deny his previous comments. More that that was then and this was now. Just get used to it.

You can say one thing one day and the opposite the next. It’s up to the other person to work out which one was the truth. Or maybe neither, or maybe both. After all, that’s precisely what The Donald does. Contradiction is his modus operandi. And it’s got him to the White House. So if it works for Trump, why not for Burnham? Sincerity can be an overrated virtue for a world leader. You don’t always need a Love, Actually moment to make your feelings known.

“So I’m looking forward, actually, to my first meeting [with Trump],” said Andy. And he probably is. His cards are on the table and he has nothing to hide. Plus, he has a sense of humour and self-deprecation, which also might confuse the US president, who has neither.

It also feels as if there’s less at stake with this meeting than there was with many of Starmer’s. Back in the early days of Trump’s presidency, it was as if much of the world was holding its breath for what he might do next. Now, not so much. We’ve all learned to adapt to The Donald. Even to his never-ending war with Iran, which has jacked up the cost of living. All his bad habits are now priced in. And suddenly he looks more vulnerable. A man who has found the world doesn’t automatically bend to his will. A man who is under pressure on the domestic front, with many Americans fed up with his foreign wars and angry at the cost of petrol (never get between an American and their car). A president facing tricky midterm elections and in danger of becoming a lame duck.

For Burnham, it’s also the home front that is occupying most of his attention. Good vibes are a decent start, but sooner or later he has to do something different to Starmer while boxing himself in with the same fiscal rules. So who knows? The meeting between Andy and The Donald may be less tricky than first imagined. A welcome distraction for both of them.

Uefa preparing to bring criminal claims against Gianni Infantino over World Cup sale

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 14:06:37 GMT

Uefa says claims will be made in Switzerland

It says claims relate to alleged criminal mismanagement

Uefa is preparing to make a criminal complaint against Gianni Infantino for alleged “criminal mismanagement” in connection with his failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan and has applied for the release of documents related to its conception.

In an explosive escalation of the war engulfing football’s governing bodies, Uefa has made separate applications in the United States for information, including from Fifa and the investment firm Thrive Capital.

The request explains Uefa and other interested parties are “preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possible other Fifa officials and advisers for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code”.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Thrive Capital, led by Joshua Kushner, was to be the lead investor in Infantino’s plan. Uefa has used a “section 1782” order in seeking release of the relevant documents. Such a request lets an interested party in a foreign legal proceeding ask for discovery of information from an entity based in the US.

The court documents pay particular attention to the “absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn” (£14.7bn) implied by Infantino’s scheme to sell a 20% chunk of Fifa tournaments for $4.2bn. The figure is claimed to be “neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer”.

Uefa claims “a valuation exceeding $30bn is readily supportable” through assessment of Fifa’s financial performance and market conditions. Additionally, comparisons are drawn with the deal Infantino pursued in 2018 with a consortium led by the Japanese firm SoftBank. The submission points out that the proposal, which was dropped, would have committed about $25bn for a 12-year interest in the Nations League and an expanded Club World Cup.

Infantino is accused of a “stunning dereliction of duty” in sidelining the Fifa Council when tabling the plan. In a surgical walk-through of what is known about FFE’s conception and its withdrawal, the documents also highlight the expedited timeline member associations were given to back the scheme and the $40m “inducement” they were offered to do so.

This month Uefa’s lawyers had told Infantino and Fifa to “take immediate steps to identify, locate and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or Fifa’s possession, custody, or control”. They had named 14 executives who were required to “specifically preserve all such materials in their possession, custody, or control”.

On Thursday Uefa filed a request for discovery in US District Court for the Eastern District of New York, which if granted would enable it to subpoena Kushner and Thrive for documents relating to Fifa’s FFE proposal, and allow Uefa attorneys to depose Kushner.

In a 56-page filing that contains a section headlined “the enduring history of corruption among Fifa officials”, Uefa’s attorneys describe FFE as “a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from Fifa’s most valuable assets to the detriment of Fifa, its members, and other parties within the football family”.

Uefa clarifies that “neither Thrive nor Kushner is an anticipated defendant in the contemplated Swiss criminal proceeding”.

Uefa’s executive committee and about 35 presidents of its members were informed of the latest developments at a meeting in Monte Carlo on Thursday, shortly before the Champions League draw. It was also confirmed that, as reported by the Guardian, the proposed boycott of Fifa tournaments has been shelved after Fifa provided the necessary assurances that no version of FFE would be tabled. “This position will remain under constant review and may be reconsidered immediately if circumstances so require,” Uefa said.

The statement said Uefa proposed to explore using funds from Fifa’s reserves, estimated to total about $5bn, to benefit its member associations. Uefa also confirmed its intention to ensure Infantino faces an opponent if he is still in position when the election for Fifa’s leadership is held in March.

“Should the current Fifa president nevertheless seek another mandate, Uefa will join forces with its partner confederations to ensure that member associations are offered a credible alternative – one committed to integrity, accountability, development and genuine institutional change,” it said.

Fifa and Thrive Capital have been contacted for comment.

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 14:00:16 GMT

The actor on which star he’d devour first on a lifeboat, why he prefers pigeons to dogs and how Trainspotting put the Scottish accent on the map

You’re stranded on a lifeboat with Ewan McGregor, Ewen Bremner, Jonny Lee Miller, Kevin McKidd, Peter Mullan, James Cosmo, Keith Allen and Irvine Welsh. Who do you eat first? DarkAnaemicI77I suppose you have to think about who’s the healthiest and has looked after their body best. I reckon Ewan would be a wee bit too chewy, and Irvine a wee bit pickled. Did you really not like Zippy the West Highland terrier who played Wee Jock in Hamish Macbeth? Campbell97

I was in the Youth Opportunities Programme touring theatre company at Glasgow Arts Centre shortly after you in the early 80s and it shaped my future. What was it like to look in the mirror and see John Lennon staring back at you in Yesterday? MegMayI don’t particularly look like John Lennon, but apparently there’s something about the bridge of my nose that looks a bit like his, which is what the wonderful prosthetics people focused on. PettyDabblerI’ve been phenomenally lucky to work with some fantastic directors such as Ken Loach, Danny Boyle and Alan Parker, who you would be foolish not to learn from. Directing myself in The Legend of Barney Thomson was certainly different to just acting, because directors have 500 fires to put out each day, so I was thinking more about the directing than the performance.

Your performance as Albie Kinsella in Cracker, a man traumatised by Hillsborough, was terrifying and incredibly moving. How did you go about creating him? LiffeyBearI remember watching the Liverpool game at Hillsborough on TV back in 1989, but not fully appreciating what had happened. Certainly, the way the Sun reported it was disgusting, accusing Liverpool fans of pissing on police officers and stuff like that. I took those terrible stories and the behaviour of the police as my starting point, along with the anger people across Liverpool felt at what had happened.

We’d come on, take off our ties, the audience would get excited and then we would cut for half an hour to set up the next shot. We took off our shirts, then our hats. NepthsolemI worked in Scottish theatre for years and later had my own theatre company. But then TV and film came into my life and I’ve gone down that road ever since. I wouldn’t want to short-change the audience by going into a piece that I had to do twice a day for months, and that I didn’t really love.

What happened to you recommending new bands every week on your Saturday Tunes on Twitter/X? FFreundThat began during the pandemic. I know a lot of young musicians through my kids, and I became acutely aware that there were no gigs, no money, no music. Did Blur get cross when you were in an Oasis video? TopTrampYes. I know Damon very well. Afterwards, he said: “Why did you do that? They recorded a bit of Little By Little – the video I’m in – and when they showed me, it almost made me cry, too.

It’s shite being Scottish! Discuss. TheReturnOfDrWhatsonIt’s shite being from any country really, isn’t it? I think it depends on your lot in life. You could equally say it’s beautiful and fantastic being Scottish. You see that when the Scottish national team play, the pride people have – they just love being Scottish. But it depends on your social circumstances. If life is socially difficult for you, then of course it’s shite being Scottish. But equally, it can be a brilliant thing, too.

The best mattress for side sleepers – and how to choose one, according to doctors and osteopaths

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 14:00:16 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Do you need a soft mattress if you sleep on your side, or are firm models better for your back? And what about pillows? Here’s what the experts say

The best mattresses, tested The best mattresses for back pain

Most of us, me included, sleep on our sides. Drooling into your pillow and giving yourself a dead arm may not be as photogenic as Sleeping Beauty lying prettily on her back, but it’s probably better for you. Studies have found that sleeping on your left side can help reduce snoring, sleep apnoea and acid reflux, and the experts I spoke to for this article say side sleeping is good for your back and your sleep.

Side sleeping brings its challenges, though, and I don’t just mean the drool. The curves of your body need somewhere to go. If your mattress isn’t cushioning your hips and shoulders, or your knees are pressing against each other, you may struggle to sleep well and experience aches and pains. An overly soft surface can also cause problems, as you’ll know if you’ve ever spent the night on a friend’s concave sofa.

To find out why, I asked osteopaths, doctors and sleep experts what’s going on at a musculoskeletal level when you spend the night snoozing on your side. Here, I’ll reveal how their advice can help you find your ideal mattress – and the pillow that’ll make it even more comfy.

As a side sleeper, you’re already doing well. “It’s the best sleeping position for back pain, as it encourages a neutral spine,” says Michael Fatica, osteopath and co-founder of the Back in Shape programme for pain relief. It doesn’t guarantee it, though.

To demonstrate, lie on the floor. First lie flat on your back, and then on your side in your usual sleeping position. When you’re on your side, your “pressure points” – hips, shoulders and knees – bear more load than when you’re on your back, and this pushes your spine into a curve instead of letting it lie straight, or “aligned”.

“Spinal alignment is even more crucial for side sleepers,” says Dr Deborah Lee, who works with online pharmacy Dr Fox and bed retailer Comfybedss. “On your side, there’s a natural tendency for the spine to curve or twist if the mattress isn’t providing the right support. This contributes to backache, neck soreness and general disrupted sleep, affecting your mood and energy levels the next day.”

Your first priority, then, is to make sure you have enough cushioning to accommodate your pressure points. “If your hips can sink a little bit [into the mattress], that helps to keep your spine steady,” says Fatica. “Women may need a softer or a more forgiving mattress, because they tend to have a more exaggerated hips-to-waist ratio than a guy. One of the things we suggest to patients, especially women, is to put a little towel or cushion in their side at waist level to even out their spine if their mattress is too hard.”

Too much cushioning is not the answer, though. “Don’t go to the opposite extreme and buy a super-soft mattress,” says Barry Rickhuss, sleep product specialist at Mattress Next Day. “If your shoulders and hips are sinking too deeply, that pulls your spine out of alignment, too.”

All the experts I spoke to recommended a medium-firm mattress for side sleepers. As I’ve discovered by testing dozens of mattresses, though, that description is a broad church. A couple of “medium-firm” models were so firm they gave me lumbar (lower back) pain, and one or two were so soft they left me with neck ache because my neck was craning upwards on to my relatively firm pillow. Rather than trust the medium-firm tag, try a mattress for yourself.

Start with your own mattress, to see if it’s still working for you. Lie on it in your usual sleeping position and ask someone to look at your back. “They’ll be able to see if your pelvis is sitting too high or low and putting a bend in your spine,” says Fatica. If your spine is neutral, it should form a relatively straight line from your neck through your back to your pelvis when viewed from behind. If your tailbone curves up, the mattress is too firm. If your bum sinks, it’s too soft.

It’s useful to be able to lie on a mattress in a showroom, especially if you take your trusty spine-checker along to check for that line when you’re lying down, but a two-minute test isn’t really long enough to judge a mattress. “You might lie down and say, ‘oh, this is comfy’,” says Fatica, “but will it be comfy after eight hours? A lot of mattresses now come with long trial periods, and that tends to be the best approach.”

Most of the best mattresses we’ve tested have free trial of 100 nights or more, and a couple (such as the Simba Hybrid Pro below) stretch to double that. In my experience the brands keep their word on these trials, collecting your mattress for free if you don’t get along with it. Just make sure to keep it in good condition: a mattress protector is essential during any trial period.

Hybrid mattresses proved particularly popular with the experts I spoke to. “A hybrid mattress, with traditional springs for support and a layer of foam for cushioning, offers the right amount of sink for your hips and shoulders when you sleep on your side,” says Rickhuss. A foam layer is also recommended by Hannah Hayden, mattress and bedding buyer at Dreams. “Memory foam is particularly effective in adapting to body contours and relieving pressure,” says Hayden, “although hybrids with a plush comfort layer provide good support while maintaining some responsiveness.”

The prices below reflect current bank holiday offers

Otty’s flagship hybrid mattress combines tall pocket springs with layers of foam to create a delicious balance of support and cushioning. As with most of the hybrids I’ve tested, the Otty is a “bed-in-a-box” mattress that comes vacuum-shrunk, so you can get a king or even a super king size up narrow stairs before you open it.

Read our full Otty Original Hybrid review

Simba’s luxurious hybrid mattress was love at first sleep for me. It was just soft enough to accommodate the curves of my small side-sleeping body, but had enough pushback to make my back feel well supported. It may be a little too soft for some side sleepers, but the 200-night free trial gives you ample time to find out.

Read our full Simba Hybrid Pro review

If you have a firm pocket-sprung mattress that’s still in good nick but need a little more cushioning, a mattress topper could prove to be an excellent buy. Simba’s topper contains a layer of micro-springs as well as foam, so it feels wonderfully responsive and robust. It comes with a 10-year guarantee, too.

For more, read our guide to the best mattress toppers

The way you lie in bed is an important factor when choosing a mattress, but not the only one. Your body size, for instance, has a big (or petite, if you like) impact on how firm your mattress should be. Generally speaking, the lighter you are, the less firmness you need, especially if you sleep on your side.

If you have joint pain, particularly at side-sleeping pressure points such as hips, shoulders and knees, you may find relief in a well-cushioned mattress. “Pressure relief should be a top priority when choosing a mattress [if you have joint pain],” says Lisa Artis, deputy CEO of the Sleep Charity, which partners with Simba. “Materials that adapt to your body’s shape can be particularly helpful.”

Memory foam is notably adaptive and pressure-relieving, although if you choose a foam mattress you’ll want to make sure it’s supportive enough for you. In my experience, soft and “sinky” memory foam is wonderful for relieving pain, but can aggravate lower back pain and neck ache if you sink too far into it. The best foam and hybrid mattresses have plenty of support in the form of pocket springs or dense support foam, especially if you’re a larger sleeper.

Adaptive foam is also brilliant at absorbing movement (motion isolation), so it’s a great choice if you share with someone who tosses and turns in bed. As a fidgety side sleeper who shares with another fidgety side sleeper, I can confirm that a sufficiently supportive foamy mattress can help prevent arguments as well as discomfort.

Memory foam cradles your body in a low-pressure way that almost feels like being suspended. The medium edition all-foam SmartCool left me craving more firmness, but it could be ideal for you if pressure relief is a priority.

Read our full Tempur Pro Plus SmartCool review

Panda’s 5cm memory foam topper is an excellent buy for adding softness to a mattress that feels too hard. It’s brilliant for motion isolation, too, and its cooling foam and bamboo fabric cover are designed to help control your body temperature when the nights get too warm.

Read our full Panda Bamboo mattress topper review

For more, read our guide to the best mattresses for back pain

Finding the perfect mattress and then slapping a lumpy old pillow on top is like covering a gourmet meal with ketchup. Sure, you might like ketchup (and you may love your lumpy old pillow), but it defeats the point. If you’re putting effort and money into getting the best mattress for your body, give your sleepy head the same honour, too.

It’s not just your head that benefits from a good pillow, or even just your head and neck, but your whole body – especially if you sleep on your side. “A pillow gives more than comfort; it provides support between your head and mattress,” says Louise Silver, a product technologist at the bed brand Feather & Black. “Side sleepers shouldn’t go without a pillow altogether, as it creates an immediate issue with alignment. When you lie on your side, there’s a natural gap between the ear and the outer shoulder. Without a pillow to support that space, the head drops down towards the mattress, the shoulder rolls forward and the spine curves out of its neutral position. This puts strain on your neck, shoulders and upper back, which can lead to stiffness, tension and poor-quality sleep over time.”

How should you choose the ideal pillow, then? “A pillow that’s too flat, particularly if you’ve overused it, can cause a drop and strain the neck muscles,” says Dr Deborah Lee. “A pillow that’s too thick can push the head upward, though, creating the same problem but in the opposite direction.

“Side sleepers should look for pillows labelled medium to firm, with enough loft to maintain the natural alignment,” says Lee. “Many side sleepers also find that placing a pillow between the knees can reduce hip and lower back strain.”

In his test to find the best pillows, Edward Munn hailed Otty’s memory foam pillow as “supportive and bouncy, but not excessively tall, which means it works best for those who sleep mainly on their back and side, as I do.”

If you find Otty’s pillow too boxy, perhaps because you’re on the small side like me, here’s a great idea from Emma: an adjustable pillow containing layers that you can add and remove until you find the ideal height for your neck and shoulder. The filling is microfibre rather than memory foam, so it feels a bit less dense and closer to the cloud-like sensation of feathers.

Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 13:58:33 GMT

Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure

Nobody likes to have the full plot of a movie spoiled before they’ve even seen it. However, sometimes this can be taken to the extreme. Take the new Paul Greengrass movie, The Uprising, for example. It is two weeks away from its US release and not only does nobody know the plot, but nobody seems to know what it is even about. Seriously, nobody at all. The film’s distributors just spent yesterday squabbling in public about whether Robin Hood was in it or not.

Here’s what we know so far. Initially, all the trailers and promotional materials made The Uprising look like a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that tore through England in 1381. And this was very exciting, since the revolt was a thrilling moment in history that has been bizarrely underserved by Hollywood over the years. Most exciting of all, though, it sounded like it fit exactly into Greengrass’s wheelhouse: full of action and realism and political awareness.

But that all changed this week, when the film’s US distributor, Focus Features, announced the film’s full title on social media. What had once simply been The Uprising was now The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood. It added a new synopsis, reading: “Set against the true events of the Uprising that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood, [Andrew Garfield’s character] forms an army of the people to face the King’s might in a fight for justice.”

Needless to say, this was both confusing and frustrating. Frustrating because it sounded like a historically grounded and socially relevant film would now contain a character best known for once being played by a cartoon fox, and confusing because the stories of Robin Hood were set during the reign of Richard the Lionheart, who died nearly two centuries before the Peasants’ Revolt took place.

Andrew Garfield’s character seemed to be at the centre of the mix-up. Officially credited as “The Ploughman”, we can assume that he has been named after William Langland’s poem Piers Plowman, which was written in the years leading up to the revolt. The poem is known for containing the first unambiguous literary reference to Robin Hood. It is also worth pointing out that, in 2022 when the film was first announced, The Uprising was set to be called The Hood.

Realistically, several things might have happened here. The first is that Greengrass took a deeply uncharacteristic swing while making this film, and decided to augment the story of Wat Tyler with a time-traveling Robin Hood, blazing into the future to help the downtrodden people of England in their hour of need. The second is that he’s suggesting the Peasants’ Revolt helped reshape a mythical figure into a symbol of working-class resistance, at which point the distributors figured, “Screw it, let’s just tell everyone that Robin Hood is in it.”

This backfired immediately. Not only because people were exasperated by the thought of yet another Robin Hood movie – not for nothing did this year’s A24 movie The Death of Robin Hood flop hard, recouping less than half of its production budget worldwide – but because the film’s UK distributor is adamant that the film has absolutely nothing to do with the guy at all.

Contacted by Metro yesterday, Entertainment Film Distributors issued a statement reading: “The Uprising is a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, not Robin Hood. The UK marketing campaign does not make any reference to Robin Hood. Marketing materials posted by other countries that may appear in the UK online and on social media referencing Robin Hood are not issued or approved by us.”

This article includes content hosted on platform. x. com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

What we’re left with is a film that urgently needs to define exactly what it is before it comes out. As things stand, somebody is almost certainly going to feel conned.

If the UK distributor is right, there will be those who hear this week’s new title, rush to the cinema in the hope of watching a Robin Hood film and leave disappointed because they were actually presented with a muddy meditation on class warfare based on a 700-year-old allegorical poem.

But if the US distributor is right, then there will be those who rush to the cinema to watch a historically rigorous reenactment of one of the most important moments in British history and leave disappointed because Garfield turns up in a DeLorean halfway through, winks directly at the camera and then gets off with a busty maiden.

The Uprising might be one of those things. It might be both. For all anyone knows, given the utter ineptitude of its own communications, it could even turn out to be Cloverfield 4 and climax with a scene where the peasants, the aristocrats, Robin Hood, King Arthur and Paddington Bear all team up to defeat a howling kaiju. At this point, who would even care?

AI-proof? Younger workers desert the digital world for traditional crafts

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 13:38:30 GMT

In a disrupted job market people are turning to heritage crafts such as bookbinding, metalwork and boatbuilding

It’s a bleak moment for young people entering the workforce for the first time. For decades, a university degree seemed to promise a stable career – but entry-level white-collar jobs across almost all sectors are being disrupted by AI. Budding accountants, software engineers and junior lawyers increasingly find themselves displaced by cheap automation.

Even creative fields are struggling against AI tech that can produce artwork, lengthy prose or complex design briefs in seconds.

But many young workers have responded by turning to what they see as “AI-proof” heritage crafts. These are the centuries-old, hands-on jobs, such as boat-making, metalwork or bookbinding, that require specialist knowledge built on creative judgment and dexterity, skills not yet mastered by AI.

Eryn Lawley, a 27-year-old politics graduate, said future-proofing her career meant walking away from the digital world. She is now a second-year bookbinder apprentice at Ludlow Bookbinders in Shropshire, learning a trade whose core techniques have not changed for centuries.

“Even just staring at a screen too long was bad for me,” she said. “I always wanted to do something more material, and I think there is something more inherently valuable to something when it is made by a person.”

The work at Ludlow is slow, detailed and tactile. The bookbinding process is almost entirely by hand, using Victorian-built presses, foil-blocking machines and glue brushes.

“People are discovering that, as everything is already decided for you by a computer or algorithm, being able to make or own something physically is good,”

Lawley said. “And it is very satisfying to repeat a task to perfection. It is meditative as a job so it is extremely low-cortisol.”

Paul Kidson, Ludlow chief executive and a fourth-generation bookbinder, said an influx of interest from young people represented a lifeline for a rapidly shrinking industry. He estimates there are now fewer than 50 handcraft-operating bookbinders in Britain today.

“British bookbinding has a terrific reputation across the world, but like so many things in the 50s, 60s and 70s, the training just started to dry up,” Kidson said. “All the formal apprentice schemes collapsed in the early 1980s, and the industry got no training at all.

“We have to train our own people because you can’t recruit at volume because there aren’t any [courses]. Fortunately there is now a desire among a lot of people to want to have the satisfaction of actually making something.”

There is no lack of commercial demand. High-end publishers are betting that shoppers will pay a premium for objects that are crafted by human hands. Joanna Reynolds, chief executive of the Folio Society book publisher – which partnered with Ludlow for a limited edition release of a Game of Thrones book – said the company rejected generative AI tools in its creative processes.

“We do not use AI in terms of our art,” she said. “We believe in the importance of supporting the creative world, and we know there is huge pressure on them at the moment. Their skills and their abilities need to be supported by as many people as possible.”

The number of young people hoping to fill these creative posts is growing rapidly. Cox London, a design house that specialises in artistic metalwork, started its apprenticeship scheme last year. Nicola Cox, a co-founder, said this year the company received more than 160 applications for two apprenticeship places.

“People want to make things and work with materials, [to] have that closeness with it,” she said. “There is AI-proofness about art that is made with someone’s hands. There is a real resonance in something that has a mark and the energy of human hands.”

For Lucky Emerson, an apprentice at Cox London, there is a “worrying feeling” that AI is taking over the creative world.

“The physicality of actually making things is incomparable, especially when people crave originality. Even though technology has advanced, handcrafted art is considered a lot more valuable and will always remain that way.”

Nazifa Tabassum, also an apprentice at Cox London, said she did not think AI would replace her work, but that it could change it.

“For me it isn’t just about making things with my hands,” she said. “It’s about continuously developing my skills, and using technology where it adds value, while still providing the expertise and craftsmanship that people can’t easily automate.

“I see AI as a tool that can assist, but not something that replaces, the satisfaction and value of skilled manual, handcrafted work.”At the National Theatre in London, technical apprenticeships span everything from IT to traditional wig-making, costume design, prop-making and metalwork.

“Our apprenticeships are partly about the need to create a more representative workforce, both for the National Theatre and for the [wider] creative sector,” said Kath Geraghty, head of technical qualifications.

“It is also about plugging the skill gap. These theatre crafts are dying out – our metalworkers are all over 50, wig-making as a skill is really dying. There’s a real need to create our own talent.

“And it’s always been about creating a skilled workforce for the wider creative sector beyond theatre, such as film, TV and broadcast.”

Sarah Ray-Dobson, a 27-year-old apprentice prop-maker at the National Theatre, said she felt her practice had been shielded from AI disruption that affected other creative pursuits.

“Everything I’ve been doing for the past two years is very hands-on,” she said. “At my level, it has not been affected by AI.”

But Geraghty adds that, like many employers, the National Theatre is struggling with the huge number of AI-generated applications for its apprenticeship programme.

“We used to think that 100 applicants was a popular apprenticeship,” she said. “In this most recent round of recruitment, we had 728 applications for one role.

“We haven’t yet worked out how to manage it, because it’s not viable for our staff to read 700 applications with care and attention. But the job market that young people are in is difficult, and they are applying for anything they can.”

An $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for it

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 13:11:16 GMT

This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world

Not many people would count paying $18bn they didn’t expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreement with 52 US attorneys general to settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children, and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts.

Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay will be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in its case coughing up too. The cash is chump change for Meta, which made around $60bn in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep us on its platforms.

Under-18s in the US will face a default two-hour daily limit on Facebook and Instagram, with access blocked overnight – unless a parent changes the setting. Teachers will be glad to hear notifications will be muted during school hours, while teenagers will be nagged as much by the platform itself as their parents about exactly how long they have spent staring at their screens.

All of these are significant changes that materially change how the company’s products work – and all of them should be welcomed. But in lots of ways, Meta has got off lightly with this agreement, both in what it’s been asked to do and the fine it must pay.

What the decision shows, just months after Meta chose to fight its corner in court, and lost significantly, is how the economics of fighting social media litigation have changed. This settlement signifies an important and deliberate shift in strategy. In August, Meta went to court in New Mexico – a decision that cost it dearly. The judge there ordered the firm to pay $942m and overhaul some protections for children – a decision it is appealing. The fact that Meta lost that case, and was found to have done wrong, was far more damaging than this week’s settlement without liability, even if the amounts involved were smaller. Still, thousands more cases involving social media addiction claims are still wending their way through US courts.

And chastened by a couple of losses, it looks – at least in this instance – like Meta has taken the approach that a pyrrhic victory is better than the risk of another real loss. Settlements without admission of fault avoid judgments and a legal situation that could quickly spiral out of control for Meta’s product offering.

While Meta has had to make significant changes to its platforms as a result of this week’s settlement, it still ultimately has control over what changes are made, and has sought to limit them to the bare minimum. Settling, however expensive, is a way of protecting its core business proposition.

Meta now faces a Hobson’s choice when it comes to litigation. It can gamble on a jury and risk vast damages, damaging internal disclosures and a judge deciding which parts of Instagram or Facebook must change. Or it can pay an eye-watering but manageable sum to settle, negotiate the product changes on its own terms and staunch the bleeding.

That $18bn is certainly more than most companies could pay, but it pales in comparison with the $1.5tn Meta’s own PR team warned the case could cost it had it gone through the courts – and the more realistic $200bn the prosecuting lawyers sought to squeeze from the firm. And even more than that, Meta has managed to make some of the bill somebody else’s problem. About a third of the settlement it has agreed to pay is conditional on TikTok and YouTube introducing similar restrictions and each making matching payments. Meta is publicly calling on both companies to sign up.

As this is a negotiated settlement – and one in which no one wins, but Meta certainly doesn’t lose – not everyone has been won over. While attorneys general from 48 US states agreed to Meta’s proposition, Florida’s representative has publicly rejected the deal and intends to continue pursuing Meta. James Uthmeier dismissed the settlement as “peanuts” and said “We’ll see them at trial.”

Nor is this necessarily just an American story. The settlement formally applies only to the participating US states and territories. A Meta spokesperson told me it already offers strong protections for teenagers elsewhere. It will watch how the new measures work before deciding what comes next internationally.

after newsletter promotion

But running substantially different versions of Facebook and Instagram around the world is hardly attractive. And Meta has now demonstrated putting these restrictions in place is possible. Given the drive towards child safety online in the UK and Australia, it seems likely that politicians will soon ask why American teenagers get them and children in their own countries don’t. The UK’s own Online Safety Act is a useful stick for the government to wield in this instance, adding extra leverage to bring those changes here, too.

And it’s that which may prove the settlement’s biggest consequence. Meta has paid billions to manage to duck liability in one court case. But in doing so, it may have opened up the possibility of change in a raft of other countries.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

‘I fight pain and fear with art’: how Yayoi Kusama blazed a trail for neurodivergent artists

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 12:42:26 GMT

The pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena Kalu

Yayoi Kusama – who has died at the age of 97 – was 10 when she first started experiencing vivid hallucinations consisting of visual and aural disturbances, which she described as “flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots”. A drawing from 1939, of a woman in a kimono assumed to be her mother, shows her obliterated by those dots; they would become Kusama’s artistic obsession. She hallucinated flowers, too. “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe”, she once said, when asked about that recurring motif. “I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”

For Kusama, art making was a means of survival. “I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live”, she said in a 2012 interview. In so doing, she became one of the most acclaimed and admired contemporary artists, staging happenings and influencing the pop art movement as a pioneering figure in the New York avant garde. Her exhibitions and major retrospectives draw huge crowds. In 2022, due to enormous public demand, Tate Modern in London extended her Infinity Mirror Rooms show for a whole extra year (it ended up running until 2024).

Kusama leaves a planet that is far more enlightened about mental illness and neurodivergence than that which she entered. Different ways of seeing are increasingly embraced by the art world, which is beginning to understand how the brilliant, beautiful diversity of the human brain can feed into groundbreaking artistic practice. Neurodivergent, disabled and autistic artists are nominated for major prizes, and last year Nnena Kalu, who is autistic and has a learning disability, won the Turner prize. Furthermore, artists such as Louis Wain, who was schizophrenic, and Andy Warhol – who had traits consistent with autism – are increasingly viewed through the lens of neurodiversity.

“Artists like Kusama, much like our own Nnena Kalu, have shown that great art does not come from a single source or follow a traditional route,” said a spokesperson for ActionSpace, a London organisation who support and facilitate work by learning disabled artists. “The art world is richer for it, and their work continues to challenge us to recognise and celebrate the many voices that shape it.”

Despite the historically unfair stigma of mental illness, Kusama was always vocal about her struggles and how they fed into her work, in the 1970s voluntarily checking herself into a mental-health facility in Tokyo and working in a studio nearby. Processing the “obliteration” she experienced involved repetitive ways of working – those signature dots and flowers covering everything including her own clothing – while her extraordinary infinity rooms installations of mirrors and lights took the concept of sensory overload and turned it into something magical and all-encompassing. In this way, we were granted a powerful glimpse through Kusama’s eyes.

“Kusama’s practice seemed to channel the intrinsic auditory, repetitive and hallucinatory compulsions that she experienced,” says Kate Adams, director and co-founder of Project Art Works, a collective of artists with complex needs, and their collaborators who were nominated for the Turner prize in 2021. “Rather than create an escape from these, her installations shaped and described for others a sometimes beautiful, sometimes overwhelming world of intensity, pattern and form.

“This has parallels with the way in which stimming, hyper focus and innate sensory sensitivities find a way into the rich practices of neurodivergent artists and makers,” she continues. Adams points out that mental illnesses such as OCD are not necessarily the same as neurodivergence – we should be wary of grouping them all together. There can be parallels though, in Adams’ words “when anxiety overwhelms wellbeing”. Often diagnoses can overlap.

This is true of my brother, who is profoundly autistic: non-verbal, with OCD. Although he is unable to tell me, I have always instinctively known that he sees the world differently. He had a childhood fascination with the way light is reflected on water, and his fear of the dark knots in the wood of the pine bathroom’s walls saw my mother frantically painting them over the moment she realised what was going on. That ASD comes with sensory differences has long been known in the autism community, but awareness has now reached a point where sensory rooms are cropping up in schools, hotels and airports. Exploring Kusama’s infinity rooms at Tate Modern with my son, who was then a baby, was a meaningful moment for me. The older children at his nursery had also been to visit, and for a while the walls were covered with pictures of dots that they had made as a tribute to Kusama.

Kusama often referenced how art had saved her, saying: “If it were not for art, I would have killed myself a long time ago.” Although disabled and neurodivergent artists still face major barriers, and still experience moments of sadness and despair that are shared by those of us that love them, Kusama’s work and enduring influence stand as a lasting tribute to the complex magnificence of human perception and experience.

A Britain of wildfires and flood risks: be sure, the climate crisis is real, and we will deal with it

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 12:05:25 GMT

Reform and the Conservatives are willing to mislead the public, but as environment secretary, I believe we must be honest – and act boldly

This long, hot summer has brought our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries. We’ve seen wildfires burn down homes and now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.

No one who has experienced this summer in the UK should be in any doubt that our climate is already changing. We know the future holds warmer, wetter winters, hotter, drier summers, and more extreme weather.

Honesty about what is required to deal with this changing reality is the least we should expect from our politicians. But last week we saw an astonishing response from Reform UK’s deputy leader, who told people to “enjoy” the scorching heatwaves and described this government’s efforts to combat the climate crisis as “arrogant”.

This response isn’t just ignorant; it is insulting.

Insulting to the firefighters risking their lives to fight blazes up and down the country. Insulting to the public whose lives are disrupted by scorching temperatures that were once a rare occurrence. And insulting to our farmers struggling to turn a profit as drought damages their crops.

This government’s response is not to throw in the towel and accept the chaos caused by extreme weather. It is to work to build and manage landscapes so they are resilient enough to withstand it and recover.

We know that healthy ecosystems retain more water and can help act as natural firebreaks. That resilience does not just protect us from the impacts of wildfire. It guards against flooding and pollution, too.

But some, including the Conservatives, have made the argument that rewilding lowers resilience to fire and that we should reverse restrictions on burning heather on our moors and peatlands. The exact opposite is true.

The evidence clearly shows that wetter, healthy peatlands hold more water and are less likely to develop species that are vulnerable to fires. The damage that has been done to these vital habitats by decades of burning has made them more vulnerable to wildfires in the long term, not less.

The solution to raging wildfires is not more burning of our countryside. It is to restore and better manage our environment.

Where rewilding has been prioritised, as at the National Trust’s Holnicote estate, you can clearly see the stark difference that it makes to the ability to withstand extreme weather. In areas where rivers and wetlands have been restored, the plants are green and blooming. Elsewhere, the ground is brown and dry.

As environment secretary, most of what comes across my desk is underpinned by the need to adapt to our changing climate – and this government is taking these challenges head on.

That’s why the prime minister this month convened an emergency Cobra meeting, bringing together senior ministers, firefighters, weather forecasters and other experts to make sure we’re doing all we can to keep the country safe from wildfires. That includes a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.

We are spending almost £100m to strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to wildfires and extreme weather.

And we are backing our farmers during the drought with a £65m funding boost, rule changes to make building on-site reservoirs easier and the largest nature-friendly budget in history to make our farms more resilient to extreme weather and to protect our food security.

Adapting to our changing climate demands sustained attention, effort and investment. Others may simply deny the problem or stick their heads in the sand, but this government will rise to the challenge.

Angela Eagle is the secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs

‘He could arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once’: Tim Curry’s five best screen roles

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 11:29:08 GMT

The actor fully embraced his physical talents and outsized personality with a line in theatrical baddies teetering deliciously on the edge of serious and silly

Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80 Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardom Clowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in pictures

As Dr Frank-N-Furter, the gender-nonconforming alien mad scientist who presides over Richard O’Brien’s glam rock musical, admits two innocents to his gothic castle and induces them into all sorts of delicious naughtiness, Curry is so thrillingly liberated as to seem a menace. An irresistibly appealing menace. Apparently able to arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once, Curry wraps his mouth around the double-entendres and belts out the lyrics with lip-smacking relish, and fully fleshes out this avatar of sexual confidence. The film earned one of the original cult fandoms, the stage musical endures and many other actors have pulled on Frank’s corset and high heels – but the role indelibly and for ever belongs to Curry.

A physical actor bursting with personality, Curry was at his best inhabiting outsized roles. He near fills up the entire frame as the prowling Lord of Darkness who kidnaps a princess and torments innocent forest child Tom Cruise in Ridley Scott’s visually sumptuous high fantasy.

The debonair manner and hint of a self-amused smile that were seemingly Curry’s birthright were deployed to delightful effect as Wadsworth, the butler who is just about a half a step ahead of everyone else in this madcap murder-mystery comedy, reputedly worked on by Tom Stoppard, and inspired by the board game that’s called Clue in North America and Cluedo everywhere else.

Inculcating coulrophobia in an entire generation of kids who stayed up late to watch this TV Stephen King adaptation, Curry played a shapeshifting child-murdering interdimensional entity – but ever a devotee of the theatrical arts, he did it in clown makeup. Charming baddies were his metier, and Pennywise the Clown was the baddest of the lot.

It was Curry’s great gift as an actor to always know exactly how seriously to take a role – certainly no more than necessary but never any less either. As the devious West Country buccaneer Long John Silver in a Muppets movie, he was fully on board with the make-believe, fully on board with the silliness.

If MPs want to take on Nigel Farage over his dodgy finances, they need to clean up their own act

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 10:03:11 GMT

It’s hard to beat back charges that MPs are ‘all the same’ when they have accepted £400k in freebies this year – £100k up on last year

How has your summer been? Done anything nice? As MPs prepare to head back to parliament next week, you’ll be relieved to hear that some of the most prominent figures in British politics have been enjoying the season’s cultural highlights – and without paying a penny. MPs throughout the Commons have received £400,000 of “freebies” to concerts, sports matches and other events so far this year, according to the most recent disclosures.

Over the summer alone, Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, enjoyed the Chelsea flower show thanks to Lloyds Banking Group covering the £1,839 cost, as did the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride. Lucy Powell, who has since become deputy leader of the Labour party and education secretary, accepted £858-worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group. Meanwhile, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, nabbed seats at Wimbledon worth £1,360 from the All England Club.

Totalled up, MPs have been gifted £100,000 more so far this year than in the whole of 2025, with recipients seemingly learning few lessons from Keir Starmer’s “passes for glasses” scandal, in which a Labour peer gifted the then prime minister designer eyewear and clothes before being spotted in Downing Street with a temporary security pass.

Like many of these types of stories, there’s some nuance lurking behind the headlines. MPs quite rightly go to events linked to their constituency or local area. Andy Burnham accepting £3,800 tickets to the Brit awards in Manchester – when he was the regional mayor – to spotlight the city hosting the event for the first time is not the same as Streeting presumably just really wanting to meet Monty Don.

The increase can also partly be explained by the fact MPs have become more consistent about declaring hospitality on the parliamentary register after Starmer changed the rules, while ticket prices are well known to have gone up across the board. And yet, wade through the details of gigs and horse racing and it’s hard not to conclude some MPs are simply practising blatant grifting. Call it a treat for a seat, where our elected officials are enjoying must-see shows as a kind of unofficial bonus.

That much of this stuff was gifted by big business, including gambling firms and banks, makes the whole thing feel considerably grubbier. Why did the betting company Flutter want to shower then local backbencher and now chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, with high-priced tickets to the Grand National and Cheltenham?

Public perception of such luxury perks will be even more unforgiving against a backdrop of an ongoing cost of living crisis. A night at the Ivor Novello awards may not be the duck house-level opulence of 2009’s expenses scandal, but the optics are little better. While much of the population are struggling to pay their electric and food bills, MPs are getting out the fascinators for Ladies’ Day at Aintree.

Politicians, of course, are human. Who among us wouldn’t be tempted by Harry Styles? The electorate, for its part, tends to want leaders to connect with everyday life. There’s a reason why Malcolm Tucker in The Thick of It – based on the rumour Alastair Campbell got Tony Blair clips of EastEnders and reality shows – makes a “zeitgeist tape” to help his useless ministers seem “in touch”. But it would be disingenuous to pretend MPs are driven to accept hospitality gifts as a bid to be down to earth, or that balancing such demands from the public is somehow a complex, grey area. Most people like to see their MP letting loose at a concert – they just want them to have paid for their ticket.

With the standards watchdog due to question Nigel Farage when parliament reopens – an inquiry he temporarily dodged by calling a byelection – the coming weeks will very likely see a renewed focus on what MPs receive and the transparency around it.

On paper, Farage’s gifts are in another league to his colleagues’ freebies: forget a ticket to the tennis, we’re talking £5m from a crypto billionaire and further “financial support” from a convicted fraudster. And yet to a public who have for decades seen front-page stories about politicians’ finances – from expenses and second jobs to tax avoidance – the idea that the Reform UK leader is an outlier worth investigating rather than one of a bad bunch can feel at best a hard sell and, at worst, hypocritical.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

If MPs wish to be able to hold Farage to account with credibility, they will need to show they care about cash and transparency in every form. That means the government looking harder into how some MPs are using their influence to make extra money, not least when it’s linked with the growth of the far right. Just this week it emerged that the Restore leader, Rupert Lowe, is set to earn as much from his – anti-migrant – posts on X as he does from his MP’s salary (which he gives to charity) since Elon Musk took over and financially rewarded some high-reach posts. “Gifts” come in many forms.

Winning public trust will also require MPs to be squeaky-clean themselves and stop accepting hospitality unless it’s linked to their constituency – even if that means watching the Chelsea flower show on iPlayer like the rest of us.

Because every time an MP goes to an event for free, it comes with a hidden cost: a public with ever-decreasing faith in the political class, who are more likely to greet outright corruption or cronyism with a weary shrug. “They’re all the same” is a dangerous public mood for a democracy and one that, once embedded, can be deeply hard to dislodge.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked

The Guardian Thu, 27 Aug 2026 10:00:11 GMT

The senator’s remarks reflect a turning point in Democrats’ attacks on the president. What should we make of them?

Apparently, he likes to say her name with a French accent. “Na-tah-lee!” the president cries out, in that affected tone of faux-formality that one might use with a person they love but do not quite respect, and she comes running, her thin legs teetering on her heels.

Natalie Harp, Trump’s 35-year-old “executive assistant”, was an odd recurring character in the latest blockbuster Trump administration book, Regime Change, by the New York Times’ Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. In the book, Harp features like a silent sentinel, ever present but eerily quiet as Trump rants and raves. It’s not exactly clear what the scope of her responsibilities are; though, as Jamelle Bouie points out, the fact that she evidently helps run the president’s social media accounts, which can sway markets and influence his foreign counterparts, makes her one of the most powerful people in the federal government.

But the dignity of Harp’s character does not often seem to equal the gravity of her influence: once, she was caught on video sprinting across a golf course on foot, chasing the golf cart that was speeding the president away to the next hole. For a while, she was called the “human printer” among Trump aides, in reference to the portable printer that Harp carries around with her: one of the primary ways she spends her time appears to be searching for flattering news stories and social media commentary about the president online, and printing it out to nourish his self-regard. But from Haberman and Swan’s reporting, it was not always clear exactly what Harp was thinking. Though many Trumpworld insiders are clearly identifiable as off-the-record sources in their book, Harp does not seem to be among them.

But recently, more of Harp’s own words have come to light. The Daily Beast published the full text of two letters from Harp to Trump, whose existence had previously been reported by Haberman and Swan. In the letters, Harp is rapturously worshipful, sycophantic, almost slavish. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote to Trump. She called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”. (The capitalization is in the original.) It’s long been known that Trump prizes devotion among his underlings, that he seeks out flattering commentary about himself, and that he is surrounded, particularly in his second term, exclusively by the kind of people who will never tell him anything that he does not want to hear. Still, the spectacle of Harp’s obsequiousness – her willingness to debase herself for an 80-year-old man whose vulgarity, misogyny, racism, narcissism and impulsiveness have damaged her country in ways it will probably never recover from – is disturbing and grotesque.

Still, Harp herself might be less unsettling than the near certainty that there are others like her – White House staffers and federal bureaucrats and petty functionaries of the Maga machine – who have made flattery of Trump a large portion, if not the entirety, of their jobs. Probably, few Americans would ever have heard of Harp if it were not for Jon Ossoff, the Democratic Georgia senator running for re-election and widely assumed to be mulling a presidential bid, who mentioned Harp in a pointed barb in a campaign stump speech in Atlanta. Trump, Ossoff said, doesn’t want to do the job of president; he wants, instead, to “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie”.

We do not need to be stupid: it strains credulity, and discredits the considerable savvy of Ossoff’s team, to claim that this remark was not meant to arouse salacious suspicion about the nature of Harp’s relationship with the president, and speculation that it might be sexual. Ossoff’s wording retained plausible deniability; still, I think he knew exactly what he was doing. Ossoff, in his campaign, has styled himself as firm-minded, resolute and morally ambitious – an inheritor to Barack Obama. But in this remark, he diverged noticeably from Michelle Obama’s famous mantra “when they go low, we go high,” which has long been a shibboleth for the kind of Democratic politicians who have preferred dignity over effectiveness in the Trump era. Ossoff was going low.

It is shocking how well it worked. The evocation of Harp in Ossoff’s speech triggered a slew of news stories about the aide, delivered by White House reporters who seemed almost giddy to be able to cite as newsworthy something that before had been merely creepy. Asked about Harp on television, Haberman referred to her as Trump’s “binky” and “comfort blanket”, infantilizing him in humiliating terms. Trump surrogates were dispatched to defend Harp with a ferocity and insistence that couldn’t help but suggest that the president himself was angered. Ossoff, it seemed, had struck a nerve. At the beginning of Trump’s rise to power, many in politics gawked at his seemingly sui generis ability to dictate the news cycle: to say outrageous things, or make bizarre provocations, and send reporters, commentators, surrogates and his opponents into a frenzy trying to respond to them. The effect was that Trump determined the subject of discourse; everyone else responded to him. Ossoff turned the tables, and he made it look easy.

One of the allegations that Trump’s aides spewed in their responses to the remark was that in insinuating that something inappropriate was afoot between Trump and Harp, Ossoff was being sexist. Those on the left rushed to discount this: no one, after all, really believes that Donald Trump, he of “grab ’em by the pussy”, is leading a movement that has serious or sincere concerns for women’s dignity. But to say that Ossoff’s remark contained no misogyny would be naive, if not dishonest: if his suggestion was made deliberately, then he was using Harp’s gender to undermine her professionalism, and to evoke a sex scandal. Of course there is misogyny in this gesture, the suggestion that a young woman is not entirely serious. That Harp’s character and conduct suggest this much more than her sex does need not force us to pretend not to see things that we do.

What is the moral consequence of this kind of sexism, the kind that Ossoff evoked – obliquely, subtly, but definitely – with his remark? For my part, I do not see any equivalence between the misogyny imposed on American women by the Trump regime – or, for that matter, the misogyny imposed on American women by Trump personally – and the minor distastefulness of Ossoff. It’s like comparing a dropper of water to the Pacific Ocean. Every woman, every feminist, knows that she has accepted things out of necessity or convenience that the most stringent adherence to principle would require her to reject. And I confess, I am more encouraged by Ossoff’s pugnaciousness than I am put off by the gendered undertones of the remark. After all, it is a grim reality of our gendered world that wherever there is a straight man who esteems himself to be godlike and extraordinary, there will be a straight woman somewhere not far behind who inexplicably believes him. We must work on building a world where this is not true. The first step might be getting this guy out of the White House.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist
